| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| material_system | str | Material and composition studied (e.g., GeSn, SiGeSn, Ge1-xSnx; include x and any Si/Ge fractions if given). |
| growth_method_and_structure | str | Film/heterostructure description and growth method (e.g., CVD/MBE/RP-CVD; thickness; buffer/substrate; strain state if noted). |
| annealing_conditions | str | Anneal temperature(s) and time(s), ambient (N2, Ar, vacuum, forming gas), ramp rates if given; explicitly capture 400–700 C when present. |
| capping_or_surface_treatment | str | Cap/passivation details (material, thickness, deposition method, whether in-situ/ex-situ; e.g., Si cap, Ge cap, SiO2, SiN, Al2O3) or explicitly 'uncapped'. |
| stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn | str | Reported outcomes related to substitutional Sn stability after anneal: Sn segregation to surface/interface, Sn precipitation (β-Sn) or Sn-rich clusters, composition change, relaxation, roughening; include qualitative and quantitative results (e.g., % Sn retained, substitutional fraction). |
| measurement_methods | str | Characterization methods used to assess Sn site/stability/defects (e.g., RBS/channeling, XRD, TEM/STEM-EDS/EELS, APT, SIMS, XPS, Raman, PL, PAS/positron annihilation, DLTS). |
| evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding | str | Any direct or indirect evidence/claims about Sn-vacancy (Sn–V) binding (e.g., from DFT, positron annihilation, inferred from diffusion/segregation trends); include extracted binding energy values if reported (with units). |
| sn_vacancy_binding_energy | str | Numerical Sn–vacancy binding energy (and charge state if specified) including units and method (DFT/experiment). Null if not reported. |
| vacancy_concentration_or_generation | str | Reported vacancy concentrations, formation energies, sources (implantation damage, growth-related defects), or anneal-induced vacancy generation/annihilation; include numbers/units when available. |
| sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim | str | Stated/assumed Sn diffusion mechanism(s): vacancy-mediated, interstitial, interstitialcy/kick-out, pair diffusion (Sn–V), grain-boundary diffusion; include how the paper supports the claim. |
| sn_diffusion_coefficients | str | Any reported Sn diffusivity/diffusion coefficients (D) or diffusion lengths in GeSn/SiGeSn (or related Ge/SiGe), with temperature, units, and whether effective or intrinsic. |
| activation_energies_diffusion_or_reaction | str | Activation energies extracted for Sn diffusion, segregation, precipitation, clustering, or decomposition processes; include value, units, and how extracted (Arrhenius fit, model). |
| models_or_simulations_used | str | Any kinetic/thermodynamic or atomistic models used (DFT defect energetics, kinetic Monte Carlo, rate equations, continuum diffusion/segregation model, CALPHAD, phase-field) and key assumptions. |
| capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion | str | Reported influence of capping on vacancy concentration, defect injection/gettering, surface recombination of vacancies/interstitials, suppression/enhancement of Sn out-diffusion or segregation; include proposed mechanism. |
| comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped | str | Side-by-side comparison outcomes for capped vs uncapped (or different cap types): differences in Sn retention, precipitation onset temperature, diffusion profiles, roughness, crystallinity; include quantitative deltas when available. |
| temperature_thresholds_for_instability | str | Any reported onset temperatures/time thresholds for Sn precipitation/segregation/decomposition (e.g., 'β-Sn appears above 500 C for 10 min'); include dependence on cap/composition/strain. |
| role_of_strain_and_relaxation | str | Mentions of strain state (compressive/tensile), relaxation, dislocations, and how these affect Sn stability/diffusion/precipitation; include evidence. |
| role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces | str | Mentions of interface-driven effects (film/substrate, cap/film) such as Sn pile-up, sink/source behavior for vacancies, interfacial reactions; include which interface and observations. |
| counterevidence_or_alternative_explanations | str | Any findings that challenge vacancy-mediated or Sn–V binding explanations, or propose alternative drivers (e.g., strain energy, surface energy, oxidation, Sn chemical potential, dislocation pipe diffusion). |
| key_figures_or_tables | str | Pointers to the most relevant figures/tables (by number) that contain diffusion profiles, Arrhenius plots, PAS spectra, substitutional fractions, or capped/uncapped comparisons. |

s2_metadata.abstract: Abstract We review the technology of Ge1−xSnx-related group-IV semiconductor materials for developing Si-based nanoelectronics. Ge1−xSnx-related materials provide novel engineering of the crystal growth, strain structure, and energy band alignment for realising various applications not only in electronics, but also in optoelectronics. We introduce our recent achievements in the crystal growth of Ge1−xSnx-related material thin films and the studies of the electronic properties of thin films, metals/Ge1−xSnx, and insulators/Ge1−xSnx interfaces. We also review recent studies related to the crystal growth, energy band engineering, and device applications of Ge1−xSnx-related materials, as well as the reported performances of electronic devices using Ge1−xSnx related materials.

s2_metadata.abstract: GeSn compounds have made many interesting contributions in photodetectors (PDs) over the last ten years, as they have a detection limit in the NIR and mid-IR region. Sn incorporation in Ge alters the cut off wavelength. In the present article, p–i–n structures based on GeSn junctions were fabricated to serve as PDs. Arsine (As) is incorporated to develop n-GeSn compounds via a metal induced crystallization (MIC) process followed by i-GeSn on p-Si wafers. The impact of As and Sn doping on the strain characteristics of GeSn has been studied with high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy analyses. The direct transitions and tuning of their band energies have been investigated using diffuse reflectance UV-vis spectroscopy and photoluminescence (PL). The barrier height and spectral responsivity have been controlled with incorporation of As. Variation of As incorporation into GeSn Compounds shifted the Raman peak and hence affected the strain in the Ge network. UV-vis spectroscopy showed that the direct transition energies are lowered as the Ge–As bonding increases as illustrated in Raman spectroscopy investigations. PL and UV-vis spectroscopy of annealed heterostructures at 500 °C showed that there are many transition peaks from the UV to the NIR region as result of oxygen vacancies in the Ge network. The calculated diode parameters showed that As incorporation leads to an increase of the height barrier and thus dark current. Spectral response measurements show that the prepared heterojunctions have spectral responses in near UV and NIR regions that gives them opportunities in UV and NIR photodetection-applications.

s2_metadata.abstract: The revival of interest in Ge1−xSnx alloys with x ≥ 10% is mainly owed to the recent demonstration of optical gain in this group-IV heterosystem. Yet, Ge and Sn are immiscible over about 98% of the composition range, which renders epilayers based on this material system inherently metastable. Here, we address the temperature stability of pseudomorphic Ge1−xSnx films grown by molecular beam epitaxy. Both the growth temperature dependence and the influence of post-growth annealing steps were investigated. In either case we observe that the decomposition of epilayers with Sn concentrations of around 10% sets in above ≈230 °C, the eutectic temperature of the Ge/Sn system. Time-resolved in-situ annealing experiments in a scanning electron microscope reveal the crucial role of liquid Sn precipitates in this phase separation process. Driven by a gradient of the chemical potential, the Sn droplets move on the surface along preferential crystallographic directions, thereby taking up Sn and Ge from the strained Ge1−xSnx layer. While Sn-uptake increases the volume of the melt, single-crystalline Ge becomes re-deposited by a liquid-phase epitaxial process at the trailing edge of the droplet. This process makes phase separation of metastable GeSn layers particularly efficient at rather low temperatures.

s2_metadata.abstract: Germanium-Tin (GeSn) alloys have emerged as a promising material for future optoelectronics, energy harvesting and nanoelectronics owing to their direct bandgap and compatibility with existing Si-based electronics. Yet, their metastability poses significant challenges calling for in-depth investigations of their thermal behavior. With this perspective, this work addresses the interdiffusion processes throughout thermal annealing of pseudomorphic GeSn binary and SiGeSn ternary alloys. In both systems, the initially pseudomorphic layers are relaxed upon annealing exclusively via thermally induced diffusional mass transfer of Sn. Systematic post-growth annealing experiments reveal enhanced Sn and Si diffusion regimes that manifest at temperatures below 600°C. The amplified low-temperature diffusion and the observation of only subtle differences between binary and ternary hint at the unique metastability of the Si-Ge-Sn material system as the most important driving force for phase separation.

s2_metadata.abstract: GeSn alloys are among the most promising materials for the fabrication of high-efficiency silicon-based light sources. However, due to the tendency of Sn to segregate to the surface during growth, it is challenging to achieve a high Sn concentration while maintaining high-quality GeSn alloys. Both theoretical and experimental studies have confirmed that non-substitutional Sn defects (VSnV) are the primary driving factors in Sn surface segregation. However, there is a discrepancy between existing theoretical and experimental findings regarding the variation in VSnV concentration with total Sn concentration. To clarify this issue, we first prepared GeSn materials with varying Sn concentrations using molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and subjected them to annealing at different temperatures. Subsequently, we characterized the VSnV concentration and Sn surface segregation. The results indicate that a higher total Sn concentration and temperature lead to an increased VSnV concentration, and the proportion of VSnV relative to the total Sn concentration also increases, which is consistent with existing theoretical research. To explain these phenomena, we employed first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the effect of varying the total Sn concentration on the formation of substitutional Sn (Sns) and VSnV in GeSn alloys, while simultaneously studying the migration kinetics of Sn atoms. The results demonstrate that as the total Sn concentration increases, the formation of Sns becomes more difficult, while the formation of VSnV becomes easier, and Sn atoms exhibit enhanced migration tendencies. The analysis of binding energies and charge density distribution maps reveals that this is due to the weakening of Ge-Sn bond strength with increasing Sn concentration, whereas the binding strength of VSnV exhibits the opposite trend. These findings demonstrate excellent agreement with experimental observations. This study provides both theoretical and experimental references for GeSn material growth and VSnV defect control through a combined theoretical–experimental approach, offering significant guidance for enhancing device performance.

s2_metadata.abstract: We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. We investigated strained and partially relaxed epi-layers with Sn content in the 5 at. %-12 at. % range. In relaxed samples, we observe a further strain relaxation followed by a sudden Sn segregation, resulting in the separation of a β-Sn phase. In pseudomorphic samples, a slower segregation process progressively leads to the accumulation of Sn at the surface only. The different behaviors are explained by the role of dislocations in the Sn diffusion process. The positive impact of annealing on optical emission is also discussed.We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. s2_metadata.abstract: Ge1-xSnx and Si1-x-yGeySnx alloys are promising materials for future opto- and nanoelectronics applications. These alloys enable effective band-gap engineering, broad adjustability of their lattice parameter, exhibit much higher carrier mobility than pure Si, and are compatible with the CMOS technology. Unfortunately, the equilibrium solid solubility of Sn in Si1-xGex is less than 1% and the pseudomorphic growth of Si1-x-yGeySnx on Ge or Si can cause in-plane compressive strain in the grown layer, degrading the superior properties of these alloys. Therefore, post-growth strain engineering by ultrafast non-equilibrium thermal treatments like pulse laser annealing (PLA) is needed to improve the layer quality. In this article, Ge0.94Sn0.06 and Si0.14Ge0.8Sn0.06 thin films grown on silicon-on-insulator substrates by molecular beam epitaxy were post growth thermally treated by PLA. The material is analyzed before and after the thermal treatments by transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD), Rutherford backscattering spectrometry, secondary ion mass spectrometry, and Hall effect measurements. It is shown that after annealing, the material is single-crystalline with improved crystallinity than the as-grown layer. This is reflected in a significantly increased XRD reflection intensity, well-ordered atomic pillars, and increased active carrier concentrations up to 4x1019 cm-3.

s2_metadata.abstract: This paper benchmarks various epitaxial growth schemes based on n-type group-IV materials as viable source/drain candidates for Ge nMOS devices. Si:P grown at low temperature on Ge, gives an active carrier concentration as high as 3.5 x 1020 cm-3 and a contact resistivity down to 7.5 x10-9 Ω.cm2. However, Si:P growth is highly defective due to large lattice mismatch between Si and Ge. Within the material stacks assessed, one option for Ge nMOS source/drain stressors would be to stack Si:P, deposited at contact level, on top of a selectively grown n-SiyGe1-x-ySnx at source/drain level, in line with the concept of Si passivation of n-Ge surfaces to achieve low contact resistivities as reported in literature [K. Martens et al. Appl. Phys. Lett., 98, 013504 (2011)]. The saturation in active carrier concentration with increasing P (or As)-doping is the major bottleneck in achieving low contact resistivities for as-grown Ge or SiyGe1-x-ySnx. We focus on understanding various dopant deactivation mechanisms in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx alloys. First principles simulation results suggest that P deactivation in Ge and Ge1-xSnx can be explained both by P-clustering and donor-vacancy complexes. Positron annihilation spectroscopy analysis, suggests that dopant deactivation in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx is primarily due to the formation of Pn-V and SnmPn-V clusters.

s2_metadata.abstract: The 2 μm wavelength band (1800–2100 nm) emerges as a promising candidate for next‐generation optical communication. As a result, silicon photonic platforms acquire great interest since they offer the ultimate minimization of photonic systems for 2 μm band applications. However, the large bandgap and indirectness of the band structure of the conventional SiGe alloy prevent their utilization for efficient photodetection in the 2 μm wavelength band. To overcome this drawback, complementary metal‐oxide semiconductor (CMOS)‐compatible GeSn waveguide photodetectors (WGPDs) with a vertical p–i–n heterojunction configuration that can operate in the 2 μm wavelength band is demonstrated. The proposed photodetector incorporates 5.28% Sn into the GeSn active layer, which redshifts the photodetection range to 2090 nm. In addition, the longer light–matter interaction length and good optical confinement of the proposed GeSn WGPD enhance the optical responses significantly. As a result, the proposed GeSn WGPD achieves a responsivity up to 0.52 A W−1 and a detectivity up to 7.9 × 108 cm Hz½ W−1 in the 2 μm wavelength band at room temperature. These promising results indicate that the developed GeSn WGPDs are promising candidates for integrated photonics in the 2 μm wavelength band.

s2_metadata.abstract: (Si)GeSn semiconductors are finally coming of age after a long gestation period. The demonstration of device-quality epi-layers and quantum-engineered heterostructures has meant that tunable all-group IV Si-integrated infrared photonics is now a real possibility. Notwithstanding the recent exciting developments in (Si)GeSn materials and devices, this family of semiconductors is still facing serious limitations that need to be addressed to enable reliable and scalable applications. The main outstanding challenges include the difficulty to grow high-crystalline quality layers and heterostructures at the desired content and lattice strain, preserve the material integrity during growth and throughout device processing steps, and control doping and defect density. Other challenges are related to the lack of optimized device designs and predictive theoretical models to evaluate and simulate the fundamental properties and performance of (Si)GeSn layers and heterostructures. This Perspective highlights key strategies to circumvent these hurdles and hopefully bring this material system to maturity to create far-reaching opportunities for Si-compatible infrared photodetectors, sensors, and emitters for applications in free-space communication, infrared harvesting, biological and chemical sensing, and thermal imaging.

s2_metadata.title: Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17504, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

s2_metadata.abstract: $\text{SiGeSn}$ alloys are promising silicon-compatible semiconductors for monolithic infrared photonics. However, their metastable nature limits the thermal budgets available for post-growth device processing, and the mechanisms governing their thermal degradation remain unresolved. Here, we investigate the thermal stability of $\text{Si}_{0.08}\text{Ge}_{0.83}\text{Sn}_{0.04}$ alloys using in situ spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) during isothermal annealing at 550 {\deg}C. We show that adding an ultrathin oxide cap kinetically suppresses Sn exchange with the free surface while leaving bulk diffusion pathways largely unaffected. Uncapped films undergo phase separation after 50 min, accompanied by void formation, a 60% thickness reduction, and a 400 meV blueshift of the $E_{2}$ critical point (CP) transition, consistent with substitutional Sn depletion from the probed volume through surface segregation. In contrast, oxide-capped films exhibit a small compositional change (<1 at.% Sn) and optical shift (<20 meV) over the same period, with suppressed void formation, strain relaxation, and alloy decomposition. This surface-kinetic control additionally yields a 25-fold reduction in contact resistivity relative to annealed uncapped alloys. These results identify surface Sn transport as the dominant degradation pathway in SiGeSn and demonstrate that an ultrathin oxide cap extends the thermal stability of metastable group-IV alloys, providing a practical route toward their integration into advanced silicon photonic and electronic platforms.

extracted_data.name_full: GeSn films formed by metal-induced crystallization (MIC) and annealed at 500 °C
extracted_data.brief_description: Experimentally formed GeSn (and Si/Ge/GeSn) multilayer films produced by thermal evaporation and metal-induced crystallization (Sn/As diffusion) then annealed at 500 °C (24 h, low vacuum); characterized for Sn incorporation, strain, oxidation and electrical/optical properties. The work compares different layer stacks/caps (As cap, Sn cap, Si or Ge buffer) and reports microstructure, d-spacing/strain, PL/UV-vis, Raman, XRD and electrical outcomes.
extracted_data.citation_title: Controlling barrier height and spectral responsivity of p–i–n based GeSn photodetectors via arsenic incorporation
extracted_data.material_system: GeSn-containing multilayers (configurations: Si(250 nm)/Sn(100 nm)/Ge(250 nm)/As(10 nm); Si/Sn/Ge/Sn (with post-anneal As 10 nm); Ge/Sn/Ge/As; Ge/Sn/Ge/Sn with post-anneal As), resulting in GeSn crystallites with measured atomic % (EDX) Sn ≈ 11.64% and As ≈ 10.46% in a sampled area; referred to as Ge1-xSnx/SiGe1-xSnx-type systems (x not globally specified).
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Thermal evaporation of stacked metal/semiconductor layers followed by metal-induced crystallization (MIC). Multilayer stacks on p-Si substrates (and some stacks with Ge base in place of Si). Layer thickness examples: Si 250 nm, Sn 100 nm, Ge 250 nm, As cap 10 nm. Anneal forms strained GeSn crystallites with orientations (001),(111),(333),(220); SAED/XRD show GeSn (220) dominant.
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: Annealed at 500 °C for 24 h inside an evacuated jar at low vacuum (4.6 × 10^-2 mbar); initial deposition vacuum 6.5 × 10^-5 mbar. (Temperature relevant to 400–700 °C window: 500 °C used.)
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Variants: (a) Ge layer capped by 10 nm As deposited prior to anneal (As cap present during MIC), (b) Ge layer capped by Sn (Sn cap present during anneal) with 10 nm As deposited after anneal to form n-GeSn, (c) some stacks have no Si buffer (Ge base instead). Caps deposited by thermal evaporation; As cap sometimes present in-situ before anneal (first config), in other configs As was deposited after anneal (second/ fourth configs).
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: Reported outcomes: formation of GeSn crystallites (evidence: HRTEM/SAED/XRD) with increased d-spacing compared to pure Ge indicating Sn incorporation (d-spacing increases e.g., GeSn(220) d ≈ 0.2221–0.2234 nm vs Ge reference 0.2006 nm). EDX local composition shows substantial Sn (~11.64 at% in probed area). One configuration (Si/Sn/Ge/Sn/As) exhibited evidence of 'free Sn clusters' (interpreted from lower Ge–Sn bonding in Raman and correlated with much higher dark current: 4.87 × 10^-4 A cm^-2 at −3 V), implying partial Sn precipitation/segregation in that case. Oxygen incorporation (low vacuum anneal) fills vacancies and forms GeOx/GeO2 which is reported to widen the band gap and alter optical response. No quantitative global substitutional fraction or Sn-retention vs initial metastructure reported beyond local EDX numbers.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: HRTEM, SAED, EDX elemental analysis and mapping, XRD (Williamson–Hall strain analysis), Raman spectroscopy, diffuse reflectance UV-vis (Kubelka–Munk), photoluminescence (PL), Hall effect (carrier concentration, mobility), I–V electrical measurements (potentiostat), spectral responsivity measurements.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: Qualitative statements only: paper repeatedly refers to 'vacancies in the Ge network' being occupied by oxygen during low-vacuum anneal (i.e., oxygen incorporation and formation of GeOx/GeO2 and oxygen vacancies). No numeric vacancy concentrations or formation energies reported.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Paper describes Sn (and As) transport as 'diffused in the semiconducting layers forming an intrinsic GeSn layer' via metal-induced crystallization (MIC) and interdiffusion during annealing; does not assert or quantify a vacancy-mediated mechanism (no explicit mention of vacancy-mediated, interstitial, or Sn–V pair diffusion).
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: No kinetic/atomistic simulations or DFT/CALPHAD models reported; analysis is experimental and uses Williamson–Hall for microstrain; Kubelka–Munk model for diffuse reflectance band gap extraction.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Observations: An As cap present during anneal leads to deeper As incorporation, increased n-type carrier concentration (Hall: −2.465 × 10^14 e cm^-3) and modifies strain (Raman peak shifts) and optical band gap (reduction). As incorporation during anneal increases GeSn Raman peak intensity and shifts peaks to lower wavenumbers (indicative of strain/chemical effects). A Sn cap (or configuration with Sn cap) is associated with reduced Ge–Sn bonding (Raman) and formation of free Sn clusters (inferred) leading to higher dark current; oxygen in low-vacuum anneal fills vacancies producing GeOx which widens band gap. Overall, capping material (As vs Sn) strongly affects chemical incorporation, strain and electrical/optical outcomes; mechanisms proposed are chemical doping (As), altered solubility and bonding and oxidation-driven vacancy filling rather than explicit vacancy-gettering kinetics.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: Comparisons among four stack configurations: (see Table 2 values) • Si/Sn/Ge/As on p-Si (As cap present during anneal): dark current at −3 V = 5.29 × 10^-7 A cm^-2; barrier height 0.77 eV; turn-on 3.65 V. • Si/Sn/Ge/Sn/As on p-Si (Sn cap during anneal, As deposited after): dark current at −3 V = 4.87 × 10^-4 A cm^-2 (much higher); barrier height 0.61 eV; turn-on 3.95 V. • Ge/Sn/Ge/As on p-Si (As cap during anneal, Ge base): dark current 8.26 × 10^-8 A cm^-2; barrier height 0.84 eV; turn-on 3.35 V. • Ge/Sn/Ge/Sn/As on p-Si (Sn cap during anneal): dark current 1.98 × 10^-7 A cm^-2; barrier height 0.81 eV. Raman intensities and XRD peak shifts/d-spacing also differ: As-incorporated configurations show stronger GeSn Raman peaks and wavenumber shifts consistent with altered strain/bonding. Quantitative deltas: orders-of-magnitude higher dark current in Sn-capped then-As-deposited-after sample vs As-capped-during-anneal sample (≈3 orders of magnitude).
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Only 500 °C anneal (24 h) examined (within 400–700 °C window). No explicit onset temperatures for Sn precipitation/β-Sn formation or Sn loss thresholds reported. The paper notes that annealing at 500 °C reduces strain, increases electron mobility and enables MIC-driven Sn incorporation; but no Arrhenius thresholds for instability were given.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Strain plays a central role: Sn incorporation increases d-spacing in Ge planes (HRTEM/SAED); compressive strain inferred from left shift of GeSn (220) XRD peak; Williamson–Hall calculated microstrain values: 4.37 × 10^-3 and 4.01 × 10^-3 for two configurations. The paper states that thicker Ge layers and relaxation allow incorporation of more Sn (more relaxation => more Sn accepted), and strain changes are supported by Raman peak shifts (GeSn mode shifting lower wavenumbers with Sn/As incorporation). Strain relaxation is linked to altered Sn incorporation and crystallite orientation.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Interfaces and buffers matter: Si buffer reduces Sn solubility relative to Ge leading to differences in Sn incorporation (configurations with Si buffer show different Raman intensities and Sn incorporation behavior). Surface As (cap) forms n-GeSn layer (As on surface or diffused in) and modifies carrier concentration and barrier heights. Oxygen at surfaces during low-vacuum anneal leads to oxidation (GeOx/GeO2) at/near surfaces and vacancies being filled by oxygen, affecting optical gaps and presumably defect chemistry. The paper also reports ‘free Sn clusters’ near surface/interface in one configuration implied by Raman and electrical behavior.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: The paper attributes observed Sn clustering/poor device behavior in some stacks to 'lower bonding between Ge and Sn' and to incomplete incorporation (leading to free Sn clusters) and to oxygen/oxidation effects, rather than invoking vacancy-mediated Sn–V binding; oxygen filling of vacancies and oxidation is invoked as an alternative/major driver of altered optical/electrical properties. No experimental evidence supporting vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion or Sn–vacancy binding is presented; vacancy effects are discussed only qualitatively in context of oxygen occupying vacancies.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Fig. 2 (HRTEM, SAED, EDX spectra and atomic %), Table 1 (d-spacing), Fig. 3 (elemental mapping), Fig. 4 (XRD patterns, GeSn (220)), Fig. 5 (Raman spectra), Fig. 7 (UV-vis diffuse reflectance direct transitions), Fig. 9b (PL spectra), Fig. 10 & Fig. 11 (I–V data, log I–V), Table 2 (diode parameters: turn-on, ideality, barrier height, dark current) — these contain the most relevant microstructural/compositional and capped/uncapped comparisons.
extracted_data.additional_notes: No positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS), DFT, diffusion coefficients, activation energies, or explicit Sn–V binding energies are provided in this paper. All mentions of vacancies relate to oxygen/vacancy filling (GeOx formation) rather than quantified vacancy-mediated diffusion of Sn.

extracted_data.name_full: Free-running liquid Sn droplet mediated liquid-phase-epitaxy (LPE) phase separation
extracted_data.brief_description: Experimentally observed mechanism in uncapped MBE-grown Ge0.9Sn0.1 films where liquid Sn droplets form above the Ge–Sn eutectic and migrate across the surface, dissolving Ge1-xSnx at the leading edge and re-depositing nearly pure Ge at the trailing edge, producing β-Sn precipitates and Ge trails (LPE-like directional transport).
extracted_data.citation_title: Free-running Sn precipitates: an efficient phase separation mechanism for metastable Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$ epilayers
extracted_data.material_system: Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$, primarily Ge$_{0.9}$Sn$_{0.1}$ (x = 10%), also reference data for 4.9% ≤ x ≤ 14.5%
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) on commercial Ge(001) substrates; typical epilayer thickness d = 30 nm (Series A) or 50–100 nm (Series B–D); films grown fully coherent / pseudomorphic and compressively strained prior to decomposition; 50 nm GeSn films (Series B–D) on a 50 nm (or 50 nm Ge buffer then Ge substrate) structure as described in Table S1.
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: In-situ anneals in MBE: 15 min at T_A = 200–350°C (Series C); ex-situ real-time anneals in SEM: experiments near 250°C ±25°C (Videos V1–V3) and at 350°C ±25°C (V4); Series D real-time SEM anneals at ≥230°C; video time scales: individual sequences covering 9–28 min (frame cadence ~20–26 s). No data in the 400–700°C range in this paper.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: All experiments in this paper performed on uncapped films (transfer from MBE to SEM in <5 min ambient to minimize surface reactions). Authors discuss capping conceptually but did not apply caps in this study.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: Above the Ge–Sn eutectic (~231°C) metastable Ge0.9Sn0.1 films decompose into mobile liquid Sn droplets (which solidify into β-Sn after cool-down) and re-deposited crystalline Ge with negligible Sn (EDXS/TEM: trail region x ≤ 1%). Large droplets can penetrate the full film thickness down to the Ge buffer/film interface. Estimated melt Ge content during movement >11% (supersaturated) although equilibrium solubility in this T window is 2–3%; morphological outcomes include trails with {001}, {105}, {113} facets, trenches ~60 nm confining trails, surface roughening, and loss of pendellösung fringes in XRD indicating loss of homogeneous strained GeSn layer.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: X-ray diffraction (rocking curves), Rutherford backscattering (RBS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with inLens and SE2 detectors (real-time imaging), atomic force microscopy (AFM), transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM, STEM-EDXS), focused ion beam (FIB) lamella preparation.
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: No direct experimental evidence for Sn–vacancy binding is provided. The paper notes that point defects may play a role for solid-state Sn diffusion in low-temperature MBE material, but supplies no measurements or binding-energy data.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: Not quantified. The authors suggest that low-temperature MBE growth may produce a higher density of point defects that could influence solid-state Sn diffusion, but no vacancy concentrations or formation energies are reported.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Primary mechanism observed: liquid-mediated transport (liquid Sn droplets dissolving GeSn and re-depositing Ge — a coupled LPE feeding/growth process). The authors contrast this with solid-state diffusion mechanisms (e.g., vacancy-mediated) and argue the droplet/LPE process dominates above the eutectic; they mention solid-state (vacancy-mediated) diffusion may be relevant in low-temperature MBE material but present no direct evidence for it in this work.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_coefficients: None reported. No numerical diffusion coefficients (D) or diffusion lengths for Sn in Ge/GeSn are given in this paper.
extracted_data.activation_energies_diffusion_or_reactio: No activation energies for diffusion, segregation, or precipitation are reported in this work.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: Thermodynamic, phenomenological LPE-based model: Gibbs free-energy expressions for epitaxial Ge growth at trailing edge (ΔG^Ge = (μ_s^Ge − μ_l) + Δγ_ls^Ge < 0) and for dissolution at leading edge including strain and interface terms (ΔG^{GeSn} expression with μ_s^{GeSn}, Δγ_ls^{GeSn}, E_ls, γ_ss). Supplementary Material S7 develops decomposition thermodynamics including ΔG^{Ge+Sn(l)} = ΔG_i^{Ge} − ΔH_{mix}^{GeSn}. No atomistic DFT or kinetic Monte Carlo simulations presented.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Conceptual: authors state (i) capping of GeSn epilayers is expected to affect Sn diffusion in the solid phase and thus delay formation of sufficiently large Sn precipitates needed to initiate the droplet-mediated transformation; (ii) CVD growth with hydrogen termination likely suppresses surface segregation of Sn, reducing initial surface Sn that would form molten droplets, and far-from-equilibrium CVD conditions reduce point-defect densities that may assist solid-state Sn diffusion. These are suggestions/commentary; no experimental capping data in this work.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: No experimental capped-versus-uncapped comparison performed in this paper. The authors only report uncapped-film results (rapid decomposition above eutectic) and cite literature (Ref. 9 and others) indicating that CVD-grown/hydrogen-terminated materials can delay precipitation to higher temperatures (e.g., suppression up to ≥390°C in cited CVD work), but do not provide side-by-side data.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Decomposition/phase separation observed to set in above ≈230°C (the Ge–Sn eutectic T_EC ≈ 231°C). Growth at T_G > 230°C produced phase separation during MBE growth (samples grown at 250–300°C show β-Sn droplets and trails). In-situ anneal: stable at 200°C; at T_A ≥ 250°C (videos at 250±25°C) droplets appear and move; at 350°C droplet density increases and transformation is very efficient. No data for 400–700°C.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Strain is an important driving term in the thermodynamic model for dissolution: strain energy terms (E_ls) and solid-solid interface energy (γ_ss) enter ΔG^{GeSn} making dissolution of the strained GeSn layer into the melt favorable; trails behind droplets are virtually strain-free Ge (x ≤ 1%). The metastability of substitutional Sn (x = 10%) in strained diamond lattice is a precondition for the observed phase separation; relaxation/defects at higher Sn contents (>~14%) reduce film quality.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Critical: droplets must contact both an intact GeSn region and a corrugated trail region to move. The liquid–solid interfaces at droplet leading/trailing edges control dissolution (leading) and epitaxial re-deposition (trailing). Large droplets often penetrate to the Ge buffer/film interface; after cool-down droplets solidify as β-Sn and are surrounded by a Ge 'collar' from precipitation of dissolved Ge. Surface segregation is the source of initial molten Sn and is implicated in initiation of droplets.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Authors explicitly argue that the observed rapid, directional phase separation is not typical solid-state precipitation driven by vacancy-mediated or slow bulk diffusion, but rather governed by liquid droplet-mediated LPE; they note that some literature reports solid-state Sn precipitation and trails, but their in-situ SEM/TEM observations show mobile liquid droplets as the efficient mechanism in their samples. They acknowledge that solid-state diffusion (possibly vacancy-mediated) might be relevant in other materials/conditions (e.g., low-T MBE point-defect rich films) but provide no direct support.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Main text: Fig.1 (XRD rocking curves), Fig.2 (SEM/AFM of droplets and trails), Fig.3 (TEM/EDXS composition & FFT showing trail nearly pure Ge), Fig.4 (cross-sectional image and schematic). Supplementary: Table S1 (growth/anneal parameters), Figs. S3 (cross-section TEM of β-Sn precipitate), S4 (AFM of trail facets), S5 (SEM video start frames / V1–V4 descriptions), Supplementary Material S7 (thermodynamic model).

extracted_data.name_full: Surface capping and hydrogen-terminated CVD surface passivation (conceptual mentions)
extracted_data.brief_description: Authors discuss capping (or hydrogen surface termination during CVD) as potential strategies to suppress Sn surface segregation and delay precipitation/phase separation of metastable GeSn, but provide no experimental capped samples in this study.
extracted_data.material_system: General Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$ films (discussion focused on Ge$_{0.9}$Sn$_{0.1}$ and literature CVD GeSn up to ~390°C)
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Not experimentally applied in this paper; discussed in context of comparing MBE (uncapped) results with CVD-grown, hydrogen-terminated films from literature (Ref. 9).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: No capped sample anneals reported. Authors reference literature where CVD-grown GeSn was reported stable up to at least 390°C during growth.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Not applied here — experiments performed on uncapped films; conceptual capping and hydrogen termination during CVD are discussed as mechanisms that could suppress surface segregation.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: No experimental data in this paper. Authors suggest that capping could delay formation of sufficiently large Sn precipitates and thus shift onset of phase separation to higher temperatures; literature-cited CVD/hydrogen-terminated growth reportedly suppresses Sn precipitation during growth to at least 390°C (Ref. 9).
extracted_data.measurement_methods: No capped-sample measurements in this paper; suggestion based on comparison to literature and authors' own characterization of uncapped samples.
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: None provided; capping discussion focuses on surface segregation suppression and point-defect density reduction rather than direct vacancy-binding effects.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No quantitative data. Authors hypothesize that far-from-equilibrium CVD growth reduces point-defect density compared with low-T MBE, which may reduce solid-state Sn diffusion mediated by point defects.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Authors suggest capping/H-termination mainly suppress surface segregation (reducing initial molten Sn source) and that reduced point-defect density in CVD may reduce solid-state Sn diffusion; they do not claim a specific atomic-scale diffusion mechanism under capped conditions.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: No models for capping effects presented; the suggestion is qualitative and literature-supported.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Qualitative claim: capping (and hydrogen termination during CVD) is expected to (i) reduce surface segregation of Sn and thus reduce initial molten Sn formation and (ii) allow higher growth temperatures and fewer point defects, thereby reducing pathways for solid-state Sn diffusion and delaying precipitation. No experimental verification in this paper.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: No direct experimental comparison in this paper. Authors cite external reports (Ref. 9) suggesting CVD/hydrogen-terminated material can be grown at higher temperatures with suppressed precipitation (e.g., up to ~390°C during growth), implying improved stability versus uncapped MBE films which decompose above ~231°C.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: No capped-sample thresholds reported. Cited literature suggests suppression of precipitation during CVD growth up to at least 390°C (reference 9) but authors caution this may delay but not fully suppress Sn precipitation during subsequent processing.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Authors hypothesize that higher growth temperatures allowed by suppressed surface segregation may lower point-defect densities and thus influence defect-assisted diffusion and relaxation pathways, but no data provided.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Capping/hydrogen termination is discussed as modifying surface energetics and suppressing surface segregation which is the initial source for molten Sn droplets; the surface is therefore implicated as a critical control parameter.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Authors note that while CVD/hydrogen termination can suppress segregation and extend metastable growth range, literature suggests Sn precipitation may be delayed but not fully suppressed under subsequent thermal processing.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: No figures in this paper show capped-sample data; related discussion points to Ref. 9 in main text. Relevant materials: Table S1 (shows that all studied films here are uncapped); discussion paragraphs in main text describing possible mitigation measures.

extracted_data.name_full: Vacancy-mediated or point-defect mediated solid-state Sn diffusion (mentioned possibility)
extracted_data.brief_description: The paper mentions that point defects generated during low-temperature MBE growth may play a role in solid-state Sn diffusion (potentially vacancy-mediated), but provides no direct experimental or computational evidence, nor any quantitative defect/diffusion parameters.
extracted_data.material_system: Low-temperature MBE-grown Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$ (context: Ge$_{0.9}$Sn$_{0.1}$ films grown at ~120–200°C)
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: MBE-grown uncapped films; authors note these low-T conditions may yield higher densities of point defects compared to far-from-equilibrium CVD.
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: No explicit anneals uniquely attributed to vacancy-mediated diffusion; general anneals described (200–350°C) where droplet-mediated LPE dominates above eutectic.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Experiments uncapped; authors state that capping or hydrogen termination during CVD may reduce point-defect density and thus defect-mediated diffusion.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: No quantitative link established between vacancy-mediated diffusion and observed decomposition in this paper; observed decomposition is dominated by droplet-mediated transport above the eutectic.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: No direct methods used here to probe vacancies (no positron annihilation spectroscopy, no DLTS, no channeling-RBS for vacancy quantification).
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: No evidence reported. The paper only posits that point defects may influence solid-state Sn diffusion but provides no experimental or theoretical binding data.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: Not measured or quantified. Authors suggest low-T MBE may produce point defects but provide no numbers or formation energies.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Mentioned as a possible mechanism for solid-state Sn diffusion in low-temperature MBE materials, but authors do not present data supporting vacancy-mediated diffusion and instead emphasize droplet/LPE as the experimentally observed dominant pathway above the eutectic.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: No atomistic defect/diffusion modeling presented for vacancy-mediated diffusion in this work.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Authors suggest capping and hydrogen-terminated CVD could reduce point-defect densities (thereby potentially reducing vacancy-mediated diffusion) but no experimental validation provided.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: None presented experimentally in this paper; only qualitative suggestions and references to literature.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Not applicable specifically to vacancy-mediated diffusion in this paper; overall decomposition onset observed above ~231°C and is dominated by droplet-mediated mechanism here.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Authors note strain energy contributes to the thermodynamic driving force for dissolution into the melt; they do not quantify interactions between strain and vacancy-mediated diffusion.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Paper emphasizes surfaces and surface segregation as initial source of molten Sn; vacancy-mediated bulk diffusion is not the observed primary pathway in these experiments.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: The direct observation of liquid Sn droplets moving and effecting phase separation provides counterevidence that slow vacancy-mediated bulk diffusion is the dominant mechanism under the studied conditions. The authors explicitly contrast LPE-like droplet transport with solid-state diffusion-driven precipitation.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: No figures directly demonstrate vacancy-mediated diffusion; relevant figures show droplet motion and composition changes: Fig.2 (SEM/AFM trails), Fig.3 (TEM/EDXS composition showing trail Ge x ≤1%), Supplementary Table S1 (growth/anneal parameters).
