extracted_data.brief_description: DFT (VASP) calculations (GGA/PBE and HSE06) performed in this work compare formation enthalpies of Sn_n-V, P_n-V and mixed Sn_nP_n-V complexes in Ge; conclusion: Sn–V complexes are less favorable (higher formation enthalpy) than P_n-V clusters, so Sn is not an efficient vacancy trap to boost P activation.
extracted_data.material_system: Epitaxial Ge and Ge1-xSnx (x up to ~0.07; specific studied composition Ge0.93Sn0.07)
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Epitaxial films grown by CVD on Ge virtual substrates (Ge-VS). Typical thicknesses: Ge:P ≈100 nm, Ge1-xSnx:P ≈80 nm. Ge1-xSnx layers grown at 315 °C (Sn ≤ 0.08).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: This paper did not perform dedicated high-temperature Sn anneals; post-epi processing for CTLM included dielectric deposition up to 400 °C (maximum reported in-process thermal budget). Literature cited (Refs. 31,32 in paper) reports undoped Ge1-xSnx (Sn ≤ 6 at%) stable up to 500 °C for anneals up to 30 min. A referenced external report (Yu et al.) mentions a Ti/Si:P post-metal anneal at 475 °C for 1 min (literature, not this work).
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: No dedicated cap used on PAS/DFT samples in this study (effectively uncapped epi films on Ge-VS). The paper separately discusses use of thin Si:P as a contact liner/cap in stacks (see separate entry), but not as an experimental cap to study Sn stability.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: DFT formation enthalpy trends: P_n-V clusters (P-decorated vacancies) have the lowest ΔH_f (most stable), Sn_nP_n-V are intermediate, and pure Sn_n-V complexes have the highest ΔH_f (least favorable). Practically, Sn alloying (at studied low x) does not increase P activation; PAS shows Sn is present around mono-vacancies (mixed Sn_pP_n-V) but does not prevent vacancy-mediated P deactivation. No evidence in this work for Sn segregation, β‑Sn precipitation, or large-scale Sn loss after the mild processing used; no quantitative substitutional fraction for Sn reported.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: First-principles DFT (VASP; PAW; GGA/PBE and HSE06 hybrid), calculation of formation enthalpies; experimental Positron Annihilation Spectroscopy (DOBS and CDOBS) and TCDFT positron modeling; supporting SIMS and RBS for composition, Reciprocal Space Mapping (XRD) for strain, MR-CTLM and micro-Hall for electrical properties.
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: Mixed evidence: DFT formation enthalpies indicate Sn_n-V complexes are thermodynamically less favorable than P_n-V clusters (i.e. Sn does not strongly 'trap' vacancies compared to P). However, PAS-derived annihilation spectra for Ge1-xSnx show the presence of Sn at first-nearest-neighbor sites around mono-vacancies (i.e. experimental evidence of Sn in vacancy environments), inferred from increased high-momentum intensity relative to Ge:P with similar P levels. The paper explicitly states 'Sn does not have the desired effect of trapping vacancies' and reports that Sn–V pair binding energies are 'clearly higher' (i.e. less favorable) than for dopant (P)-vacancy complexes.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No absolute vacancy concentrations reported. PAS shows mono-vacancy sized open-volume defects are the dominant positron traps. Experimental thresholds from PAS: for P doping 3.2×10^19–6×10^19 cm^-3, mono-vacancies are decorated by at least 2 P atoms; for P > 9×10^19 cm^-3, at least 3 P atoms decorate vacancies. For the Ge1-xSnx sample with highest P (1.5×10^20 cm^-3) PAS indicates at least one Sn atom around some mono-vacancies. Vacancies are associated with growth/incorporation (as-grown films), not implantation.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: The paper discusses the hypothesis (motivation) that Sn could trap vacancies to reduce vacancy-mediated P deactivation (i.e., vacancy-mediated mechanisms were considered), but the combined DFT and PAS results argue against effective Sn vacancy trapping. The paper does not present direct measurements of Sn diffusion mechanisms (no diffusivities or mechanism-resolved experiments); it therefore does not provide affirmative support for vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion in these films.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: DFT atomistic energetics: VASP PAW calculations in 216-atom Ge supercells; both GGA/PBE and HSE06 functionals used; formation enthalpy (ΔH_f) calculations for P_n, Sn_n, P_n-V, Sn_n-V and mixed Sn_nP_n-V complexes. Positron annihilation modeling using two-component DFT (TCDFT) within local-density approximation to compute Doppler spectra; no kinetic models or diffusion simulations were used.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: This work did not present experiments using caps to affect Sn–V behavior. It does note that Sn inward relaxation around vacancies reduces open-volume size and can suppress positron trapping. No claim that capping (oxide, Si, SiO2, Al2O3 etc.) alters Sn–V binding or Sn stability is presented.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: No direct anneal-induced Sn instability observed in this work; the paper cites literature that undoped Ge1-xSnx (Sn up to 6 at%, thickness ~40 nm) is thermally stable up to 500 °C for anneals up to 30 min with 'no evident changes in surface morphology, lattice parameter and layer composition' (Refs. 31,32). The authors' CTLM post-processing maximum temperature was 400 °C and did not report Sn decomposition or segregation at that process step.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Sn alloying introduces compressive strain (undesirable for n‑Ge FinFETs). For Sn atoms near vacancies, DFT and PAS show inward atomic relaxation of Sn toward the vacancy, effectively reducing the open-volume size and altering positron trapping signatures. Strain/elastic effects also explain Sn–Sn configurational energetics (elastic origin of local minima for certain neighbor separations).
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: The paper discusses possible instabilities in layer composition and strain relaxation induced during post-epi CTLM processing (interface-related), but does not provide direct evidence of Sn segregation to surfaces or interfaces in their experiments. PAS signatures implicate Sn at first-nearest-neighbor sites around bulk vacancies rather than implying surface pile-up.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Although the initial idea was that Sn could trap vacancies and improve P activation, DFT formation enthalpies and PAS experiments show P_n‑V complexes are energetically preferred and that Sn does not significantly increase active carrier concentration; thus vacancy-attraction by P (not Sn) explains dopant deactivation. Also inward relaxation of Sn reduces apparent positron trapping, complicating simple interpretations that Sn 'binds' vacancies strongly.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Fig. 11 (formation enthalpies ΔH_f for P_n-V, Sn_n-V, Sn_nP_n-V complexes), Fig. 13 (DOBS and CDOBS experimental and calculated momentum distributions showing P_n-V and Sn_pP_n-V signatures), Fig. 10 (Sn–Sn configurational energetics), Table I (compositions and processing conditions for Ge and GeSn layers).

extracted_data.name_full: Positron annihilation spectroscopy identification of P-decorated vacancies and Sn-containing vacancy complexes
extracted_data.brief_description: Depth-resolved Doppler and coincidence Doppler PAS measurements identify mono-vacancy sized open-volume defects in epitaxial Ge and Ge1-xSnx films that are decorated by multiple P atoms (2–4) depending on P concentration; in Ge1-xSnx at high P there is also evidence for Sn presence around vacancies (mixed Sn_pP_n-V).
extracted_data.material_system: Epitaxial Ge:P and Ge1-xSnx:P (example composition Ge0.93Sn0.07:P), films on Ge-VS; layer thickness ≈100 nm (Ge:P) and ≈80 nm (Ge1-xSnx:P).
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: CVD growth on 300 mm Ge virtual substrates; Ge:P grown at 440 °C (GeH4), Ge1-xSnx:P grown at 315 °C (GeH4 + SnCl4), Si:P grown at 450 °C when present.
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: PAS was performed on as-grown films. The processing/CTLM flow includes a maximum post‑epi processing temperature of 400 °C; no dedicated anneal series in the 400–700 °C range were performed in this study.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Samples for PAS were effectively uncapped (as-grown epi on Ge-VS). No dedicated capping/passivation was applied to study effects on vacancy/Sn behavior.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: PAS does not show macroscopic Sn precipitation or Sn loss in these as-grown films. Instead, mixed Sn_pP_n-V complexes (Sn at nearest-neighbor positions around mono-vacancies) are observed in Ge1-xSnx films at high P concentrations; presence of Sn around vacancies does not increase electrical activation of P.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: Doppler Broadening Spectroscopy (DOBS) depth profiling with mono-energetic positrons (0.5–25 keV), Coincidence DOBS (CDOBS) for momentum distributions, and TCDFT positron state modeling to compute expected spectra for modeled defect complexes. Supporting SIMS for dopant concentrations and RBS for Sn percentage.
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: Indirect: CDOBS spectra for Ge1-xSnx show increased high-momentum intensity relative to Ge:P with similar P content; comparison with calculated momentum distributions indicates presence of Sn atoms at or near vacancies (i.e. Sn_pP_n-V clusters). The PAS data thus provides experimental evidence that Sn atoms can occupy sites adjacent to vacancies, but does not quantify binding energies.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No absolute vacancy concentrations reported. PAS indicates mono-vacancy sized open-volume defects dominate annihilation signal. Experimental PAS-derived compositional-in-defect thresholds: P_n-V complexes with n≥2 for P ≈3.2×10^19–6×10^19 cm^-3, and n≥3 for P >9×10^19 cm^-3. For highest P (≈1.5×10^20 cm^-3) in Ge1-xSnx sample, at least one Sn atom is present around some vacancies.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: PAS measurements do not provide direct diffusion mechanisms. The observed Sn in vacancy environments implies Sn can occupy near-vacancy sites during growth/incorporation, but paper does not claim vacancy-mediated bulk Sn diffusion during anneal.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: Comparison of experimental CDOBS spectra to calculated momentum distributions for modeled single-defect types (P1-V, P2-V, Sn_pP_n-V, etc.) using TCDFT and periodic supercell calculations.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Not studied experimentally with PAS in this work; samples were uncapped. The paper does note (separately) processing stacks that include Si:P liners for contact resistivity but these were not used to study vacancy/Sn behavior.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Not reported from PAS experiments (performed on as-grown material). See paper's citation of literature indicating Ge1-xSnx (Sn ≤6 at%) films 40 nm thick are stable up to 500 °C / 30 min (Refs. 31,32).
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: PAS analysis and DFT indicate Sn atoms relax inward around vacancies whereas P relaxes outward; these relaxation directions alter the apparent open-volume size and positron trapping strength (inward Sn relaxation reduces open-volume and positron trapping).
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: PAS depth profiling distinguishes signal from top epi layer (0.5–5 keV positron energy) versus Ge-VS and substrate; signatures attributed to vacancy decoration occur in top epi layers. No specific evidence of interface-driven Sn pile-up or surface segregation during processing in these measurements.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: While PAS shows Sn at vacancy-neighbor sites, DFT formation enthalpies indicate Sn_n-V complexes are less stable than P_n-V complexes; therefore presence of Sn near vacancies does not imply Sn is the dominant vacancy sink or that Sn will prevent P_n-V formation. The net experimental electrical outcome (no improved P activation in Ge1-xSnx vs Ge) supports this counterevidence.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Figure 13 (panels a–f: DOBS W-parameter depth profiles and CDOBS momentum distributions compared with calculated spectra for P_n-V and Sn_pP_n-V), Figures referenced in PAS sections; data linked to Fig. 4 (P concentration vs activation) for contextual composition.

extracted_data.name_full: Reported thermal stability of undoped Ge1-xSnx films up to 500 °C (literature)
extracted_data.brief_description: The paper cites literature reports that undoped Ge1-xSnx layers (Sn up to ~6 at%, thickness ~40 nm) exhibit thermal stability (no evident changes in surface morphology, lattice parameter or composition) for anneals up to 500 °C and anneal durations as long as 30 min.
extracted_data.material_system: Undoped Ge1-xSnx, Sn up to ~6 at%, thickness ~40 nm (literature examples cited in paper).
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Referenced undoped Ge1-xSnx films (details in cited literature; not reproduced in this paper).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: Literature-cited anneal window: 300–500 °C (stability observed); reported anneal durations up to 30 minutes at 500 °C with no evident compositional/structural changes.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Not specified in the paper's citation text (presumably as-grown uncapped or standard surface conditions in cited studies).
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: According to cited literature, no detectable Sn segregation, precipitation, surface roughening or lattice-parameter change for undoped Ge1-xSnx up to 500 °C for the reported thicknesses and durations.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: Cited literature used surface morphology analysis, lattice-parameter (XRD/RSM) and composition (likely RBS/SIMS) — paper states 'no evident changes in surface morphology, the lattice parameter and the layer composition'.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Cited stability boundary: no instability observed up to 500 °C (for examples with Sn up to ~6 at% and film thickness ~40 nm for durations up to 30 min). The paper itself used 400 °C maximum processing temperature without reporting Sn decomposition.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Not detailed in the citation summary; the paper elsewhere notes Sn alloying introduces compressive strain in Ge films.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Not detailed in the citation summary.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Not given in this paper for the cited stability claims; the authors caution that precise mechanisms for contact resistivity degradation in Sn-containing stacks remain not fully understood.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Text references in body (discussion around CTLM processing stability); no specific figure in this paper (authors cite Refs. 31,32).

extracted_data.name_full: Silicon:P capped/liner layers used as passivation/contact liners on Ge and Ge1-xSnx
extracted_data.brief_description: Thin in-situ P-doped Si layers (Si:P) grown on Ge or Ge1-xSnx are used as contact liners/passivation to achieve low contact resistivity, but these Si:P caps are grown non-selectively and are often defective on Ge (lattice mismatch); the paper reports stack contact resistivities for Si:P on Ge or Ge1-xSnx.
extracted_data.material_system: Si:P deposited on Ge:P or Ge1-xSnx:P and on Si0.08Ge0.90Sn0.02:P (stacks), Si:P layers grown on Ge substrates
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Si:P grown by CVD: Si2H6 (450 °C) for low-temperature high-activation Si:P; SiH2Cl2 at 675 °C used for other recipes. Si:P layers in this work are thin (too thin for SIMS) and were grown in-situ (non-selective on patterned devices).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: Si:P stacks measured as-grown; literature example (Yu et al.) reports post-metal anneal at 475 °C for 1 min that reduced contact resistivity further. The authors' CTLM processing included dielectrics deposition up to 400 °C (no dedicated Si:P anneal series reported here).
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Si:P used as a cap/liner at contact level; deposition was in-situ during CVD growth (non-selective). The paper also discusses difficulties achieving selective Si:P (attempted cyclic deposition and etch with Cl2), and that Si:P on Ge is highly defective due to lattice mismatch.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: Paper does not report direct effects of Si:P caps on substitutional Sn stability. Si:P caps do improve electrical contact resistivity when stacked on Ge:P or SiGeSn:P layers, but the authors do not present data showing suppression or enhancement of Sn segregation/precipitation by Si:P capping.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: MR-CTLM for contact resistivity, micro-Hall for carrier concentration, SEM cross-sections to inspect conformality and etch effects; electrical benchmarking vs literature.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: No experimental data in this paper showing that Si:P capping modifies vacancy concentrations or Sn diffusion/segregation. The cap is used to lower contact resistivity; the paper notes Si passivation concept in literature but does not claim a role in stabilizing substitutional Sn during anneal.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: Comparative electrical results: Si:P on Ge:P or Si0.06Ge0.94Sn0.02:P stacks show low contact resistivities approaching ~1×10^-8 Ω·cm^2 (as-grown); Table I reports specific ρ_c values (e.g., Si:P on Ge0.93Sn0.07:P stack ρ_c ≈1.3×10^-8 Ω·cm^2). No microstructural comparison (Sn retention/segregation) between capped and uncapped films reported.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Not reported for Sn-related stability with Si:P cap. The paper only reports processing temperatures (max ~400 °C in their flow) and literature 475–500 °C anneals referenced externally.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Si:P layers on Ge are highly defective due to lattice mismatch; this defectivity and strain mismatch complicate the use of Si:P as a selective liner at S/D level. No direct linkage to Sn stability provided.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Si:P is used to passivate the metal/semiconductor contact interface to reduce contact resistivity. The paper discusses difficulties removing amorphous Si:P on oxide/nitride areas during selective etch, and notes aggressive Cl2 etch removes Ge fins if exposed.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Although Si:P liner improves contact resistivity, it cannot be implemented selectively with the highest-activation Si:P recipes used here because of non-selective growth and etch challenges; no evidence provided that such caps influence Sn-V binding.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Table I (electrical properties and contact resistivities for stacks), Figure 5 (SEM cross-sections showing conformal Si:P deposition and etch-induced removal of Ge fins).

extracted_data.name_full: Sn diffusion and stability in pseudomorphic Ge1-xSnx (Ge0.914Sn0.086 / Ge0.94Sn0.06)
extracted_data.brief_description: Experimental study of thermally activated Sn interdiffusion and lattice relaxation in coherently grown GeSn thin films showing two diffusion regimes (low-T enhanced and high-T conventional vacancy-mediated) and measurable Sn loss/segregation depending on capping and relaxation state.
extracted_data.material_system: Ge0.914Sn0.086 (RSM/SIMS experiments); Ge0.94Sn0.06 (diffusion experiments, 30 nm layer)
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Reduced-pressure CVD (AIXTRON Tricent, reactive gas precursors Ge2H6 and SnCl4); pseudomorphic (coherently strained) thin films grown on Ge-buffered Si(001) wafers; film thicknesses: 30 nm (diffusion samples), other samples <50 nm; Ge virtual substrate / Ge buffer with low threading dislocation density (<1E7 cm^-2).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: Rapid thermal processing (Mattson Helios RTP) in N2 ambient; temperature range studied 350–850 °C; times 3–30 min. Specific reported conditions: 10 min @ 500 °C (RSM shift noted), 10 min @ 600 °C (SIMS: ~40 nm Sn penetration into Ge buffer), experiments focusing on 500–800 °C for diffusion (no distinct effect <500 °C). Low-temperature enhanced diffusion regime defined below ~650 °C; high-temperature regime above ~650–700 °C.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Both diffusion-dedicated samples were in-situ capped with Ge: Ge/GeSn/Ge structure — Ge cap 300 nm for GeSn samples (grown at same temperature as alloy to avoid surface influence). Some earlier samples (RSM/SIMS in Fig.1) were uncapped and showed surface segregation at >600 °C.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: Pseudomorphic (low-TDD) layers relax elastically via Sn interdiffusion rather than by plastic relaxation; gradual Sn loss from alloy during anneals. Observations: (uncapped) surface segregation of Sn observed above ~600 °C; (capped) Sn diffuses into surrounding Ge cap/buffer rather than segregating to free surface. Quantitative: Sn atoms diffuse ~40 nm into Ge buffer for 10 min @ 600 °C (uncapped sample, Fig.1c); in capped 30 nm Ge0.94Sn0.06 sample the Sn peak concentration reduced by more than a factor of two after annealing at 600 °C for 10 min (Fig.2a). Annealing above ~700 °C reduces mean Sn content to ≈1 at.% (thermodynamic solid solubility), leading to strongly enhanced diffusion.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: High-resolution X-ray diffraction reciprocal space maps (RSM) around (224) to probe strain/coherency; Secondary Ion Mass Spectroscopy (SIMS) for Sn depth profiles; rapid thermal processing (RTP) for anneals. (Paper cites positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) and atomistic studies in literature but did not perform them here.)
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: Indirect / inferential only: authors state that vacancies are expected to attract/relax around larger Sn atoms and thereby an attractive Sn–vacancy interaction is anticipated; vacancy presence in GeSn noted citing PAS work (Ref. 42). No direct experimental Sn–V binding measurement in this paper.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No numeric vacancy concentrations reported. Qualitative: vacancies are expected to be present due to low-temperature epitaxy and have been directly observed in GeSn via positron annihilation in cited literature (Ref.42). The Ge buffer TDD is given as <1E7 cm^-2 (defines dislocation-related diffusion contribution upper bound).
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Paper attributes Sn diffusion predominantly to vacancy-mediated mechanisms in the high-temperature regime (EA comparable to literature for Sn in Ge). In the low-temperature enhanced regime the authors attribute the enhancement to metastability / chemical potential gradients and strain effects that lower point-defect formation energies; vacancy mediation is still considered important but not uniquely explanatory. For partially relaxed material, dislocation-pipe diffusion (along dislocations) dominates and leads to rapid clustering/β-Sn precipitates.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_coefficients: Diffusion coefficients extracted by fitting 1D diffusion solutions to SIMS profiles; Arrhenius plots shown (Fig.2c). Specifics: D(T) reported as Arrhenius with parameters in Table I (see activation energies and D0). Observed behavior: low-T regime (<~650 °C) shows enhanced effective diffusivity (reduced EA); high-T regime (>~650 °C) diffusivities similar to implanted-Sn-in-Ge literature. Also observed diffusion lengths: ~40 nm penetration into Ge buffer for 10 min @ 600 °C (uncapped).
extracted_data.activation_energies_diffusion_or_reactio: From Arrhenius fits (Table I) for Sn diffusion: High-T (Ge/GeSn/Ge): E_A = 3.10 ± 0.07 eV, D0 = 264 ± 220 cm^2/s; High-T (Ge/SiGeSn/Ge): E_A = 2.87 ± 0.03 eV, D0 = 12 ± 5 cm^2/s. Low-T: Ge/GeSn/Ge E_A = 1.81 ± 0.09 eV; Ge/SiGeSn/Ge E_A = 1.13 ± 0.11 eV. (Methods: Arrhenius fits to diffusion coefficients determined from 1D diffusion equation fits to SIMS profiles.)
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: 1D continuum diffusion modeling (solutions of the diffusion equation per Crank) to fit SIMS profiles and extract effective diffusion coefficients; Arrhenius model D = D0 exp(-E_A/k_BT) used to extract EA and D0. No DFT or atomistic simulations performed in this paper, though atomistic literature is cited for interpretation.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Ge caps (in-situ, thick) were used to suppress surface segregation and to probe pure interdiffusion into Ge rather than loss to free surface. With Ge cap, Sn diffuses into surrounding Ge layers and no pronounced surface segregation/precipitation is observed at temperatures where uncapped samples show surface Sn segregation (>600 °C). Authors grew the Ge caps at same temperature as alloy to minimize cap-induced effects. Proposed mechanism: cap removes free-surface sink for Sn and for point-defects (vacancy/interstitial exchange), forcing Sn to diffuse into the adjacent Ge matrix.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: Uncapped samples (Fig.1c) show surface segregation of Sn above ~600 °C and rectangular-to-smeared profiles with ~40 nm penetration into Ge buffer for 10 min @ 600 °C. In-capped diffusion samples (Ge/GeSn/Ge in Fig.2a) showed suppression of surface segregation and allowed measurement of interdiffusion into Ge; in capped samples Sn peak concentration decreased by >2× after 10 min @ 600 °C. No quantitative comparison table provided; observations are qualitative/semiquantitative.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Surface segregation observed in uncapped films above ~600 °C (10 min). Strongly enhanced diffusion and drop of mean Sn to ≈1 at.% occurs upon annealing above ~700 °C. Low-T enhanced diffusion regime exists below ~650 °C (reduced activation energies reported).
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: All diffusion experiments were on coherently strained (compressive) films with strain ≈ -0.90% (Ge0.94Sn0.06) and -0.89% (SiGeSn). Authors argue that in low-TDD coherently strained layers, relaxation occurs elastically via Sn diffusion rather than by dislocation formation. In partly relaxed films, pre-existing dislocations enable rapid strain relaxation via dislocation multiplication/glide and serve as fast diffusion pathways (pipe diffusion), promoting Sn clustering and β-Sn precipitates.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Free surface acts as sink for Sn causing surface segregation/precipitation in uncapped samples above ~600 °C. Ge cap and Ge buffer act as adjacent Ge matrix that receives diffusing Sn (cap/buffer as sink), modifying where Sn accumulates. Interfaces with dislocations (in partially relaxed material) act as fast diffusion channels and clustering initiation sites.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Authors note that while vacancy-mediated diffusion is consistent with high-T activation energies, the marked reduction of activation energy in low-T regime cannot be solely explained by strain-driven vacancy formation; they attribute major role to metastability / chemical potential gradients (low Sn solubility) and note possible differences in vacancy formation/migration between GeSn and SiGeSn (not directly measured). For partially relaxed layers, dislocation-mediated diffusion (pipe diffusion) explains abrupt phase separation better than vacancy-mediated bulk diffusion.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Figure 1 (RSM and SIMS of Ge0.914Sn0.086, showing strain and surface segregation behavior), Figure 2a and 2c (Sn SIMS diffusion profiles for Ge0.94Sn0.06 and Arrhenius plot of D), Table I (activation energies and D0 for Sn diffusion high/low T).

extracted_data.name_full: Sn (and Si) diffusion and stability in pseudomorphic SiGe1-xSnx (Si0.040Ge0.895Sn0.065 / Si0.10Ge0.81Sn0.09)
extracted_data.brief_description: Experimental characterization of Sn interdiffusion from coherently grown SiGeSn ternary thin films showing qualitatively similar behavior to GeSn but with lower activation energies (especially in low-T regime), indicating easier Sn loss and stronger metastability in ternaries.
extracted_data.material_system: Si0.040Ge0.895Sn0.065 (30 nm diffusion sample, Ge/SiGeSn/Ge capped), Si0.10Ge0.81Sn0.09 (RSM sample)
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Reduced-pressure CVD (AIXTRON Tricent); pseudomorphic coherent thin films grown on Ge-buffered Si(001); thickness 30 nm for diffusion samples; capped in-situ with Ge (150 nm cap for SiGeSn diffusion sample).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: RTP in N2 ambient; temperature range 350–850 °C; diffusion experiments focused on 500–800 °C; anneal times 3–10 min for diffusion experiments; observed enhanced diffusion below ~650 °C and strong diffusion above ~650–700 °C.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: In-situ Ge cap (150 nm) grown at same temperature as ternary film to avoid cap-induced surface effects; used to suppress surface segregation and probe interdiffusion into Ge.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: Ternary layers show Sn loss and interface smearing upon annealing. Compared to binary GeSn, Sn diffusion in SiGeSn 'sets in relatively easier' with peak Sn concentration decreasing more rapidly at lower temperatures; low-T activation energy for Sn is lower (1.13 eV) indicating enhanced instability. No direct observation of β-Sn precipitates in coherent capped samples; in partially relaxed material clustering/β-Sn formation associated with dislocations reported in literature.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: XRD RSM for strain/coherency; SIMS for Sn depth profiles; RTP anneals; diffusion coefficient extraction by fitting 1D diffusion equation solutions and Arrhenius analysis.
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: Indirect: authors suggest difference in activation energies (ternary < binary) may indicate larger number of vacancies in ternary; also note expected attractive Sn–vacancy interaction. No direct Sn–V binding measurements given for SiGeSn in this work.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No quantitative vacancy concentrations reported. Authors propose SiGeSn may have larger vacancy population than GeSn based on lower activation energies; vacancy presence (general) attributed to low-temperature epitaxy and cited PAS observations in GeSn (Ref.42).
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Same as binary: vacancy-mediated diffusion considered main mechanism in high-T regime (EA similar to impurity diffusion in Ge). In low-T regime vacancy formation energies possibly lowered by strain/metastability causing enhanced vacancy-mediated diffusion; additionally Si diffusion (vacancy-mediated) may interact with Sn diffusion.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_coefficients: Extracted via 1D diffusion fits and Arrhenius analysis. Activation energies and D0 in Table I: High-T (Ge/SiGeSn/Ge) Sn E_A = 2.87 ± 0.03 eV, D0 = 12 ± 5 cm^2/s. Low-T (Ge/SiGeSn/Ge) Sn E_A = 1.13 ± 0.11 eV. Observed qualitative faster decrease of Sn peak at lower temperatures compared to binary.
extracted_data.activation_energies_diffusion_or_reactio: Sn: High-T E_A = 2.87 ± 0.03 eV; Low-T E_A = 1.13 ± 0.11 eV (Table I). Si: High-T E_A = 3.27 ± 0.03 eV; Low-T E_A (Si) = 0.50 ± 0.10 eV. Extraction via Arrhenius fits to diffusion coefficients from SIMS.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: Continuum 1D diffusion modeling (Crank) and Arrhenius fits. Paper cites atomistic-level work (Ref.41) showing repulsive Si–Sn interactions used to interpret Si diffusion anomalies, but no new atomistic simulations performed here.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Ge capping (150 nm) suppresses surface segregation and forces Sn to interdiffuse into Ge cap/buffer; cap grown in-situ at same temperature to minimize additional surface effects. Authors used capping specifically 'to investigate diffusion into the surrounding Ge matrix and suppress surface segregation'.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: Capped SiGeSn samples showed suppression of surface segregation and a clearer measurement of interdiffusion into Ge. Uncapped counterparts (general observations from uncapped GeSn sample) show surface segregation above ~600 °C. The ternary loses Sn more rapidly at lower temperatures than binary (qualitative comparative conclusion).
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Low-T enhanced diffusion regime below ~650 °C; surface segregation in uncapped samples observed above ~600 °C; annealing above ~700 °C reduces mean Sn to ≈1 at.% (thermodynamic solubility) with strongly enhanced diffusion.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Ternary sample compressive strain similar to binary (-0.89%); authors argue metastability (lower Sn solubility in SiGe) explains stronger low-T diffusion enhancement in ternary vs binary rather than strain alone. In partially relaxed ternaries, dislocation-mediated diffusion would increase clustering/precipitation.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Ge cap and Ge buffer act as sinks for diffusing Sn; free surface (if uncapped) is a sink causing segregation/precipitation. Interfaces containing dislocations act as rapid diffusion/segregation sites in partly relaxed films.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: While vacancy-mediated diffusion explains the high-T activation energies, the authors argue that the large reduction in EA at low-T cannot be fully explained by strain-induced vacancy formation alone; chemical potential gradients from metastability and Si–Sn interactions are invoked as alternative/more important drivers.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Figure 1b (RSM of Si0.10Ge0.81Sn0.09), Figure 2b (Sn SIMS diffusion profiles for Si0.040Ge0.895Sn0.065), Figure 2c (Arrhenius plot comparing binary/ternary), Table I (activation energies and D0 for Sn and Si).

extracted_data.name_full: Mentions of vacancies and expected Sn–vacancy (Sn–V) interactions in (Si)GeSn
extracted_data.brief_description: Paper discusses the expected attractive interaction between Sn atoms and vacancies, notes vacancy presence from low-temperature growth and cites positron annihilation spectroscopy evidence in the literature, but provides no direct binding-energy measurements.
extracted_data.material_system: General (Si-Ge-Sn alloys / GeSn and SiGeSn thin films)
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Low-temperature epitaxial thin films (as used in this study); vacancy presence attributed to low-temperature growth but no experimental vacancy quantification performed here.
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: Vacancy-related discussion in context of RTP anneals 350–850 °C (this study); no direct vacancy anneal experiments reported.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Discussion mentions that caps modify surface sinks (which can affect vacancy/interstitial exchange) but provides no quantitative cap–vacancy coupling data.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: Authors infer that an attractive Sn–vacancy interaction could locally relax strain around large Sn atoms and thus influence Sn diffusion and clustering, but no direct substitutional-fraction measurements or Sn–V binding quantification are provided.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: The paper itself did not perform vacancy-specific measurements, but cites positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) observations of vacancies in GeSn alloys (Ref.42) as supporting evidence for vacancy presence.
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: Indirect / theoretical expectation: 'Since vacancies can locally relax the strain surrounding the larger size Sn atoms, an attractive interaction between Sn atoms and vacancies is expected in GeSn alloys.' Citation of PAS work evidencing vacancies; no experimental Sn–V binding energies reported.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No numeric vacancy concentrations reported in this paper. Vacancy generation is ascribed qualitatively to low-temperature epitaxy and possibly enhanced by strain; PAS in literature (Ref.42) is cited as direct observation of vacancies in GeSn.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Vacancy-mediated diffusion is considered the dominant microscopic mechanism in the high-T regime by analogy to impurity diffusion in Ge and Si (and supported by activation energies), and vacancies are invoked as mediators in low-T enhanced diffusion although other drivers are important.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: No new atomistic calculations in this work; the expectation of Sn–V attraction is based on atomistic reasoning and literature references (e.g., PAS observation and cited atomistic studies elsewhere).
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Paper states that capping removes the free-surface sink and thus alters vacancy/interstitial exchange dynamics, indirectly affecting Sn migration pathways; no quantitative data on vacancy injection/gettering by caps are provided.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: No direct vacancy concentration comparison; but capped samples show suppressed surface segregation (implying different surface-sink behavior) whereas uncapped samples show surface Sn segregation above ~600 °C (suggesting cap affects Sn/vacancy mass transfer paths).
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Discussion associates vacancy effects with the observed low-T enhanced diffusion regime below ~650 °C, but no specific vacancy-formation-temperature given.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Strain is discussed as lowering formation energy of point defects (vacancies), which could increase vacancy concentrations and thereby enhance vacancy-mediated diffusion (cited analogies from SiGe literature).
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Free surface is a sink for Sn and likely for point defects; Ge caps/buffers act as sinks for Sn and modify defect-mediated diffusion pathways. Interfaces containing dislocations act as fast diffusion/segregation channels.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Authors explicitly state that vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion alone cannot fully explain the pronounced low-T activation-energy drop and point to chemical potential gradients (metastability) and strain as primary drivers; also dislocation-mediated pipe diffusion explains abrupt phase separation in partly relaxed films.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Discussion text citing vacancy observations (Ref.42); relevant context in Figure 2c (Arrhenius behavior showing two regimes) and Table I (EA values) which motivate the vacancy-related discussion.

extracted_data.name_full: Effect of in-situ Ge capping on Sn segregation and diffusion
extracted_data.brief_description: Experimental demonstration that in-situ Ge caps (150–300 nm) grown at same temperature as alloy suppress surface segregation of Sn during annealing and redirect Sn interdiffusion into the Ge cap/buffer, enabling measurement of bulk interdiffusion rather than surface precipitation.
extracted_data.material_system: Ge/GeSn/Ge and Ge/SiGeSn/Ge sandwich structures (Ge cap thickness: 300 nm for GeSn, 150 nm for SiGeSn).
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: In-situ Ge caps grown in same RP-CVD reactor at same temperature as alloy layer to minimize cap-induced artifacts; sandwich geometry with Ge buffer and Ge cap around the 30 nm alloy layer.
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: RTP in N2; diffusion experiments primarily at 500–800 °C, times 3–10 min. Caps used to study diffusion behavior in this temperature window (noted effects at 600 °C and >700 °C).
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Ge cap (in-situ), thicknesses: 300 nm (GeSn) and 150 nm (SiGeSn); caps grown at same temperature as alloy layer.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: With Ge cap: suppressed surface segregation and prevention of immediate surface β-Sn precipitation during anneals where uncapped films showed surface segregation (>600 °C). Observation: Sn redistributed into adjacent Ge layers; in capped Ge0.94Sn0.06 sample the Sn peak concentration decreased by more than a factor of two after 10 min @ 600 °C.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: SIMS depth profiling to show suppressed surface segregation and interdiffusion into Ge cap/buffer; XRD RSM to demonstrate retained coherency/strain during gradual Sn loss.
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: No direct evidence provided that capping changes Sn–V binding energy; authors discuss capping as altering sinks/sources for Sn and defects but do not quantify vacancy effects.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No quantitative data; implication that cap reduces surface sink for point defects but no measured vacancy concentrations reported.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Capping shifts the observed outcome from surface segregation to bulk interdiffusion into Ge, implying that surface-mediated sinks (and possibly surface-mediated vacancy annihilation/injection) play a role in where Sn migrates; underlying atomistic diffusion mechanism (vacancy-mediated) is still assumed for bulk movement.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_coefficients: Same extracted diffusion coefficients as reported for capped Ge/GeSn/Ge and Ge/SiGeSn/Ge samples (see Table I and Fig.2c); capping enabled extraction of these effective diffusivities by preventing surface loss.
extracted_data.activation_energies_diffusion_or_reactio: Activation energies reported in Table I for capped sandwich samples: see Sn E_A values (high and low T) listed for Ge/GeSn/Ge and Ge/SiGeSn/Ge.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: 1D diffusion modeling assuming the sandwich geometry and composition-dependent diffusion to fit SIMS profiles; caps grown to enforce boundary condition of no free-surface sink.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Cap suppresses free-surface sink for Sn (and likely for point-defects), causing Sn to diffuse into adjacent Ge layers instead of segregating/precipitating at the top surface; caps grown at same temperature to avoid introducing cap-formation defects which might alter diffusion.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: Uncapped: surface segregation observed above ~600 °C (SIMS Fig.1c), rectangular profiles preserved up to ~600 °C with surface segregation at higher T. Capped: no surface segregation; instead Sn redistributes into Ge cap/buffer with strong reduction of Sn peak (more than 2× reduction after 10 min @ 600 °C in Ge0.94Sn0.06). Quantitative deltas: ~40 nm Sn penetration into Ge buffer reported for uncapped sample @ 600 °C / 10 min; capped samples show diffusive broadening and >2× reduction in peak but no surface pile-up.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Surface segregation in uncapped films noted above ~600 °C; capping prevented segregation in that range but high-T anneals >700 °C still reduce mean Sn to ~1 at.% (thermodynamic limit) and produce strongly enhanced diffusion.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Capped pseudomorphic films remained coherently strained while losing Sn by diffusion rather than by defect-mediated relaxation. Cap did not prevent elastic relaxation via diffusion but prevented surface-precipitation routes tied to free-surface sinks and dislocation-mediated relaxation.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Free surface (uncapped) is active sink causing Sn segregation and precipitation; Ge cap provides a bounded Ge matrix into which Sn diffuses; Ge/film interfaces act as diffusion pathways/hosts for redistributed Sn.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Authors note that even with caps, at higher temperatures (>~700 °C) thermodynamics drive Sn content to solubility ~1 at.% and diffusion is strongly enhanced; caps cannot prevent reaching equilibrium composition or the associated enhanced diffusion. Additionally, in samples with high TDD or partial relaxation, dislocation-mediated phase separation can still lead to clustering and surface/bulk precipitates irrespective of caps.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Figure 2a and 2b (Sn diffusion profiles in Ge/GeSn/Ge and Ge/SiGeSn/Ge capped sandwiches), Figure 1c (uncapped SIMS showing surface segregation), Figure 2c (Arrhenius plot demonstrating regimes), Table I (activation energies and D0 for capped sandwich experiments).

extracted_data.name_full: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys
extracted_data.brief_description: Combined experimental (MBE-grown GeSn films, RTA anneals, XRD/Raman/optical/SEM) and DFT (SQS + NEB/VASP) study showing that higher total Sn concentration and higher anneal temperature promote formation of non-substitutional Sn-vacancy clusters (VSnV), lower Sn migration barriers, and enhanced Sn surface segregation; reports quantified substitutional Sn retention after 60 s RTA at 400/600/800 °C and DFT formation/migration energetics across compositions.
extracted_data.citation_title: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys
extracted_data.material_system: Ge1-xSnx (GeSn) films; experimental samples with substitutional Sn (Sn_s) measured as ~4.50%, 7.20%, 8.6% (XRD); DFT supercells simulated from nominal ~3.2% to 16.1% Sn (Ge60Sn2 to Ge52Sn10 models).
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) on Si(100) substrates; 30 nm Ge buffer grown at 300 °C, then 100 nm GeSn grown at 180 °C by co-deposition of Ge and Sn beams; films are continuous epitaxial layers (no cap reported).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: Rapid thermal anneal (RTA) at 400 °C, 600 °C and 800 °C for 60 s each (ambient not specified in text), reported because the study focuses on 400–800 °C; no ramp rates given.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: uncapped (no cap/passivation reported or applied for the samples studied).
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: Substitutional Sn (Sn_s) decreases with anneal temperature and with higher initial Sn: XRD-measured Sn_s (samples labelled 1/2/3) before anneal = 4.50%, 7.20%, 8.6%; after 400 °C: 4.50%, 7.20%, 6.6%; after 600 °C: 2.6%, 2.8%, 0% (sample 3 lost all measurable substitutional Sn); after 800 °C: 1.30%, 1.20%, 0%. SEM/optical images show surface Sn segregation points appearing at 600 °C for lower-Sn samples and already at 400 °C for the highest-Sn sample, with clustering and growth of Sn-rich surface particles at 800 °C. The paper interprets decreased Sn_s as conversion into VSnV and other clusters and reports qualitative crystal-quality degradation (XRD peak broadening) with increasing initial Sn.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: X-ray diffraction (004 and 224 scans) for quantitative Sn_s and lattice constant; Raman spectroscopy for semi-quantitative Sn (Ge-Ge phonon shifts); optical microscopy and SEM for surface segregation/cluster imaging; DFT (VASP/PBE/PAW) with SQS supercells for defect energetics; NEB for migration barriers; charge-density maps visualized (VESTA).
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: Multiple lines: (1) literature evidence cited that VSnV are dominant non-substitutional defects (Decoster, Assali, Ventura, etc.); (2) DFT formation energies show VSnV formation energy decreases (becomes more favorable) with increasing total Sn concentration, while Sn_s formation energy becomes less favorable; (3) DFT binding-energy analysis (E_VSnV computed, Fig.11) shows VSnV binding strength increases with Sn concentration; (4) charge-density maps show increased electron density around VSnV with higher Sn, interpreted as stronger binding; (5) experimental conversion of Sn_s to non-substitutional defects with anneal (Table 1, Fig.7) consistent with VSnV formation. All binding/formation trends derived from DFT (PBE/VASP) calculations.
extracted_data.sn_vacancy_binding_energy: No single scalar experimental Sn–vacancy binding energy reported; DFT-derived formation energies for VSnV (Table 3) are given as E_F(VSnV) vs total Sn concentration (DFT/PBE): 3.2%: -4.244 eV; 4.8%: -4.403 eV; 6.5%: -4.837 eV; 8.1%: -5.128 eV; 9.7%: -5.374 eV; 11.3%: -5.528 eV; 12.9%: -5.783 eV; 14.5%: -5.916 eV; 16.1%: -6.279 eV. The paper also reports that computed 'binding energy of VSnV' increases with Sn concentration (qualitative / plotted in Fig.11); method = DFT using formation-energy-based definition (Equation 6).
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No absolute vacancy-number densities reported. Experimentally inferred vacancy-related clustering quantified indirectly by conservation: VSnV concentration after anneal = initial Sn_s(before) - Sn_s(after). Using XRD data (this paper) the converted (interpreted as VSnV) fractions after 60 s RTA are: sample1 (init 4.50%): 400 °C -> 0% converted; 600 °C -> 1.9% converted (alpha = 1.9/4.5 = 0.422); 800 °C -> 3.2% converted (alpha = 0.711). sample2 (init 7.20%): 400 °C -> 0%; 600 °C -> 4.4% (alpha = 0.611); 800 °C -> 6.0% (alpha = 0.833). sample3 (init 8.6%): 400 °C -> 2.0% (alpha = 0.233); 600 °C -> 8.6% (alpha = 1.0); 800 °C -> 8.6% (alpha = 1.0). These alpha values were plotted in Fig.7 and interpreted as increasing VSnV fraction with temperature and with total Sn. Sources of vacancies are treated implicitly as intrinsic/non-substitutional defect formation (thermodynamically favored VSnV) during anneal; no implantation damage in these MBE-grown films.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Vacancy-mediated diffusion is asserted for Sn in Ge and GeSn (consistent with prior literature cited); supported by DFT/NEB calculations performed in this work showing vacancy-mediated hopping path and computed energy barriers. The paper cites earlier theoretical/experimental works indicating vacancy-mediated Sn migration and that Sn preferentially binds to vacancies to form Sn–V clusters.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_coefficients: No explicit diffusion coefficients (D) or Arrhenius prefactors reported in the paper. The work reports migration energy barriers and activation energies (see next field) but not diffusivities.
extracted_data.activation_energies_diffusion_or_reactio: NEB-calculated migration energy barriers (vacancy-mediated hop) for two compositions: Ge60Sn2-VSnV: migration energy barrier = 0.286 eV; Ge55Sn7-VSnV: migration energy barrier = 0.179 eV (NEB). Using an activation-energy formula from references [23,35] the paper reports corresponding activation energies: 0.927 eV (Ge60Sn2-VSnV) and 0.832 eV (Ge55Sn7-VSnV). Methods = DFT NEB (migration barriers) and derived activation energies using literature kinetic model.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: DFT (VASP 5.4, PBE functional, PAW, plane-wave cut-off 300 eV, 4x4x4 k-mesh), Special Quasirandom Structure (SQS) to generate random alloy supercells (six realizations per composition), formation-energy calculations (Equation 4), NEB for migration paths and transition states, binding-energy calculations for Ge–Sn and VSnV (Equations 5 and 6), charge-density analysis (VESTA visualization).
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: No capping or passivation studied; samples were uncapped and the paper does not provide experimental or computational data on cap-induced suppression or enhancement of Sn out-diffusion. Therefore no capping-effect data are reported.
extracted_data.comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped: Not available in this work — no capped samples studied, so no direct comparisons (capped vs uncapped) are provided.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Experimentally observed onset: for the highest-Sn sample (initial ~8.6% Sn_s), visible surface Sn particles/segregation already appear at 400 °C (60 s). For the lower-Sn samples (4.5% and 7.2% initial), surface segregation features are reported to appear at ~600 °C (60 s) and become much more pronounced at 800 °C; by 600 °C large reductions in substitutional Sn are observed (sample1: retained Sn_s 2.6% from 4.5%; sample2: retained 2.8% from 7.2%; sample3: Sn_s gone at 600 °C). Thus 400–600 °C is the critical range where composition-dependent instability is observed in uncapped films.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: The paper notes that substitutional Sn (Sn_s) strongly affects lattice constant (used to extract Sn_s by XRD) and that increased Sn_s leads to XRD peak broadening indicating poorer crystallinity. However, detailed quantitative analysis of strain-driven diffusion/precipitation is not presented; strain is discussed primarily as context (lattice-constant shifts) rather than as a separate driving mechanism for segregation. No direct measurement of dislocations or relaxation-driven vacancy injection is reported.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Surface acts as the observed sink for segregated Sn: optical and SEM images show Sn-rich particles/clusters on the film surface after anneal (Figures 5 and 6). The paper interprets VSnV formation and vacancy-mediated diffusion as driving Sn migration toward the surface where Sn accumulates/segregates; interfaces (film/substrate, cap or passivating layers) are not experimentally varied in this study, so interfacial reactions are not quantified.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: The paper discusses contradictory experimental results from Decoster et al. (ion-implantation + emission channeling) who reported a roughly constant VSnV proportion across total Sn concentrations and anneal temperatures; the authors argue that discrepancies arise from implantation-induced lattice damage and non-homogeneous doping in that prior study, making those results less applicable than their MBE-grown films. No alternative diffusion mechanisms (e.g., interstitial or dislocation pipe) are supported by data in this paper.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Table 1 (XRD/Raman Sn_s concentrations vs anneal), Table 3 (DFT formation energies of Sn_s and VSnV vs total Sn concentration), Figure 3 (XRD spectra vs anneal), Figure 4 (Raman spectra vs anneal), Figure 5 & 6 (optical microscope and SEM images showing Sn surface segregation), Figure 7 (ratio alpha = VSnV/total Sn after anneal), Figure 10 (NEB diffusion path and migration-energy profiles), Figure 11 (binding-energy trends Ge-Sn and VSnV vs Sn concentration), Figures 12/13 (charge-density distributions).

extracted_data.name_full: VSnV (non-substitutional Sn defect: Sn bonded with two vacancies; quasi-cubic/β-Sn-like cluster)
extracted_data.brief_description: A non-substitutional defect in GeSn consisting of a Sn atom associated with two vacancies (Sn–V–V, often denoted VSnV) that forms a quasi-cubic octahedral structure similar to white tin and is reported to be the dominant non-substitutional Sn cluster driving surface segregation and Sn precipitation in GeSn.
extracted_data.citation_title: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys
extracted_data.material_system: VSnV in Ge1-xSnx alloys across simulated compositions (DFT supercells from ~3.2% to 16.1% Sn) and experimentally inferred in MBE-grown GeSn films (initial Sn_s 4.5–8.6%).
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Experimentally observed in uncapped MBE-grown GeSn films after RTA; modeled in 64-atom supercells with SQS distributions and with one VSnV defect per supercell (notation e.g., Ge57Sn5-VSnV).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: VSnV formation inferred and quantified after RTA at 400 °C, 600 °C, 800 °C for 60 s (experimental), with VSnV fraction increasing with T and with higher total Sn; DFT formation energies computed at T=0 K (thermodynamic quantities) across compositions.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: uncapped (no cap applied in experiments; VSnV formation and surface segregation observed in uncapped films).
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: VSnV interpreted as the product of conversion of substitutional Sn during anneal; fraction of Sn converted to VSnV increases with anneal temperature and with total Sn (alpha values computed from Table 1 and plotted in Fig.7). VSnV formation correlates with loss of substitutional Sn and with surface segregation/precipitation of Sn-rich clusters.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: Experimentally: indirect inference from XRD and Raman (Sn_s drop) and SEM/optical (surface clusters) combined with mass conservation to estimate VSnV fraction; literature references to PAS as a direct probe (Assali et al.). The paper uses DFT formation-energy calculations and charge-density distributions to characterize VSnV energetics and binding.
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: DFT formation energies (Table 3) show VSnV formation energy becomes more negative (more favorable) as total Sn increases (from -4.244 eV at 3.2% to -6.279 eV at 16.1%); binding-energy calculations (Equation 6 and plotted in Fig.11b) show an increasing binding strength of VSnV with Sn concentration; charge-density maps show increased electron density around VSnV with higher Sn, consistent with stronger binding. Prior experimental PAS and emission-channeling studies (cited) support VSnV as a dominant defect type.
extracted_data.sn_vacancy_binding_energy: Paper provides DFT-based formation energies for VSnV (interpreted as binding/formation strength) across compositions (Table 3): 3.2%: -4.244 eV; 4.8%: -4.403 eV; 6.5%: -4.837 eV; 8.1%: -5.128 eV; 9.7%: -5.374 eV; 11.3%: -5.528 eV; 12.9%: -5.783 eV; 14.5%: -5.916 eV; 16.1%: -6.279 eV. Method: DFT (PBE) formation-energy definition and binding-energy expression (Equation 6). No single experimental binding-energy number given.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No absolute vacancy concentrations presented. Paper infers VSnV concentrations from decreases in substitutional Sn measured by XRD after anneal (see experimental conversions and alpha values in first result). The paper notes that higher Sn concentrations and higher anneal temperatures favor VSnV formation thermodynamically (via lower formation energy) and kinetically (lower migration barriers).
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: VSnV is central to vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion story: Sn atoms bind to vacancies to form Sn–V clusters (VSnV), which promote Sn migration/segregation; supported by DFT showing favorable VSnV formation energies and literature on vacancy-mediated Sn mobility.
extracted_data.activation_energies_diffusion_or_reactio: Not reported specifically for VSnV cluster formation as an isolated reaction barrier; paper reports migration barriers and activation energies for vacancy-mediated Sn hops (see other result): NEB barriers and activation energies indicate more facile Sn motion at higher Sn concentration, facilitating VSnV formation.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: DFT (VASP/PBE/PAW) SQS supercells with one VSnV defect per cell; formation-energy formalism (Eq.4); binding-energy definition for VSnV (Eq.6); charge-density analysis; averaging over multiple SQS realizations for statistical robustness.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: No data — VSnV formation and behavior reported only for uncapped films in this work. The paper does not provide capping/passivation experiments or modeling.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Experimentally, VSnV fraction (inferred) increases with anneal T: negligible conversion at 400 °C for low-Sn samples, substantial conversion at 600 °C (e.g., sample1 42% of initial Sn_s converted to VSnV at 600 °C; sample2 61%; sample3 fully converted by 600 °C). These are inferred VSnV-formation thresholds in uncapped MBE-grown films for 60 s anneals.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: VSnV vs Sn_s have different coordination and different effects on lattice constant; Sn_s strongly affects lattice parameter whereas VSnV has minimal effect. The paper does not provide a detailed coupling between strain relaxation/dislocation generation and VSnV formation beyond noting lattice-constant-based Sn_s extraction.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: VSnV formation is linked to Sn migration toward the surface; surface accumulation of Sn-rich particles observed by SEM is interpreted as the macroscopic consequence of VSnV-assisted vacancy-mediated transport and segregation to the film surface.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Paper cites Decoster et al. who found near-constant VSnV fraction vs total Sn in ion-implanted Ge — presented as contradictory prior experimental evidence; authors argue implantation-created damage and inhomogeneity make those results not directly comparable. No other strong alternative mechanisms proposed in the paper.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Table 3 (VSnV formation energies vs Sn concentration), Figure 7 (VSnV/total Sn ratio after anneal inferred from XRD/Raman), Figure 11b (binding energy of VSnV vs Sn concentration), Figures 12/13 (charge density maps showing enhanced VSnV electron density).

extracted_data.name_full: Vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion pathway and energetics from DFT/NEB calculations
extracted_data.brief_description: DFT nudged-elastic-band (NEB) calculations in this paper identify a vacancy-mediated ring-type diffusion path for Sn in GeSn supercells and quantify composition-dependent migration energy barriers and derived activation energies, showing lower barriers/activation energies at higher Sn concentrations and thus increased Sn mobility and surface segregation tendencies.
extracted_data.citation_title: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys
extracted_data.material_system: Vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion modeled in Ge60Sn2-VSnV and Ge55Sn7-VSnV DFT supercell models (representing low and higher Sn concentrations).
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Computational only (NEB path constructed between initial and final vacancy-mediated Sn hop configurations in SQS-generated supercells).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: Not directly simulated (DFT provides energetics at 0 K); experimental annealing contexts are RTA at 400/600/800 °C for 60 s, used to interpret kinetic relevance of computed barriers.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: Not applicable (computational study of bulk-like diffusion/hop in supercell); no cap modeled.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: Lower NEB migration barriers and activation energies at higher Sn concentration imply easier removal of Sn from substitutional sites and greater likelihood of conversion to VSnV and subsequent surface segregation during anneal.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: NEB transition-state calculations in VASP (DFT-PBE) to obtain migration energy barriers; activation energies calculated using an activation-energy formula from references [23,35].
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: NEB path explicitly involves vacancy-mediated hopping; lower computed migration barriers at higher Sn (0.286 eV → 0.179 eV) and lower activation energies (0.927 eV → 0.832 eV) are consistent with enhanced Sn mobility and stronger Sn–vacancy interactions enabling diffusion.
extracted_data.sn_vacancy_binding_energy: No explicit single 'binding energy for Sn–V pair' value reported for the diffusion transition state; formation energies and E_VSnV (Table 3) and trends in binding-energy plots (Fig.11) are provided instead (see other entries).
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: Not directly computed as absolute concentrations; vacancy presence is modeled explicitly as the hop-mediating species (VSnV in the supercells). The paper infers experimentally that vacancy-mediated formation of VSnV increases with temperature and total Sn.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Vacancy-mediated (Sn hops via vacancy-assisted ring mechanism); supported by NEB DFT pathways and prior literature citations that Sn migration follows vacancy-mediated mechanism.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_coefficients: None reported; only migration energy barriers and activation energies are provided (no attempt to compute diffusivities or prefactors).
extracted_data.activation_energies_diffusion_or_reactio: Computed NEB migration energy barriers: Ge60Sn2-VSnV = 0.286 eV; Ge55Sn7-VSnV = 0.179 eV. Derived activation energies (using literature formula): Ge60Sn2-VSnV = 0.927 eV; Ge55Sn7-VSnV = 0.832 eV. Methods: DFT NEB for barriers; activation-energy formula from refs [23,35].
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: NEB calculations in DFT (VASP/PBE/PAW) on SQS supercells (64-atom cells with one VSnV), multiple intermediate images to map the ring diffusion mechanism, average over configurations not explicitly required for NEB path examples given.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Not studied computationally; no cap layers included in NEB models. Paper therefore gives no data on cap influence on vacancy-mediated diffusion.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: Not directly computed from kinetics, but DFT barriers/activation energies are used to rationalize experimental observation that significant Sn loss/substitutional-to-VSnV conversion occurs between 400–600 °C (60 s) depending on composition.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: NEB models are within SQS alloy supercells; the calculations do not explicitly separate strain contributions; trends are attributed primarily to weaker Ge–Sn bonding at higher Sn content which lowers migration barriers.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: NEB is a bulk-like hop calculation; interfaces/surface not included. However, experimental interpretation connects vacancy-mediated diffusion to surface segregation seen in SEM/optical images.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: No direct computational counterevidence presented; the vacancy-mediated mechanism is presented as consistent with both prior literature and the reported DFT energetics. Alternative mechanisms (interstitial-mediated, pipe diffusion) are not supported or modeled in this work.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Figure 10 (NEB diffusion path and relative energy profile with intermediate states and computed migration barriers), Figure 11 (bonding trends used to rationalize lower barriers), Table 3 (formation energies that contextualize thermodynamic driving forces).

extracted_data.name_full: Divacancy defects in Ge1-xSnx epitaxial layers
extracted_data.brief_description: Depth-profiled positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) identifies divacancies as the dominant open-volume defect in CVD-grown Ge1-xSnx (x = 0.065–0.13) films; the divacancy-related positron lifetime component τ1 ≈ 335 ps (constant vs composition) with relative intensity I1 increasing from ~65% to ~83% as Sn increases.
extracted_data.citation_title: Vacancy complexes in nonequilibrium germanium-tin semiconductors
extracted_data.material_system: Ge1-xSnx (GeSn) epitaxial layers with Sn content 6.5–13.0 at.% (reported as 6.5, 9, 11, 13 at.%)
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (CVD). Structure: Si(100) substrate; 500–700 nm Ge virtual substrate (Ge-VS) grown at 450 °C (with thermal cyclic annealing >800 °C), then 500–700 nm GeSn grown at fixed temperature in 300–330 °C range; a ~60 nm GeSn buffer used for some samples. Residual in-plane compressive strain reported as < -0.3%.
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: No deliberate post-growth anneals in the 400–700 °C range were performed on the GeSn layers in this study; the Ge virtual substrate experienced thermal cyclic annealing >800 °C during its preparation. Growth conducted below 400 °C to avoid segregation.
extracted_data.capping_or_surface_treatment: uncapped (no cap/passivation reported for the GeSn films)
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: No experimental observation of Sn surface segregation, β-Sn precipitation, or Sn-rich precipitates reported after growth or anneal in this work. Sn is stated to occupy substitutional sites (from literature) and to be randomly distributed; increasing Sn content correlates with higher fraction of divacancies (I1) and a decreased fraction of larger vacancy clusters, interpreted as Sn reducing vacancy clustering rather than driving Sn loss or precipitation under the reported conditions.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: Depth-profiled pulsed positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS/PAS), variable-energy Doppler broadening (S-parameter), X-ray diffraction (RSM, 2θ-ω), cross-sectional TEM, and references to prior structural/chemical studies (literature).
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: Indirect experimental evidence in this paper: the fraction of large vacancy clusters (τ2 component) decreases as Sn content increases while the divacancy-related component (τ1 ≈ 335 ps) becomes dominant (I1 up to ~83%), suggesting Sn locally 'freezes' or stabilizes vacancies and limits their clustering. The paper also cites prior work (Refs. 37, 38) reporting an affinity of Sn to attract/trap vacancies from experiments and ab initio calculations (emission channeling and DFT), supporting Sn–vacancy interaction hypotheses. No direct measurement of Sn–V binding energy in this study.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No absolute vacancy concentrations reported. Relative PAS-derived metrics: average positron lifetime τ_AV = 380–395 ps near surface decreasing to ~350 ps near the Ge-VS; Ge reference bulk lifetime τ_b ≈ 224–228 ps. Decomposition: divacancy-related lifetime τ1 ≈ 335±2 ps (I1 increases from ~65% to ~83% with Sn content). Larger vacancy-cluster lifetime τ2 > 450 ps with low intensity I2 that decreases with Sn content. No numeric vacancies/cm^3 provided.
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: The paper does not directly measure Sn diffusion; it discusses literature and plausible mechanisms: Sn can trap vacancies (Sn–V complexes) and occupy bound-centered or vacancy-split configurations (literature cited), implying vacancy-mediated processes could be relevant for Sn mobility or stabilization. The authors mention high activation energies for divacancy migration (>1 eV, Ref. 35), arguing vacancy mobility (and therefore vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion) is limited under small growth-temperature changes in their experiments.
extracted_data.activation_energies_diffusion_or_reactio: No activation energies measured for Sn diffusion/segregation in this work. The paper cites literature value/order: divacancy migration in Ge involves activation energies above 1 eV (Ref. 35).
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: No models/simulations performed in this paper. The authors cite prior DFT/ab initio studies (Refs. 38) and thermodynamic considerations from literature regarding Sn preference for substitutional sites and possibility to trap vacancies.
extracted_data.capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion: Not studied; samples were uncapped and no cap experiments were reported. Paper does not provide data on how capping would influence vacancy concentration or Sn loss during annealing.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: No thresholds for Sn precipitation/segregation in the 400–700 °C range reported. The paper cites literature that Sn–divacancy complexes formed in irradiated Ge anneal out at 220 K (Ref. 39), i.e., a low-temperature anneal-out, but provides no high-temperature stability thresholds for substitutional Sn in epitaxial GeSn.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Authors note compressive in-plane strain < -0.3% across samples. They propose that the larger size of Sn relative to Ge makes Sn–vacancy pairing a plausible local stress-relief mechanism; this is invoked to explain reduced vacancy clustering as Sn increases. Dislocations near the GeSn–Ge interface are noted, but are argued not to significantly affect PAS signals under measurement conditions.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Depth-dependent PAS shows increased open-volume defects near the GeSn surface and a monotonic decrease toward the Ge-VS; the S-parameter increases up to ~310 nm mean depth and then decreases toward Si substrate values. The GeSn–Ge virtual substrate interface hosts dislocations, but the authors argue these do not dominate the observed PAS lifetimes. No observations of Sn pile-up at interfaces or cap/film reactions are reported.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: The authors consider and discount a simple temperature-driven explanation for reduced vacancy cluster formation (i.e., lower growth temperature reducing mobility), arguing the 300–330 °C growth-temperature range is too narrow and that migration barriers are high (>1 eV). Thus they favor an Sn–vacancy attractive interaction explanation. They also note that monovacancies are not observed at room temperature (monovacancies pair to divacancies above ~200 K), consistent with PAS lifetimes recorded.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 (Fig.2: S-parameter vs positron energy; Fig.3: τ_AV vs depth and vs Sn content; Fig.4: lifetime decomposition for Ge-VS; Fig.5: lifetime/intensity decomposition for 13 at.% GeSn and composition dependence at 215 nm).

extracted_data.name_full: Larger vacancy clusters (multi-vacancy complexes) in Ge1-xSnx layers
extracted_data.brief_description: PAS identifies a minority population of larger vacancy clusters in as-grown GeSn (multi-vacancy complexes, >~5 vacancies) with long lifetimes τ2 > 450 ps (observed 469–750 ps depending on depth) whose relative intensity I2 decreases with increasing Sn content.
extracted_data.citation_title: Vacancy complexes in nonequilibrium germanium-tin semiconductors
extracted_data.growth_method_and_structure: Low-pressure CVD; same stack as above (Ge-VS + GeSn layers on Si(100); GeSn thickness ~500–700 nm; growth 300–330 °C).
extracted_data.annealing_conditions: No post-growth anneals in 400–700 °C performed. Ge-VS had prior high-temperature thermal cycles >800 °C during preparation.
extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: No observation of Sn precipitation; vacancy clusters are present but form a small fraction (I2 low) and their fraction decreases as Sn content increases—interpreted as Sn inhibiting formation/growth of vacancy clusters rather than promoting Sn precipitation under the studied conditions.
extracted_data.measurement_methods: Pulsed low-energy positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (depth-resolved), Doppler broadening spectroscopy, TEM, XRD.
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: Indirect: τ2 (cluster-related) intensity I2 decreases as Sn content increases while τ1 (divacancy) intensity increases, suggesting that Sn–vacancy interactions reduce the tendency of vacancies to aggregate into larger clusters. No direct chemical identification of Sn at vacancy clusters presented.
extracted_data.vacancy_concentration_or_generation: No absolute concentrations; PAS intensities show I2 (cluster fraction) is small and decreases with Sn. τ2 observed in GeSn ranges from ~490 ps (lower Sn) to ~750 ps (surface near region for certain depths) and is associated with clusters of multiple vacancies (>5).
extracted_data.sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim: Paper does not present direct Sn diffusion measurements; vacancy-cluster evolution is interpreted through trapping of vacancies by Sn which reduces vacancy mobility/aggregation, indirectly bearing on any vacancy-mediated Sn redistribution.
extracted_data.models_or_simulations_used: No kinetic simulations; interpretation references known PAS lifetime-to-defect-size assignments from literature.
extracted_data.temperature_thresholds_for_instability: None for 400–700 °C. τ2-associated clusters are present as-grown and are fewer at higher Sn content.
extracted_data.role_of_strain_and_relaxation: Authors suggest vacancy clustering tendencies are affected by local stress; larger Sn atoms may pair with vacancies to relieve local stress, reducing cluster formation.
extracted_data.role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces: Higher τ2 values and larger defect signals observed nearer the surface in some depth ranges; however, overall cluster fraction is low across film thickness and diminishes with higher Sn.
extracted_data.counterevidence_or_alternative_explanati: Authors consider reduced mobility due to slightly lower growth temperature as an alternative explanation for less clustering at higher Sn content but deem the small temperature difference (300–330 °C) insufficient given high migration barriers; thus favor Sn–vacancy interaction interpretation.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Figures 3 and 5 (Fig.3: τ_AV vs depth and Sn content; Fig.5: τ2 and I2 vs depth and composition).

extracted_data.name_full: Attractive interaction / binding between substitutional Sn atoms and vacancies in Ge
extracted_data.brief_description: The paper cites experimental (emission channeling) and ab initio (DFT) literature indicating Sn has an affinity to attract and trap vacancies in Ge, potentially forming Sn–vacancy or Sn–divacancy complexes; the present PAS data provide indirect support (reduced vacancy clustering with higher Sn).

extracted_data.annealing_conditions: No explicit annealing experiments aimed at probing Sn–V binding energies in this study; literature cited includes irradiated-Ge studies and low-T anneal-out behavior (e.g., Sn–divacancy complexes anneal out at 220 K in irradiated Ge, Ref. 39). extracted_data.stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn: Based on cited literature and the study's inference: Sn favors substitutional sites but can trap vacancies; this trapping could stabilize substitutional Sn locally and reduce vacancy-clustering driven microstructural evolution. extracted_data.measurement_methods: This paper: PAS/Doppler broadening (indirect evidence). Cited literature: ab initio/DFT calculations and emission channeling (Refs. 37, 38) and irradiated-sample PAS studies (Ref. 39).
extracted_data.evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding: Indirect: (1) PAS shows reduced formation of large vacancy clusters with increasing Sn content; (2) literature cited shows experimental and DFT evidence that Sn attracts/traps vacancies and can occupy bound-center sites in vacancy-split configurations.
