components.theory_description_plain_language: In uncapped films, Sn travels quickly along dislocations to the surface, where it is permanently removed; this leaves vacancies that form voids, and the voids make the process accelerate suddenly. A thin oxide cap blocks the surface sink and prevents this runaway feedback.

law.statement_name: Pipe-diffusion dominated Sn transport law (voiding/collapse mode)
law.theory_statement: In metastable SiGeSn (and GeSn/SiGeSn stacks) annealed at ~500–600 °C that (i) contain pre-existing dislocation networks or other continuous short-circuit paths connecting to the surface and (ii) display incubation-then-collapse near-surface Sn loss, the dominant long-range Sn transport to the near-surface region is dislocation-core (pipe) diffusion (or an equivalent short-circuit pathway), not bulk substitutional diffusion; bulk substitutional diffusion lengths on the relevant timescale are too small to account for the observed near-surface compositional collapse and microstructural changes.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: When collapse behavior happens, Sn mainly travels along dislocations/fast paths rather than slowly through the perfect crystal lattice.
law.domain_scope: Applies to metastable (Si)GeSn epitaxial films/heterostructures in the 500–600 °C regime (order-of-tens-of-minutes to hours) where (a) a connected defect network exists (misfit/threading dislocations, dislocation bunches, or other percolating short-circuit paths) and (b) near-surface probes show incubation followed by rapid Sn depletion/optical shift and voiding/roughening signatures. Not intended for low-T (<~400 °C) droplet-free regimes or for liquid droplet-mediated transport above the eutectic, nor for purely capped sandwich diffusion experiments where surface sink is removed and profiles evolve smoothly.
special_cases: If the film is demonstrably dislocation-poor and lacks percolating fast paths to the surface, this law may not apply; degradation may then proceed via slower interdiffusion into adjacent layers or via different nucleation-limited precipitation mechanisms.

If temperature/composition conditions allow liquid Sn droplet formation (eutectic-driven LPE), droplet-mediated transport can dominate and invalidate pipe-diffusion dominance for the observed morphology evolution.

supporting_evidence.text: For uncapped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 at 550 °C, authors argue bulk substitutional diffusion cannot explain the kinetics, estimating a bulk diffusion length of only ~0.3 nm over the ~50 min incubation, while TEM shows filamentary Sn-enriched paths consistent with dislocation-mediated transport to the surface.

Uncapped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 shows incubation (~50 min) then abrupt optical collapse; post-mortem TEM/EDX reveals filamentary Sn-enriched features and surface/near-surface segregation consistent with a connected fast-transport network feeding the surface sink.

GeSn thermal stability study reports that partially relaxed (dislocated) GeSn exhibits much faster Sn transport/segregation and Sn-rich clustering at both surface and interface; pseudomorphic films (lacking dislocations) show surface-only accumulation and slower evolution, supporting a dislocation-enhanced transport picture.

In uncapped pseudomorphic GeSn/SiGeSn diffusion work, surface segregation appears above ~600 °C, while capped sandwich structures suppress surface segregation and instead show smoother interdiffusion into Ge; this supports the idea that fast pathways plus a free-surface sink can dominate observed Sn redistribution when uncapped.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Dislocation pipe diffusion as a fast solute transport mechanism and its relevance to Sn segregation in relaxed GeSn are established concepts in the GeSn stability literature.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The statement narrows the mechanism to the specific incubation-then-collapse/voiding regime and elevates short-circuit transport as the necessary rate-setting pathway specifically under those kinetic signatures, contrasting it with bulk diffusion limits quantified for the same timescale.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Mechanistic ingredients are known, but the scoped claim (dominance under collapse-mode kinetics with quantified bulk-diffusion insufficiency) is a targeted, testable refinement rather than a generic restatement.
references: Zaumseil (2018) The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers [dislocation-enhanced Sn transport/segregation; short-circuit diffusion concept in GeSn]
Unknown (SiGeSn cap study) Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation [explicit argument that bulk diffusion is too small; filamentary fast paths implicated]

law.statement_name: Surface-sink–driven Kirkendall void nucleation and positive feedback
law.theory_statement: If, during annealing of an uncapped metastable (Si)GeSn film/heterostructure, the free surface acts as a strong irreversible sink for Sn (segregation/oxidation/precipitation) and Sn is delivered to that surface through fast paths at a rate that is not balanced by an inward counter-flux of matrix atoms, then vacancies generated by the flux imbalance accumulate (vacancy supersaturation) and nucleate Kirkendall-type voids; the resulting voids and microstructural disruption increase effective sink area and introduce additional fast transport routes, yielding a positive feedback that produces an abrupt acceleration (collapse) of near-surface substitutional Sn loss after an incubation period.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: When the surface keeps removing Sn, vacancies pile up and form voids; voids then make Sn loss speed up suddenly.
law.domain_scope: Uncapped metastable GeSn/SiGeSn films/stacks in an anneal window where (a) the surface is an effective irreversible sink for Sn and (b) vacancy mobility is sufficient for void nucleation and growth on experimental timescales (here evidenced at 550 °C for ~hours). Requires the presence of fast delivery pathways for Sn to the surface (dislocations or equivalent).
special_cases: If the surface is not an irreversible sink (e.g., surface sealed by an impermeable cap), net flux imbalance may be suppressed and voiding may not occur even if fast paths exist.

If inward diffusion of other species (Ge/Si) and/or defect recombination at sinks balances the outward Sn flux, vacancy supersaturation and voiding may be reduced; degradation may then proceed as slower interdiffusion without collapse kinetics.
If degradation proceeds by liquid droplet-mediated mechanisms (eutectic-driven), voiding feedback is not required to explain rapid transformation.

supporting_evidence.text: Uncapped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 annealed 550 °C/140 min exhibits voids throughout upper region; voids contain oxygen by EDX, and authors interpret voiding as Kirkendall-type vacancy supersaturation caused by unbalanced outward Sn flux along fast paths to the surface.

The same uncapped sample shows catastrophic thickness loss (~60%), strong ellipsometric E2 blueshift (+423 meV) and rapid collapse after incubation (t0≈74 min; incubation ~50 min; collapse width ~1.9 min), consistent with a nonlinear feedback process rather than steady Fickian diffusion.

GeSn thermal stability study links enhanced Sn transport/segregation to extended defects (dislocations) and vacancy-mediated dynamics, consistent with a scenario where short-circuit transport can create strong fluxes that could generate vacancy imbalances.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Kirkendall voiding due to unbalanced diffusion fluxes is a classic mechanism; voiding as an amplifier of degradation in diffusion-coupled systems is known broadly.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The explicit feedback-loop framing for metastable SiGeSn collapse kinetics—surface sink + pipe-delivered Sn flux → vacancy supersaturation → voiding → accelerated transport/sink strength—used as the principal explanation for incubation-then-collapse behavior at fixed temperature.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Uses established Kirkendall physics but applies it as a specific, falsifiable kinetic trigger for the observed abrupt ellipsometric collapse and associated void microstructure in SiGeSn.
references: Unknown (SiGeSn cap study) Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation [invokes vacancy supersaturation/Kirkendall voiding as consequence of Sn flux to surface]

law.statement_name: Nm-scale oxide cap suppresses the sink/void feedback by blocking Sn egress
law.theory_statement: A continuous nm-scale oxide cap (e.g., ~3 nm SiO2 or ~5 nm Al2O3) suppresses the voiding/collapse degradation mode in metastable SiGeSn at ~550 °C by reducing the effective free-surface sink strength for Sn: the cap kinetically blocks Sn transport to the ambient (and thus blocks irreversible surface fixation via segregation/oxide/droplet formation), which reduces net outward Sn flux along fast paths and prevents vacancy supersaturation; concomitantly, by physically separating the alloy from the ambient, the cap suppresses oxygen incorporation associated with voided regions. Therefore void nucleation, rapid near-surface Sn depletion, and strain-relaxation/roughening cascades are strongly inhibited.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: A thin, intact oxide cap removes the surface as a place for Sn to escape to, so the runaway voiding process never starts.
law.domain_scope: Metastable SiGeSn (and similar GeSn/SiGeSn stacks) annealed in nominally inert ambients around 550 °C where uncapped films exhibit incubation-then-collapse and voiding. Requires that the cap remains continuous (no pinholes/cracks), chemically stable, and sufficiently impermeable to Sn transport on the anneal timescale.
special_cases: If the cap contains pinholes, cracks, delamination, or reacts to form permeable pathways, localized sinks reappear and collapse can initiate at defects.
If cap deposition introduces high stress, defects, or interfacial damage that creates additional fast paths, it could partially offset stabilization benefits.

At substantially higher temperatures (>~700 °C) or long times where thermodynamic solubility limits dominate and interdiffusion into adjacent layers is strong, a cap may prevent surface segregation but cannot prevent bulk equilibration-driven Sn redistribution into neighboring layers (different failure mode).

supporting_evidence.text: At 550 °C/140 min under N2 purge, uncapped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 shows incubation (~50 min) then rapid collapse (t0≈74.2 min; width ~1.86 min), large E2 blueshift (~+423 meV), voids with oxygen, roughening, thickness loss, and formation of a Ge0.99Sn0.01 segregation layer; the 3 nm SiO2-capped sample shows <1 at.% Sn change over 140 min, |ΔE2|<20 meV, no voids, minimal relaxation and preserved uniformity.

Screening in the same study indicates 5 nm Al2O3 also suppresses segregation after 550 °C/30 min, supporting the idea that an oxide barrier (not only SiO2 specifically) can block the relevant surface-mediated pathway.

Conceptual discussions in GeSn droplet-mediated decomposition work suggest capping should suppress surface segregation and delay droplet/precipitate formation by reducing surface sink strength (though not experimentally tested there).

Capped Ge/GeSn/Ge sandwich diffusion experiments suppress surface segregation and redirect Sn into adjacent Ge rather than allowing surface pile-up, consistent with the general principle that removing the free surface changes the dominant degradation pathway.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Capping/passivation to suppress surface segregation is widely used; barrier layers limiting out-diffusion are standard concepts.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The explicit mechanistic attribution that nm-scale oxides stabilize by breaking a specific nonlinear feedback loop (pipe/short-circuit transport → surface sink → vacancy supersaturation → Kirkendall voiding → accelerated transport), providing an explanation for incubation-then-collapse kinetics rather than only a steady reduction in diffusion flux.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: The cap effect itself is known, but the collapse-mode feedback-loop mechanism and its suppression by ultrathin oxides is a more specific, testable causal chain tailored to the observed kinetics and microstructure.
references: Unknown (SiGeSn cap study) Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation [demonstrates oxide-cap suppression and interprets via surface-mediated pathways/voiding]

new_predictions_likely: For Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 annealed isothermally at 550 °C, a thin continuous oxide cap (e.g., 3 nm SiO2) will fall into the category 'cap suppresses the change' in in-situ SE, with the uncapped film showing a finite incubation time before the near-surface substitutional-Sn loss becomes visible (order: tens of minutes, comparable to ~50 min in the referenced 550 °C uncapped case).

If the dislocation density (or connectivity of dislocations to the surface) is increased in otherwise similar uncapped films, the incubation time before collapse will decrease and the void density in post-anneal TEM will increase; capped films will show a much weaker dependence of kinetics on dislocation density (collapse suppressed).

If an oxide cap is intentionally patterned with openings, degradation (Sn depletion, voiding) will initiate preferentially at openings and propagate laterally underneath as the local surface sink is reintroduced; capped regions away from openings remain comparatively stable.
new_predictions_unknown: In an uncapped sample annealed under extremely low oxygen chemical potential (e.g., ultra-high purity inert gas with strong oxygen getter), collapse kinetics may slow substantially and voids may show reduced oxygen decoration; if collapse is still rapid, it would imply that oxidation is not required for sink strength (segregation alone suffices).

Replacing oxide with a mechanically compressive but Sn-impermeable dielectric (e.g., thick SiNx) could either further suppress collapse (by sealing the surface) or accelerate it (if the stress generates cracks/defects that act as new fast paths). Outcome would strongly constrain whether mechanical integrity or chemical impermeability is the limiting factor.

Electrostatic effects from high fixed-charge caps could modify vacancy charge states and thus vacancy mobility/aggregation; if true, identical impermeability caps with different charge states would yield measurably different incubation times, separating 'barrier' from 'defect-chemistry' contributions.
negative_experiments: If uncapped films that show SE collapse at 550 °C do not exhibit voids (confirmed by cross-sectional TEM across the affected region), then Kirkendall voiding is not necessary for collapse and the feedback-loop hypothesis is weakened.

If capped films with verified continuous caps (no pinholes/cracks, verified by TEM/AFM and perhaps etch tests) still show the same incubation-then-collapse kinetics as uncapped, then suppression cannot be attributed to blocking the surface sink and the theory statements must be revised.

If a verified dislocation-poor/pseudomorphic film (no connected dislocation network) nevertheless shows the same collapse kinetics and filamentary transport signatures, then pipe/short-circuit transport is not the dominant pathway in this regime.

unaccounted_for.text: Droplet-mediated liquid-phase-epitaxy phase separation in high-Sn MBE Ge0.9Sn0.1 above the eutectic (~231 °C) proceeds by mobile liquid Sn droplets and is not explained by Kirkendall voiding feedback; it is a distinct degradation mode.

Two-regime Arrhenius behavior (low-T enhanced diffusion with EA ~1.1–1.8 eV and high-T conventional with EA ~2.9–3.1 eV) in capped Ge/GeSn/Ge sandwich diffusion experiments reflects bulk/interdiffusion kinetics rather than collapse-mode voiding; this theory does not aim to explain those regimes quantitatively.

conflicting_evidence.text: MBE GeSn RTA study interprets substitutional Sn loss largely via formation of non-substitutional VSnV clusters and vacancy-mediated hopping with sub-eV activation energies (0.83–0.93 eV derived) over 60 s at 400–800 °C, without invoking pipe diffusion or voiding; this indicates that in some uncapped GeSn films, bulk-like vacancy-mediated clustering may dominate over pipe-diffusion/voiding collapse.

special_cases: Capped Ge/GeSn/Ge or Ge/SiGeSn/Ge sandwich geometries (thick Ge caps) remove the free surface sink; degradation manifests as interdiffusion into Ge rather than voiding/collapse, consistent with this theory’s scope limits.
Very thin oxide caps may fail mechanically/chemically at sufficiently high temperatures or long times, reintroducing local sinks and enabling localized collapse.

In oxidizing ambients or during rapid thermal treatments in air (e.g., some PLA scenarios), Sn-rich oxide formation can dominate the surface sink behavior; whether voiding/collapse occurs will depend on timescale and defect connectivity.

references: Zaumseil (2018) The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers [dislocation-enhanced Sn transport/segregation; extended-defect role]
Unknown (SiGeSn cap study) Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation [oxide caps suppress 550 °C collapse; voiding and fast-path transport implicated]
General metallurgy literature on Kirkendall voiding [flux-imbalance-driven vacancy supersaturation and void formation; foundational mechanism]
existing_theory.what_already_exists: Pipe diffusion and Kirkendall voiding are established mechanisms; capping to suppress surface-mediated degradation is also a known processing strategy.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: A collapse-mode-specific causal chain linking (short-circuit Sn delivery) + (irreversible surface sink) → vacancy supersaturation → voiding → abrupt kinetic acceleration, and the claim that nm-scale oxide caps suppress collapse primarily by breaking this feedback loop (not merely by modestly reducing diffusion).
existing_theory.classification_explanation: The pieces are known, but the assembled feedback-loop explanation scoped to incubation-then-collapse kinetics in metastable SiGeSn and its suppression by ultrathin oxides is a more specific, testable mechanism than generic 'cap blocks diffusion' narratives.

theory-6.name: Competing vacancy traps: Sn–V vs dopant–V controls vacancy availability and Sn mobility
theory-6.description:
This specific theory covers doped GeSn/SiGeSn where vacancy-mediated Sn motion would otherwise be possible, but vacancy chemistry is dominated by other strong vacancy traps (especially high-concentration donors such as P; potentially also As/Sb depending on their complex energetics). The central mechanism is competition for the same vacancy population: (i) vacancies can enable Sn motion and/or conversion of substitutional Sn into Sn–vacancy complexes (including VSnV-like non-substitutional configurations), but (ii) vacancies can be preferentially immobilized by forming dopant–vacancy complexes (Pn–V) that are thermodynamically more stable than Sn-only vacancy complexes in the composition regime probed by PAS/DFT.

As a consequence, under conditions where bulk vacancy-mediated diffusion would matter (e.g., in capped or surface-sink-limited stacks), heavy dopant concentrations can reduce the effective concentration of mobile/free vacancies available for Sn exchange hops, thereby suppressing vacancy-mediated Sn interdiffusion and slowing the kinetics of substitutional-Sn loss via vacancy-assisted pathways. However, this vacancy-trap stabilization can be bypassed if degradation is dominated by dislocation-pipe transport to a free surface sink (surface-mediated degradation) or by liquid droplet transport (above eutectic in high-Sn GeSn).

Mechanistic dependencies: relative formation enthalpies of Pn–V vs Sn–V (and mixed Sn–P–V) complexes; dopant concentration; vacancy charge-state/Fermi-level effects (which can shift complex stability); and microstructure (dislocations/fast paths) and surface boundary conditions (capped vs uncapped).

components.theory_description_plain_language: Vacancies are needed for tin to move through the lattice. If dopants like phosphorus tie up most vacancies into dopant–vacancy complexes, tin has fewer vacancies to move with, which can slow vacancy-driven tin loss—unless fast dislocation paths or a free surface sink dominate the degradation.

law.statement_name: Vacancy capture hierarchy law (P dominates Sn in Ge/GeSn in studied regime)
law.theory_statement: In heavily P-doped epitaxial Ge and low-Sn Ge1−xSnx (x ≲ 0.07) with P in the ~10^19–10^20 cm−3 range, the dominant thermodynamic sinks for monovacancies are Pn–V complexes (n ≥ 2 at high P), while Sn is more likely to appear as a secondary neighbor/decorator in mixed Sn–P–V complexes rather than acting as the primary vacancy trap; thus the fraction of vacancies available as ‘free’ mediators for Sn-only vacancy pairing/hopping is reduced relative to undoped material.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: With very high phosphorus doping, vacancies mostly bind to phosphorus; tin shows up mainly as an additional neighbor around those vacancy complexes rather than capturing vacancies first.
law.domain_scope: Epitaxial Ge:P and GeSn:P films similar to the PAS/DFT study conditions: Sn up to ~7 at.% (example Ge0.93Sn0.07) and high P doping (~10^19–10^20 cm−3). Applies to as-grown material and post-growth thermal budgets up to at least the reported processing ceiling (~400 °C) and literature-stated stability window up to ~500 °C/30 min for low-Sn GeSn, where mono-vacancy-sized complexes remain relevant and before macroscopic phase separation dominates.
special_cases: At low P (or undoped), Pn–V trapping weakens and Sn–vacancy association can play a larger role (e.g., VSnV formation pathways in undoped MBE films).

At higher Sn contents and/or different microstructures (e.g., high defect densities, dislocation networks), vacancy sinks and transport may be dominated by dislocations/pipe diffusion and surface sinks, reducing the relevance of bulk mono-vacancy trapping competition.
Other dopants (As, Sb) can also form vacancy complexes; the hierarchy (dopant–V vs Sn–V) must be re-evaluated for each dopant and Fermi-level condition.
At sufficiently high temperatures where vacancy generation is large and dopant–V trapping saturates, the hierarchy may not limit vacancy availability.

supporting_evidence.text: DFT formation enthalpy ranking: Pn–V complexes are most stable; mixed Sn–Pn–V intermediate; Sn-only vacancy complexes least favorable; authors conclude Sn does not efficiently trap vacancies compared to P and therefore does not improve P activation via vacancy trapping.

PAS/coincedence Doppler shows mono-vacancy-sized open-volume defects decorated by multiple P atoms (2–4 depending on P level). In GeSn:P at highest P, PAS indicates at least one Sn atom near some vacancies (Sn_pP_n–V), consistent with Sn acting as a co-decorator around an already P-decorated vacancy complex rather than dominating vacancy capture.

PAS/DFT work notes inward Sn relaxation around vacancies (reducing open-volume and positron trapping), consistent with Sn being present around vacancies but not necessarily implying Sn is the dominant vacancy sink compared to Pn–V.

Literature cited in the PAS/DFT work indicates undoped low-Sn GeSn (Sn ≤ ~6 at.%) can be stable up to 500 °C for up to 30 min (context that the relevant defect complexes persist without immediate macroscopic decomposition in this composition range).

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Dopant–vacancy complexing and its dominance over other vacancy traps is established in semiconductor defect physics; the provided PAS/DFT study already reports that Pn–V complexes are thermodynamically preferred over Sn-only vacancy complexes in Ge/GeSn at low Sn content.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The statement is reframed as an explicit ‘hierarchy’ law to be used predictively for metastable GeSn/SiGeSn annealing stability: it asserts that vacancy availability for Sn-mediated transport/complexing is controlled by competition with dopant–V sinks, not solely by Sn–V affinity.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: The energetic ordering is directly supported by the provided PAS/DFT evidence; novelty lies in elevating it into a predictive stability-control principle for annealing scenarios (especially capped/surface-limited stacks).
references: PAS/DFT study (provided as 'here') [DFT formation enthalpies + PAS showing Pn–V dominance and mixed Sn_pP_n–V signatures; basis for vacancy capture hierarchy]
Decoster/Assali/Ventura (various, cited within provided works) [prior identification of dopant–vacancy complexes and non-substitutional Sn–vacancy complexes in Ge/GeSn]

law.statement_name: Dopant-controlled vacancy availability modulates vacancy-mediated Sn interdiffusion (under surface-sink-limited conditions)
law.theory_statement: For anneals where Sn redistribution is limited by bulk vacancy-mediated exchange (rather than by dislocation-pipe transport to a free surface sink or liquid droplet transport), increasing the concentration of a strong vacancy-trapping dopant (exemplified by high P) decreases the effective concentration of mobile/free vacancies, thereby increasing the apparent kinetic stability of substitutional Sn against vacancy-mediated redistribution and against vacancy-assisted formation of Sn–vacancy complexes (including VSnV-like configurations), at fixed temperature and similar microstructure.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: If the main way tin moves is by exchanging with vacancies in the lattice, then adding a dopant that locks up vacancies should slow tin motion and help keep tin substitutional—provided the surface isn’t acting as an easy escape route.
law.domain_scope: Applies to doped GeSn/SiGeSn stacks during anneals where (i) surface sinks are blocked or strongly reduced (e.g., thick caps, buried layers, diffusion-sandwich geometries), and (ii) dislocation density is low enough that pipe diffusion is not the dominant transport path. Intended temperature range: roughly 400–700 °C where vacancy-mediated diffusion is relevant in Ge/GeSn/SiGeSn, but excluding regimes where rapid surface-mediated collapse (voiding/pipe diffusion) or liquid droplet-mediated decomposition dominates.
special_cases: If degradation is dominated by dislocation networks feeding Sn to the surface (pipe diffusion) and/or by an irreversible surface sink, dopant trapping in the bulk may not prevent near-surface Sn depletion (surface-mediated theories dominate).
If dopant incorporation itself increases dislocation density or generates additional vacancies, net Sn mobility could increase despite trapping (microstructure change overrides chemistry).
At high temperatures where vacancy generation is large, dopant–V complexes may saturate, reducing the effectiveness of vacancy sequestration.

supporting_evidence.text: This statement is logically inferred (abduction/deduction) from: (1) Pn–V complexes are thermodynamically preferred over Sn-only vacancy complexes in Ge/low-Sn GeSn (vacancy capture hierarchy), and (2) vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion requires accessible vacancies as mediators; therefore sequestering vacancies into dopant–V complexes reduces vacancy availability for Sn exchange hops and Sn–V complex formation.

Vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion is identified as a relevant microscopic mechanism in GeSn stability literature; DFT/NEB in undoped GeSn shows low activation energies for vacancy-mediated Sn hops (~0.83–0.93 eV) and experimental RTA in undoped MBE GeSn shows substitutional Sn loss interpreted via formation of Sn–vacancy complexes (VSnV). These establish that vacancy-mediated routes can control Sn stability when not overridden by surface/pipe mechanisms, motivating why vacancy availability matters.

Capped diffusion-sandwich experiments (Ge/GeSn/Ge; Ge/SiGeSn/Ge) demonstrate that removing the free-surface sink shifts behavior to bulk interdiffusion with measurable activation energies (two-regime behavior) rather than immediate surface segregation—consistent with a domain where bulk vacancy-mediated kinetics can matter and therefore where vacancy sequestration by dopants could modulate Sn mobility.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Vacancy-mediated diffusion requiring vacancies and dopant–vacancy trapping reducing free-vacancy populations are established concepts in defect physics.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The explicit prediction for metastable GeSn/SiGeSn: under surface-sink-limited configurations, heavy vacancy-trapping dopants should measurably suppress Sn interdiffusion and delay substitutional-Sn loss via vacancy-mediated routes—proposed as an orthogonal control knob to capping.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Not directly measured in the provided dataset (no side-by-side doped vs undoped diffusion/retention experiment under identical caps), but it is strongly grounded in the provided PAS/DFT hierarchy plus the demonstrated relevance of vacancy-mediated Sn motion in uncapped and capped contexts.
references: PAS/DFT study (provided as 'here') [establishes dopant–V vs Sn–V energetic ordering in Ge/GeSn:P]
Study on Sn concentration vs VSnV and Sn segregation (provided as e9.0) [demonstrates vacancy-related Sn loss pathways in undoped MBE GeSn]
Pseudomorphic GeSn/SiGeSn diffusion study (provided as e8.0/e8.1) [shows capped, surface-sink-limited interdiffusion regimes where vacancy-mediated kinetics can dominate]

new_predictions_likely: In a surface-sink-suppressed geometry (e.g., Ge/GeSn/Ge diffusion sandwich or an oxide-capped stack that blocks free-surface Sn escape), increasing P doping into the high-10^19 cm−3 regime will reduce the effective Sn interdiffusion rate at 500–650 °C relative to an undoped control with similar dislocation density, because vacancies are sequestered into Pn–V complexes.

PAS/CDOBS vs P concentration in GeSn:P will show systematic increase in P decoration number (P2–V → P3–V/ P4–V) while the incremental Sn contribution around vacancies remains limited (mixed Sn_pP_n–V signal increases weakly or saturates), consistent with P-dominated vacancy trapping.

If two films have similar Sn content and microstructure but one has much higher P, the higher-P film will show reduced signatures of Sn-only vacancy complexes (or reduced kinetic conversion to such complexes during mild anneals), with vacancies predominantly residing in Pn–V or mixed Sn–P–V states.
new_predictions_unknown: Fermi-level engineering could change the vacancy charge-state distribution enough to alter the dopant–V vs Sn–V stability ordering; in some doping/strain conditions this could partially invert the hierarchy and enable electrically tunable Sn stability during annealing.

In SiGeSn, the presence of Si may modify vacancy formation energies and dopant–vacancy binding enough that P trapping is less effective (or more effective) than in GeSn, leading to composition-dependent crossovers where dopant chemistry unexpectedly accelerates Sn loss (if it increases vacancy populations more than it traps them).

Co-doping strategies (e.g., combining P with another species that preferentially binds vacancies or changes vacancy migration) might create a regime where vacancies are immobilized without generating compensating fast paths, enabling substantially higher thermal budgets for substitutional Sn retention.
negative_experiments: Prepare capped (surface-sink-limited) GeSn diffusion-sandwich samples with matched Sn content and dislocation density but different P levels; if heavily P-doped samples show equal or higher Sn interdiffusion rates than undoped samples across 500–650 °C, then vacancy sequestration by P is not limiting Sn mobility (or P increases vacancy supply/fast paths enough to dominate).

Direct defect spectroscopy/DFT under relevant Fermi-level conditions: if Sn–V (or VSnV precursor) binding becomes stronger than Pn–V stability under the actual charge states in these films, contradicting the assumed hierarchy, the theory’s mechanism fails for that regime.

If PAS after anneal shows a large increase of Sn-only vacancy complexes in heavily P-doped GeSn compared with undoped controls (at comparable vacancy supply), then P is not the dominant vacancy trap in the kinetic/thermodynamic regime relevant to annealing.

unaccounted_for.text: Oxide capping (3 nm SiO2, 5 nm Al2O3) at 550 °C can suppress surface-mediated degradation/voiding and preserve substitutional Sn in SiGeSn for 140 min; this theory does not explain that effect because it concerns bulk vacancy-trap competition, not surface-sink blocking and pipe-diffusion shutoff.
Droplet-mediated liquid transport above the Ge–Sn eutectic in high-Sn GeSn (e.g., Ge0.9Sn0.1) dominates decomposition and is not addressed by vacancy-trap competition.

conflicting_evidence.text: Undoped MBE GeSn RTA data show strong substitutional Sn loss via inferred VSnV formation and surface segregation between 400–800 °C, but provide no doped comparison; thus the key stabilizing prediction of dopant trapping is not directly corroborated (nor directly contradicted) by those results.

Some studies emphasize that Sn can attract/trap vacancies (e.g., inferred from reduced vacancy clustering with higher Sn, and literature on Sn–V affinity), which could be read as Sn being an effective vacancy trap in some regimes; this does not directly contradict P-dominance in P-rich films but signals that the hierarchy may be conditional on composition/charge state and defect type (mono- vs di-vacancies).

special_cases: Time-dependent trapping: during anneal, dopant activation/redistribution can change Pn–V populations, making vacancy sequestration non-stationary and possibly producing incubation-like kinetics.

Vacancy type dependence: PAS/DFT hierarchy is established mainly for mono-vacancy-sized complexes in P-rich material; GeSn films can contain divacancies and larger clusters (PAS in GeSn), which may interact differently with Sn and dopants, potentially shifting the competition outcome.
Microstructure override: if dislocation-pipe diffusion dominates (partially relaxed layers, high TDD), dopant-vacancy competition in the bulk may have limited impact on overall Sn transport.

Surface-sink override: if a free surface or reactive surface oxide provides a strong irreversible sink for Sn, then even reduced bulk vacancy availability may not prevent near-surface Sn depletion driven by pipe diffusion or surface segregation thermodynamics.

references: PAS/DFT study (provided as e7.0/e7.1) [shows Pn–V complexes are more stable than Sn-only vacancy complexes in Ge/GeSn:P; provides basis for vacancy-trap competition]
Zaumseil et al. (2018) The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers [discusses vacancy-mediated diffusion and defect-enhanced transport; does not develop dopant-competition control principle]

Zhang et al. (paper provided as e9.0) Study on Sn concentration on non-substitutional defect concentration and Sn surface segregation in GeSn alloys [emphasizes vacancy-mediated Sn loss/VSnV in undoped films; does not treat dopant competition]
existing_theory.what_already_exists: Dopant–vacancy complexes controlling free-vacancy populations and vacancy-mediated diffusion are established in semiconductor defect physics; the provided PAS/DFT work specifically shows Pn–V complexes are energetically favored over Sn-only vacancy complexes in Ge/low-Sn GeSn:P.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: Casting dopant–vacancy competition as a predictive control parameter for substitutional Sn stability and vacancy-mediated Sn mobility during annealing (especially under capped/surface-sink-limited conditions), and separating it mechanistically from capping/surface-sink suppression.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: The energetic premise is evidenced and thus not new, but the theory’s use as a process-control lever for metastable GeSn/SiGeSn thermal stability is an application/extension not directly demonstrated in the provided experiments.

metadata.title: Controlling barrier height and spectral responsivity of p–i–n based GeSn photodetectors via arsenic incorporation
metadata.abstract: GeSn compounds have made many interesting contributions in photodetectors (PDs) over the last ten years, as they have a detection limit in the NIR and mid-IR region. Sn incorporation in Ge alters the cut off wavelength. In the present article, p–i–n structures based on GeSn junctions were fabricated to serve as PDs. Arsine (As) is incorporated to develop n-GeSn compounds via a metal induced crystallization (MIC) process followed by i-GeSn on p-Si wafers. The impact of As and Sn doping on the strain characteristics of GeSn has been studied with high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy analyses. The direct transitions and tuning of their band energies have been investigated using diffuse reflectance UV-vis spectroscopy and photoluminescence (PL). The barrier height and spectral responsivity have been controlled with incorporation of As. Variation of As incorporation into GeSn Compounds shifted the Raman peak and hence affected the strain in the Ge network. UV-vis spectroscopy showed that the direct transition energies are lowered as the Ge–As bonding increases as illustrated in Raman spectroscopy investigations. PL and UV-vis spectroscopy of annealed heterostructures at 500 °C showed that there are many transition peaks from the UV to the NIR region as result of oxygen vacancies in the Ge network. The calculated diode parameters showed that As incorporation leads to an increase of the height barrier and thus dark current. Spectral response measurements show that the prepared heterojunctions have spectral responses in near UV and NIR regions that gives them opportunities in UV and NIR photodetection-applications.

Overall, capping material (As vs Sn) strongly affects chemical incorporation, strain and electrical/optical outcomes; mechanisms proposed are chemical doping (As), altered solubility and bonding and oxidation-driven vacancy filling rather than explicit vacancy-gettering kinetics. |

Raman intensities and XRD peak shifts/d-spacing also differ: As-incorporated configurations show stronger GeSn Raman peaks and wavenumber shifts consistent with altered strain/bonding. Quantitative deltas: orders-of-magnitude higher dark current in Sn-capped then-As-deposited-after sample vs As-capped-during-anneal sample (≈3 orders of magnitude). |

No explicit onset temperatures for Sn precipitation/β-Sn formation or Sn loss thresholds reported. The paper notes that annealing at 500 °C reduces strain, increases electron mobility and enables MIC-driven Sn incorporation; but no Arrhenius thresholds for instability were given. |

The paper states that thicker Ge layers and relaxation allow incorporation of more Sn (more relaxation => more Sn accepted), and strain changes are supported by Raman peak shifts (GeSn mode shifting lower wavenumbers with Sn/As incorporation). Strain relaxation is linked to altered Sn incorporation and crystallite orientation. |

Oxygen at surfaces during low-vacuum anneal leads to oxidation (GeOx/GeO2) at/near surfaces and vacancies being filled by oxygen, affecting optical gaps and presumably defect chemistry. The paper also reports ‘free Sn clusters’ near surface/interface in one configuration implied by Raman and electrical behavior. |

No experimental evidence supporting vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion or Sn–vacancy binding is presented; vacancy effects are discussed only qualitatively in context of oxygen occupying vacancies. |

All mentions of vacancies relate to oxygen/vacancy filling (GeOx formation) rather than quantified vacancy-mediated diffusion of Sn. |

metadata.title: Structural changes in Ge1-xSnx and Si1-x-yGeySnx thin films on SOI substrates treated by pulse laser annealing
metadata.abstract: Ge1-xSnx and Si1-x-yGeySnx alloys are promising materials for future opto- and nanoelectronics applications. These alloys enable effective band-gap engineering, broad adjustability of their lattice parameter, exhibit much higher carrier mobility than pure Si, and are compatible with the CMOS technology. Unfortunately, the equilibrium solid solubility of Sn in Si1-xGex is less than 1% and the pseudomorphic growth of Si1-x-yGeySnx on Ge or Si can cause in-plane compressive strain in the grown layer, degrading the superior properties of these alloys. Therefore, post-growth strain engineering by ultrafast non-equilibrium thermal treatments like pulse laser annealing (PLA) is needed to improve the layer quality. In this article, Ge0.94Sn0.06 and Si0.14Ge0.8Sn0.06 thin films grown on silicon-on-insulator substrates by molecular beam epitaxy were post growth thermally treated by PLA. The material is analyzed before and after the thermal treatments by transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD), Rutherford backscattering spectrometry, secondary ion mass spectrometry, and Hall effect measurements. It is shown that after annealing, the material is single-crystalline with improved crystallinity than the as-grown layer. This is reflected in a significantly increased XRD reflection intensity, well-ordered atomic pillars, and increased active carrier concentrations up to 4x1019 cm-3.

Quantitative substitutionality (Sn/Sb on Ge sites) from RBS-channeling: as-grown ξ_Sn/Sb,Ge = 0%; after PLA: ξ = 59.6% (0.15 J cm^-2), 66.4% (0.18 J cm^-2), 70.7% (0.20 J cm^-2). | evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding | No direct or indirect evidence for Sn–vacancy binding is reported in this paper. The authors do not present PAS, DFT, or binding-energy estimates for Sn–V complexes, nor do they invoke Sn–V binding to explain observed Sn behavior. |

| vacancy_concentration_or_generation | No quantitative vacancy concentrations, formation energies, or vacancy-generation rates are reported. | sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim | The paper does not claim or demonstrate a specific atomic-scale Sn diffusion mechanism (no explicit vacancy-mediated / interstitial / interstitialcy model invoked). metadata.title: Monolithic infrared silicon photonics: The rise of (Si)GeSn semiconductors
metadata.abstract: (Si)GeSn semiconductors are finally coming of age after a long gestation period. The demonstration of device-quality epi-layers and quantum-engineered heterostructures has meant that tunable all-group IV Si-integrated infrared photonics is now a real possibility. Notwithstanding the recent exciting developments in (Si)GeSn materials and devices, this family of semiconductors is still facing serious limitations that need to be addressed to enable reliable and scalable applications. The main outstanding challenges include the difficulty to grow high-crystalline quality layers and heterostructures at the desired content and lattice strain, preserve the material integrity during growth and throughout device processing steps, and control doping and defect density. Other challenges are related to the lack of optimized device designs and predictive theoretical models to evaluate and simulate the fundamental properties and performance of (Si)GeSn layers and heterostructures. This Perspective highlights key strategies to circumvent these hurdles and hopefully bring this material system to maturity to create far-reaching opportunities for Si-compatible infrared photodetectors, sensors, and emitters for applications in free-space communication, infrared harvesting, biological and chemical sensing, and thermal imaging.

metadata.title: The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers
metadata.abstract: We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. We investigated strained and partially relaxed epi-layers with Sn content in the 5 at. %-12 at. % range. In relaxed samples, we observe a further strain relaxation followed by a sudden Sn segregation, resulting in the separation of a β-Sn phase. In pseudomorphic samples, a slower segregation process progressively leads to the accumulation of Sn at the surface only. The different behaviors are explained by the role of dislocations in the Sn diffusion process. The positive impact of annealing on optical emission is also discussed.We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. We investigated strained and partially relaxed epi-layers with Sn content in the 5 at. %-12 at. % range. In relaxed samples, we observe a further strain relaxation followed by a sudden Sn segregation, resulting in the separation of a β-Sn phase. In pseudomorphic samples, a slower segregation process progressively leads to the accumulation of Sn at the surface only. The different behaviors are explained by the role of dislocations in the Sn diffusion process. The positive impact of annealing on optical emission is also discussed.

| measurement_methods | In situ high-resolution XRD (ω-2θ, asymmetric reflections), grazing-incidence XRD, TEM/STEM cross-sectional imaging, EDX line scans (STEM-EDX), Rutherford backscattering spectrometry (RBS) cited for composition agreement, micro-photoluminescence (μ-PL). |
| evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding | Indirect/interpretive: authors state that Sn diffusivity in dislocated layers is enhanced by two-to-three orders of magnitude compared to bulk (citing Ref. 20) and that this enhanced diffusion occurs 'through the mono-vacancy diffusion dynamics' (citing Ref. 21). They also argue that high point-defect (vacancy) densities from low-temperature growth can evolve into vacancy clusters that act as seeds for non-substitutional β‑Sn formation (citing Ref. 12 and Ref. 18). No direct experimental measurement of Sn–vacancy binding is provided in this paper. |
| sn_vacancy_binding_energy | None |

| sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim | Primary claim: vacancy-mediated (mono-vacancy) diffusion enhanced along/dislocation-associated 'pipe' diffusion pathways (TD/MD networks) accelerates Sn transport; evidence: (i) correlation between presence of pre-existing dislocations in partially relaxed films and rapid segregation/β‑Sn formation at interface and around MD cores (TEM/EDX); (ii) pseudomorphic films lacking dislocations show only surface segregation and slower process; (iii) literature-cited orders-of-magnitude diffusivity enhancement attributed to dislocations and vacancy-mediated dynamics. Authors also mention occupation of interstitial sites by Sn near dislocation cores enabling β‑Sn formation (local interstitial accommodation). |
| sn_diffusion_coefficients | No direct diffusion coefficients reported for Sn in these films. Paper cites literature statement that Sn diffusivity in dislocated layers is enhanced by ~2–3 orders of magnitude relative to bulk (citation only); no numerical D(T) values are given in this work. |

Analysis used linear interpolation between α-Sn and Ge lattice parameters to extract composition, and a simple CTE analysis assuming temperature-independent relaxation R and Sn content x as a probe of relaxation/segregation onset; no DFT, KMC, rate-equation or CALPHAD modeling presented. |

| temperature_thresholds_for_instability | Critical segregation temperature T_C(x) reported to decrease with increasing Sn content. Pseudomorphic films (no MD/TD) do not show plastic relaxation prior to segregation and instead exhibit progressive Sn accumulation at the surface only. Authors explicitly link dislocation cores as nucleation/accumulation sites for Sn clusters due to locally loose bonding enabling interstitial occupation and β‑Sn nucleation. |

The Ge/Si virtual-substrate interdiffusion and buffer strain state also influence behaviors discussed in text. |

metadata.title: Free-running Sn precipitates: an efficient phase separation mechanism for metastable Ge1−xSnx epilayers

tldr.text: Time-resolved in-situ annealing experiments in a scanning electron microscope reveal the crucial role of liquid Sn precipitates in this phase separation process that makes phase separation of metastable GeSn layers particularly efficient at rather low temperatures.

metadata.abstract: The revival of interest in Ge1−xSnx alloys with x ≥ 10% is mainly owed to the recent demonstration of optical gain in this group-IV heterosystem. Yet, Ge and Sn are immiscible over about 98% of the composition range, which renders epilayers based on this material system inherently metastable. Here, we address the temperature stability of pseudomorphic Ge1−xSnx films grown by molecular beam epitaxy. Both the growth temperature dependence and the influence of post-growth annealing steps were investigated. In either case we observe that the decomposition of epilayers with Sn concentrations of around 10% sets in above ≈230 °C, the eutectic temperature of the Ge/Sn system. Time-resolved in-situ annealing experiments in a scanning electron microscope reveal the crucial role of liquid Sn precipitates in this phase separation process. Driven by a gradient of the chemical potential, the Sn droplets move on the surface along preferential crystallographic directions, thereby taking up Sn and Ge from the strained Ge1−xSnx layer. While Sn-uptake increases the volume of the melt, single-crystalline Ge becomes re-deposited by a liquid-phase epitaxial process at the trailing edge of the droplet. This process makes phase separation of metastable GeSn layers particularly efficient at rather low temperatures.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Droplet-mediated LPE phase separation |
| name_full | Free-running liquid Sn droplet mediated liquid-phase-epitaxy (LPE) phase separation |
| brief_description | Experimentally observed mechanism in uncapped MBE-grown Ge0.9Sn0.1 films where liquid Sn droplets form above the Ge–Sn eutectic and migrate across the surface, dissolving Ge1-xSnx at the leading edge and re-depositing nearly pure Ge at the trailing edge, producing β-Sn precipitates and Ge trails (LPE-like directional transport). |
| citation_title | Free-running Sn precipitates: an efficient phase separation mechanism for metastable Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$ epilayers |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_system | Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$, primarily Ge$_{0.9}$Sn$_{0.1}$ (x = 10%), also reference data for 4.9% ≤ x ≤ 14.5% |
| growth_method_and_structure | Molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) on commercial Ge(001) substrates; typical epilayer thickness d = 30 nm (Series A) or 50–100 nm (Series B–D); films grown fully coherent / pseudomorphic and compressively strained prior to decomposition; 50 nm GeSn films (Series B–D) on a 50 nm (or 50 nm Ge buffer then Ge substrate) structure as described in Table S1. |
| annealing_conditions | In-situ anneals in MBE: 15 min at T_A = 200–350°C (Series C); ex-situ real-time anneals in SEM: experiments near 250°C ±25°C (Videos V1–V3) and at 350°C ±25°C (V4); Series D real-time SEM anneals at ≥230°C; video time scales: individual sequences covering 9–28 min (frame cadence ~20–26 s). No data in the 400–700°C range in this paper. |
| capping_or_surface_treatment | All experiments in this paper performed on uncapped films (transfer from MBE to SEM in <5 min ambient to minimize surface reactions). Authors discuss capping conceptually but did not apply caps in this study. |
| stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn | Above the Ge–Sn eutectic (~231°C) metastable Ge0.9Sn0.1 films decompose into mobile liquid Sn droplets (which solidify into β-Sn after cool-down) and re-deposited crystalline Ge with negligible Sn (EDXS/TEM: trail region x ≤ 1%). Large droplets can penetrate the full film thickness down to the Ge buffer/film interface. Estimated melt Ge content during movement >11% (supersaturated) although equilibrium solubility in this T window is 2–3%; morphological outcomes include trails with {001}, {105}, {113} facets, trenches ~60 nm confining trails, surface roughening, and loss of pendellösung fringes in XRD indicating loss of homogeneous strained GeSn layer. |
| measurement_methods | X-ray diffraction (rocking curves), Rutherford backscattering (RBS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with inLens and SE2 detectors (real-time imaging), atomic force microscopy (AFM), transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM, STEM-EDXS), focused ion beam (FIB) lamella preparation. |
| evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding | No direct experimental evidence for Sn–vacancy binding is provided. The paper notes that point defects may play a role for solid-state Sn diffusion in low-temperature MBE material, but supplies no measurements or binding-energy data. |
| sn_vacancy_binding_energy | None |
| vacancy_concentration_or_generation | Not quantified. The authors suggest that low-temperature MBE growth may produce a higher density of point defects that could influence solid-state Sn diffusion, but no vacancy concentrations or formation energies are reported. |
| sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim | Primary mechanism observed: liquid-mediated transport (liquid Sn droplets dissolving GeSn and re-depositing Ge — a coupled LPE feeding/growth process). The authors contrast this with solid-state diffusion mechanisms (e.g., vacancy-mediated) and argue the droplet/LPE process dominates above the eutectic; they mention solid-state (vacancy-mediated) diffusion may be relevant in low-temperature MBE material but present no direct evidence for it in this work. |
| sn_diffusion_coefficients | None reported. No numerical diffusion coefficients (D) or diffusion lengths for Sn in Ge/GeSn are given in this paper. |
| activation_energies_diffusion_or_reaction | No activation energies for diffusion, segregation, or precipitation are reported in this work. |
| models_or_simulations_used | Thermodynamic, phenomenological LPE-based model: Gibbs free-energy expressions for epitaxial Ge growth at trailing edge (ΔG^Ge = (μ_s^Ge − μ_l) + Δγ_ls^Ge < 0) and for dissolution at leading edge including strain and interface terms (ΔG^{GeSn} expression with μ_s^{GeSn}, Δγ_ls^{GeSn}, E_ls, γ_ss). Supplementary Material S7 develops decomposition thermodynamics including ΔG^{Ge+Sn(l)} = ΔG_i^{Ge} − ΔH_{mix}^{GeSn}. No atomistic DFT or kinetic Monte Carlo simulations presented. |
| capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion | Conceptual: authors state (i) capping of GeSn epilayers is expected to affect Sn diffusion in the solid phase and thus delay formation of sufficiently large Sn precipitates needed to initiate the droplet-mediated transformation; (ii) CVD growth with hydrogen termination likely suppresses surface segregation of Sn, reducing initial surface Sn that would form molten droplets, and far-from-equilibrium CVD conditions reduce point-defect densities that may assist solid-state Sn diffusion. These are suggestions/commentary; no experimental capping data in this work. |
| comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped | No experimental capped-versus-uncapped comparison performed in this paper. The authors only report uncapped-film results (rapid decomposition above eutectic) and cite literature (Ref. 9 and others) indicating that CVD-grown/hydrogen-terminated materials can delay precipitation to higher temperatures (e.g., suppression up to ≥390°C in cited CVD work), but do not provide side-by-side data. |
| temperature_thresholds_for_instability | Decomposition/phase separation observed to set in above ≈230°C (the Ge–Sn eutectic T_EC ≈ 231°C). Growth at T_G > 230°C produced phase separation during MBE growth (samples grown at 250–300°C show β-Sn droplets and trails). In-situ anneal: stable at 200°C; at T_A ≥ 250°C (videos at 250±25°C) droplets appear and move; at 350°C droplet density increases and transformation is very efficient. No data for 400–700°C. |
| role_of_strain_and_relaxation | Strain is an important driving term in the thermodynamic model for dissolution: strain energy terms (E_ls) and solid-solid interface energy (γ_ss) enter ΔG^{GeSn} making dissolution of the strained GeSn layer into the melt favorable; trails behind droplets are virtually strain-free Ge (x ≤ 1%). The metastability of substitutional Sn (x = 10%) in strained diamond lattice is a precondition for the observed phase separation; relaxation/defects at higher Sn contents (>~14%) reduce film quality. |
| role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces | Critical: droplets must contact both an intact GeSn region and a corrugated trail region to move. The liquid–solid interfaces at droplet leading/trailing edges control dissolution (leading) and epitaxial re-deposition (trailing). Large droplets often penetrate to the Ge buffer/film interface; after cool-down droplets solidify as β-Sn and are surrounded by a Ge 'collar' from precipitation of dissolved Ge. Surface segregation is the source of initial molten Sn and is implicated in initiation of droplets. |
| counterevidence_or_alternative_explanations | Authors explicitly argue that the observed rapid, directional phase separation is not typical solid-state precipitation driven by vacancy-mediated or slow bulk diffusion, but rather governed by liquid droplet-mediated LPE; they note that some literature reports solid-state Sn precipitation and trails, but their in-situ SEM/TEM observations show mobile liquid droplets as the efficient mechanism in their samples. They acknowledge that solid-state diffusion (possibly vacancy-mediated) might be relevant in other materials/conditions (e.g., low-T MBE point-defect rich films) but provide no direct support. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Main text: Fig.1 (XRD rocking curves), Fig.2 (SEM/AFM of droplets and trails), Fig.3 (TEM/EDXS composition & FFT showing trail nearly pure Ge), Fig.4 (cross-sectional image and schematic). Supplementary: Table S1 (growth/anneal parameters), Figs. S3 (cross-section TEM of β-Sn precipitate), S4 (AFM of trail facets), S5 (SEM video start frames / V1–V4 descriptions), Supplementary Material S7 (thermodynamic model). |

metadata.title: Source/Drain Materials for Ge nMOS Devices: Phosphorus Activation in Epitaxial Si, Ge, Ge1−x Sn x and Si y Ge1−x−y Sn x

journal.name: ECS Journal of Solid State Science and Technology

metadata.abstract: This paper benchmarks various epitaxial growth schemes based on n-type group-IV materials as viable source/drain candidates for Ge nMOS devices. Si:P grown at low temperature on Ge, gives an active carrier concentration as high as 3.5 x 1020 cm-3 and a contact resistivity down to 7.5 x10-9 Ω.cm2. However, Si:P growth is highly defective due to large lattice mismatch between Si and Ge. Within the material stacks assessed, one option for Ge nMOS source/drain stressors would be to stack Si:P, deposited at contact level, on top of a selectively grown n-SiyGe1-x-ySnx at source/drain level, in line with the concept of Si passivation of n-Ge surfaces to achieve low contact resistivities as reported in literature [K. Martens et al. Appl. Phys. Lett., 98, 013504 (2011)]. The saturation in active carrier concentration with increasing P (or As)-doping is the major bottleneck in achieving low contact resistivities for as-grown Ge or SiyGe1-x-ySnx. We focus on understanding various dopant deactivation mechanisms in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx alloys. First principles simulation results suggest that P deactivation in Ge and Ge1-xSnx can be explained both by P-clustering and donor-vacancy complexes. Positron annihilation spectroscopy analysis, suggests that dopant deactivation in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx is primarily due to the formation of Pn-V and SnmPn-V clusters.

| annealing_conditions | This paper did not perform dedicated high-temperature Sn anneals; post-epi processing for CTLM included dielectric deposition up to 400 °C (maximum reported in-process thermal budget). Literature cited (Refs. 31,32 in paper) reports undoped Ge1-xSnx (Sn ≤ 6 at%) stable up to 500 °C for anneals up to 30 min. Practically, Sn alloying (at studied low x) does not increase P activation; PAS shows Sn is present around mono-vacancies (mixed Sn_pP_n-V) but does not prevent vacancy-mediated P deactivation. No evidence in this work for Sn segregation, β‑Sn precipitation, or large-scale Sn loss after the mild processing used; no quantitative substitutional fraction for Sn reported. |

| sn_vacancy_binding_energy | None |
| vacancy_concentration_or_generation | No absolute vacancy concentrations reported. PAS shows mono-vacancy sized open-volume defects are the dominant positron traps. Experimental thresholds from PAS: for P doping 3.2×10^19–6×10^19 cm^-3, mono-vacancies are decorated by at least 2 P atoms; for P > 9×10^19 cm^-3, at least 3 P atoms decorate vacancies. For the Ge1-xSnx sample with highest P (1.5×10^20 cm^-3) PAS indicates at least one Sn atom around some mono-vacancies. Vacancies are associated with growth/incorporation (as-grown films), not implantation. |
| sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim | The paper discusses the hypothesis (motivation) that Sn could trap vacancies to reduce vacancy-mediated P deactivation (i.e., vacancy-mediated mechanisms were considered), but the combined DFT and PAS results argue against effective Sn vacancy trapping. The paper does not present direct measurements of Sn diffusion mechanisms (no diffusivities or mechanism-resolved experiments); it therefore does not provide affirmative support for vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion in these films. |
| sn_diffusion_coefficients | None |
| activation_energies_diffusion_or_reaction | None |
| models_or_simulations_used | DFT atomistic energetics: VASP PAW calculations in 216-atom Ge supercells; both GGA/PBE and HSE06 functionals used; formation enthalpy (ΔH_f) calculations for P_n, Sn_n, P_n-V, Sn_n-V and mixed Sn_nP_n-V complexes. Positron annihilation modeling using two-component DFT (TCDFT) within local-density approximation to compute Doppler spectra; no kinetic models or diffusion simulations were used. |
| capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion | This work did not present experiments using caps to affect Sn–V behavior. It does note that Sn inward relaxation around vacancies reduces open-volume size and can suppress positron trapping. No claim that capping (oxide, Si, SiO2, Al2O3 etc.) alters Sn–V binding or Sn stability is presented. |
| comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped | None |
| temperature_thresholds_for_instability | No direct anneal-induced Sn instability observed in this work; the paper cites literature that undoped Ge1-xSnx (Sn up to 6 at%, thickness ~40 nm) is thermally stable up to 500 °C for anneals up to 30 min with 'no evident changes in surface morphology, lattice parameter and layer composition' (Refs. 31,32). The authors' CTLM post-processing maximum temperature was 400 °C and did not report Sn decomposition or segregation at that process step. |
| role_of_strain_and_relaxation | Sn alloying introduces compressive strain (undesirable for n‑Ge FinFETs). For Sn atoms near vacancies, DFT and PAS show inward atomic relaxation of Sn toward the vacancy, effectively reducing the open-volume size and altering positron trapping signatures. Strain/elastic effects also explain Sn–Sn configurational energetics (elastic origin of local minima for certain neighbor separations). |
| role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces | The paper discusses possible instabilities in layer composition and strain relaxation induced during post-epi CTLM processing (interface-related), but does not provide direct evidence of Sn segregation to surfaces or interfaces in their experiments. PAS signatures implicate Sn at first-nearest-neighbor sites around bulk vacancies rather than implying surface pile-up. |
| counterevidence_or_alternative_explanations | Although the initial idea was that Sn could trap vacancies and improve P activation, DFT formation enthalpies and PAS experiments show P_n‑V complexes are energetically preferred and that Sn does not significantly increase active carrier concentration; thus vacancy-attraction by P (not Sn) explains dopant deactivation. Also inward relaxation of Sn reduces apparent positron trapping, complicating simple interpretations that Sn 'binds' vacancies strongly. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Fig. 11 (formation enthalpies ΔH_f for P_n-V, Sn_n-V, Sn_nP_n-V complexes), Fig. 13 (DOBS and CDOBS experimental and calculated momentum distributions showing P_n-V and Sn_pP_n-V signatures), Fig. 10 (Sn–Sn configurational energetics), Table I (compositions and processing conditions for Ge and GeSn layers). |

The PAS data thus provides experimental evidence that Sn atoms can occupy sites adjacent to vacancies, but does not quantify binding energies. |
| sn_vacancy_binding_energy | None |
| vacancy_concentration_or_generation | No absolute vacancy concentrations reported. PAS indicates mono-vacancy sized open-volume defects dominate annihilation signal. Experimental PAS-derived compositional-in-defect thresholds: P_n-V complexes with n≥2 for P ≈3.2×10^19–6×10^19 cm^-3, and n≥3 for P >9×10^19 cm^-3. For highest P (≈1.5×10^20 cm^-3) in Ge1-xSnx sample, at least one Sn atom is present around some vacancies. |
| sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim | PAS measurements do not provide direct diffusion mechanisms. The observed Sn in vacancy environments implies Sn can occupy near-vacancy sites during growth/incorporation, but paper does not claim vacancy-mediated bulk Sn diffusion during anneal. |
| sn_diffusion_coefficients | None |
| activation_energies_diffusion_or_reaction | None |
| models_or_simulations_used | Comparison of experimental CDOBS spectra to calculated momentum distributions for modeled single-defect types (P1-V, P2-V, Sn_pP_n-V, etc.) using TCDFT and periodic supercell calculations. |
| capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion | Not studied experimentally with PAS in this work; samples were uncapped. The paper does note (separately) processing stacks that include Si:P liners for contact resistivity but these were not used to study vacancy/Sn behavior. |
| comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped | None |
| temperature_thresholds_for_instability | Not reported from PAS experiments (performed on as-grown material). See paper's citation of literature indicating Ge1-xSnx (Sn ≤6 at%) films 40 nm thick are stable up to 500 °C / 30 min (Refs. 31,32). |
| role_of_strain_and_relaxation | PAS analysis and DFT indicate Sn atoms relax inward around vacancies whereas P relaxes outward; these relaxation directions alter the apparent open-volume size and positron trapping strength (inward Sn relaxation reduces open-volume and positron trapping). |
| role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces | PAS depth profiling distinguishes signal from top epi layer (0.5–5 keV positron energy) versus Ge-VS and substrate; signatures attributed to vacancy decoration occur in top epi layers. No specific evidence of interface-driven Sn pile-up or surface segregation during processing in these measurements. |

metadata.title: Thermally activated diffusion and lattice relaxation in (Si)GeSn materials
metadata.abstract: Germanium-Tin (GeSn) alloys have emerged as a promising material for future optoelectronics, energy harvesting and nanoelectronics owing to their direct bandgap and compatibility with existing Si-based electronics. Yet, their metastability poses significant challenges calling for in-depth investigations of their thermal behavior. With this perspective, this work addresses the interdiffusion processes throughout thermal annealing of pseudomorphic GeSn binary and SiGeSn ternary alloys. In both systems, the initially pseudomorphic layers are relaxed upon annealing exclusively via thermally induced diffusional mass transfer of Sn. Systematic post-growth annealing experiments reveal enhanced Sn and Si diffusion regimes that manifest at temperatures below 600°C. The amplified low-temperature diffusion and the observation of only subtle differences between binary and ternary hint at the unique metastability of the Si-Ge-Sn material system as the most important driving force for phase separation.

content.title: Sn diffusion and stability in pseudomorphic Ge1-xSnx (Ge0.914Sn0.086 / Ge0.94Sn0.06)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | GeSn_pseudo_diffusion |
| name_full | Sn diffusion and stability in pseudomorphic Ge1-xSnx (Ge0.914Sn0.086 / Ge0.94Sn0.06) |
| brief_description | Experimental study of thermally activated Sn interdiffusion and lattice relaxation in coherently grown GeSn thin films showing two diffusion regimes (low-T enhanced and high-T conventional vacancy-mediated) and measurable Sn loss/segregation depending on capping and relaxation state. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_system | Ge0.914Sn0.086 (RSM/SIMS experiments); Ge0.94Sn0.06 (diffusion experiments, 30 nm layer) |
| growth_method_and_structure | Reduced-pressure CVD (AIXTRON Tricent, reactive gas precursors Ge2H6 and SnCl4); pseudomorphic (coherently strained) thin films grown on Ge-buffered Si(001) wafers; film thicknesses: 30 nm (diffusion samples), other samples <50 nm; Ge virtual substrate / Ge buffer with low threading dislocation density (<1E7 cm^-2). |
| annealing_conditions | Rapid thermal processing (Mattson Helios RTP) in N2 ambient; temperature range studied 350–850 °C; times 3–30 min. Specific reported conditions: 10 min @ 500 °C (RSM shift noted), 10 min @ 600 °C (SIMS: ~40 nm Sn penetration into Ge buffer), experiments focusing on 500–800 °C for diffusion (no distinct effect <500 °C). Low-temperature enhanced diffusion regime defined below ~650 °C; high-temperature regime above ~650–700 °C. |
| capping_or_surface_treatment | Both diffusion-dedicated samples were in-situ capped with Ge: Ge/GeSn/Ge structure — Ge cap 300 nm for GeSn samples (grown at same temperature as alloy to avoid surface influence). Some earlier samples (RSM/SIMS in Fig.1) were uncapped and showed surface segregation at >600 °C. |
| stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn | Pseudomorphic (low-TDD) layers relax elastically via Sn interdiffusion rather than by plastic relaxation; gradual Sn loss from alloy during anneals. Observations: (uncapped) surface segregation of Sn observed above ~600 °C; (capped) Sn diffuses into surrounding Ge cap/buffer rather than segregating to free surface. Quantitative: Sn atoms diffuse ~40 nm into Ge buffer for 10 min @ 600 °C (uncapped sample, Fig.1c); in capped 30 nm Ge0.94Sn0.06 sample the Sn peak concentration reduced by more than a factor of two after annealing at 600 °C for 10 min (Fig.2a). Annealing above ~700 °C reduces mean Sn content to ≈1 at.% (thermodynamic solid solubility), leading to strongly enhanced diffusion. |
| measurement_methods | High-resolution X-ray diffraction reciprocal space maps (RSM) around (224) to probe strain/coherency; Secondary Ion Mass Spectroscopy (SIMS) for Sn depth profiles; rapid thermal processing (RTP) for anneals. (Paper cites positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) and atomistic studies in literature but did not perform them here.) |
| evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding | Indirect / inferential only: authors state that vacancies are expected to attract/relax around larger Sn atoms and thereby an attractive Sn–vacancy interaction is anticipated; vacancy presence in GeSn noted citing PAS work (Ref. 42). No direct experimental Sn–V binding measurement in this paper. |
| sn_vacancy_binding_energy | None |
| vacancy_concentration_or_generation | No numeric vacancy concentrations reported. Qualitative: vacancies are expected to be present due to low-temperature epitaxy and have been directly observed in GeSn via positron annihilation in cited literature (Ref.42). The Ge buffer TDD is given as <1E7 cm^-2 (defines dislocation-related diffusion contribution upper bound). |
| sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim | Paper attributes Sn diffusion predominantly to vacancy-mediated mechanisms in the high-temperature regime (EA comparable to literature for Sn in Ge). In the low-temperature enhanced regime the authors attribute the enhancement to metastability / chemical potential gradients and strain effects that lower point-defect formation energies; vacancy mediation is still considered important but not uniquely explanatory. For partially relaxed material, dislocation-pipe diffusion (along dislocations) dominates and leads to rapid clustering/β-Sn precipitates. |
| sn_diffusion_coefficients | Diffusion coefficients extracted by fitting 1D diffusion solutions to SIMS profiles; Arrhenius plots shown (Fig.2c). Specifics: D(T) reported as Arrhenius with parameters in Table I (see activation energies and D0). Observed behavior: low-T regime (<~650 °C) shows enhanced effective diffusivity (reduced EA); high-T regime (>~650 °C) diffusivities similar to implanted-Sn-in-Ge literature. Also observed diffusion lengths: ~40 nm penetration into Ge buffer for 10 min @ 600 °C (uncapped). |
| activation_energies_diffusion_or_reaction | From Arrhenius fits (Table I) for Sn diffusion: High-T (Ge/GeSn/Ge): E_A = 3.10 ± 0.07 eV, D0 = 264 ± 220 cm^2/s; High-T (Ge/SiGeSn/Ge): E_A = 2.87 ± 0.03 eV, D0 = 12 ± 5 cm^2/s. Low-T: Ge/GeSn/Ge E_A = 1.81 ± 0.09 eV; Ge/SiGeSn/Ge E_A = 1.13 ± 0.11 eV. (Methods: Arrhenius fits to diffusion coefficients determined from 1D diffusion equation fits to SIMS profiles.) |
| models_or_simulations_used | 1D continuum diffusion modeling (solutions of the diffusion equation per Crank) to fit SIMS profiles and extract effective diffusion coefficients; Arrhenius model D = D0 exp(-E_A/k_BT) used to extract EA and D0. No DFT or atomistic simulations performed in this paper, though atomistic literature is cited for interpretation. |
| capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion | Ge caps (in-situ, thick) were used to suppress surface segregation and to probe pure interdiffusion into Ge rather than loss to free surface. With Ge cap, Sn diffuses into surrounding Ge layers and no pronounced surface segregation/precipitation is observed at temperatures where uncapped samples show surface Sn segregation (>600 °C). Authors grew the Ge caps at same temperature as alloy to minimize cap-induced effects. Proposed mechanism: cap removes free-surface sink for Sn and for point-defects (vacancy/interstitial exchange), forcing Sn to diffuse into the adjacent Ge matrix. |
| comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped | Uncapped samples (Fig.1c) show surface segregation of Sn above ~600 °C and rectangular-to-smeared profiles with ~40 nm penetration into Ge buffer for 10 min @ 600 °C. In-capped diffusion samples (Ge/GeSn/Ge in Fig.2a) showed suppression of surface segregation and allowed measurement of interdiffusion into Ge; in capped samples Sn peak concentration decreased by >2× after 10 min @ 600 °C. No quantitative comparison table provided; observations are qualitative/semiquantitative. |
| temperature_thresholds_for_instability | Surface segregation observed in uncapped films above ~600 °C (10 min). Strongly enhanced diffusion and drop of mean Sn to ≈1 at.% occurs upon annealing above ~700 °C. Low-T enhanced diffusion regime exists below ~650 °C (reduced activation energies reported). |
| role_of_strain_and_relaxation | All diffusion experiments were on coherently strained (compressive) films with strain ≈ -0.90% (Ge0.94Sn0.06) and -0.89% (SiGeSn). Authors argue that in low-TDD coherently strained layers, relaxation occurs elastically via Sn diffusion rather than by dislocation formation. In partly relaxed films, pre-existing dislocations enable rapid strain relaxation via dislocation multiplication/glide and serve as fast diffusion pathways (pipe diffusion), promoting Sn clustering and β-Sn precipitates. |
| role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces | Free surface acts as sink for Sn causing surface segregation/precipitation in uncapped samples above ~600 °C. Ge cap and Ge buffer act as adjacent Ge matrix that receives diffusing Sn (cap/buffer as sink), modifying where Sn accumulates. Interfaces with dislocations (in partially relaxed material) act as fast diffusion channels and clustering initiation sites. |
| counterevidence_or_alternative_explanations | Authors note that while vacancy-mediated diffusion is consistent with high-T activation energies, the marked reduction of activation energy in low-T regime cannot be solely explained by strain-driven vacancy formation; they attribute major role to metastability / chemical potential gradients (low Sn solubility) and note possible differences in vacancy formation/migration between GeSn and SiGeSn (not directly measured). For partially relaxed layers, dislocation-mediated diffusion (pipe diffusion) explains abrupt phase separation better than vacancy-mediated bulk diffusion. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Figure 1 (RSM and SIMS of Ge0.914Sn0.086, showing strain and surface segregation behavior), Figure 2a and 2c (Sn SIMS diffusion profiles for Ge0.94Sn0.06 and Arrhenius plot of D), Table I (activation energies and D0 for Sn diffusion high/low T). |

| sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim | Same as binary: vacancy-mediated diffusion considered main mechanism in high-T regime (EA similar to impurity diffusion in Ge). In low-T regime vacancy formation energies possibly lowered by strain/metastability causing enhanced vacancy-mediated diffusion; additionally Si diffusion (vacancy-mediated) may interact with Sn diffusion. |
| sn_diffusion_coefficients | Extracted via 1D diffusion fits and Arrhenius analysis. Activation energies and D0 in Table I: High-T (Ge/SiGeSn/Ge) Sn E_A = 2.87 ± 0.03 eV, D0 = 12 ± 5 cm^2/s. | capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion | Ge capping (150 nm) suppresses surface segregation and forces Sn to interdiffuse into Ge cap/buffer; cap grown in-situ at same temperature to minimize additional surface effects. metadata.title: Vacancy complexes in nonequilibrium germanium-tin semiconductors
metadata.abstract: Understanding the nature and behavior of vacancy-like defects in epitaxial GeSn metastable alloys is crucial to elucidate the structural and optoelectronic properties of these emerging semiconductors. The formation of vacancies and their complexes is expected to be promoted by the relatively low substrate temperature required for the epitaxial growth of GeSn layers with Sn contents significantly above the equilibrium solubility of 1 at.%. These defects can impact both the microstructure and charge carrier lifetime. Herein, to identify the vacancy-related complexes and probe their evolution as a function of Sn content, depth-profiled pulsed low-energy positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy and Doppler broadening spectroscopy were combined to investigate GeSn epitaxial layers with Sn content in the 6.5-13.0 at.% range. The samples were grown by chemical vapor deposition method at temperatures between 300 and 330 °C. Regardless of the Sn content, all GeSn samples showed the same depth-dependent increase in the positron annihilation line broadening parameters, which confirmed the presence of open volume defects. The measured average positron lifetimes were the highest (380-395 ps) in the region near the surface and monotonically decrease across the analyzed thickness, but remain above 350 ps. All GeSn layers exhibit lifetimes that are 85 to 110 ps higher than the Ge reference layers. Surprisingly, these lifetimes were found to decrease as Sn content increases in GeSn layers. These measurements indicate that divacancies are the dominant defect in the as-grown GeSn layers. However, their corresponding lifetime was found to be shorter than in epitaxial Ge thus suggesting that the presence of Sn may alter the structure of divacancies. Additionally, GeSn layers were found to also contain a small fraction of vacancy clusters, which become less important as Sn content increases.

content.text:
