| name_short | Divacancies (GeSn) |
| name_full | Divacancy defects in Ge1-xSnx epitaxial layers |
| brief_description | Depth-profiled positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) identifies divacancies as the dominant open-volume defect in CVD-grown Ge1-xSnx (x = 0.065–0.13) films; the divacancy-related positron lifetime component τ1 ≈ 335 ps (constant vs composition) with relative intensity I1 increasing from ~65% to ~83% as Sn increases. |
| citation_title | Vacancy complexes in nonequilibrium germanium-tin semiconductors |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_system | Ge1-xSnx (GeSn) epitaxial layers with Sn content 6.5–13.0 at.% (reported as 6.5, 9, 11, 13 at.%) |
| growth_method_and_structure | Low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (CVD). Structure: Si(100) substrate; 500–700 nm Ge virtual substrate (Ge-VS) grown at 450 °C (with thermal cyclic annealing >800 °C), then 500–700 nm GeSn grown at fixed temperature in 300–330 °C range; a ~60 nm GeSn buffer used for some samples. Residual in-plane compressive strain reported as < -0.3%. |
| annealing_conditions | No deliberate post-growth anneals in the 400–700 °C range were performed on the GeSn layers in this study; the Ge virtual substrate experienced thermal cyclic annealing >800 °C during its preparation. Growth conducted below 400 °C to avoid segregation. |
| capping_or_surface_treatment | uncapped (no cap/passivation reported for the GeSn films) |
| stability_outcomes_substitutional_sn | No experimental observation of Sn surface segregation, β-Sn precipitation, or Sn-rich precipitates reported after growth or anneal in this work. Sn is stated to occupy substitutional sites (from literature) and to be randomly distributed; increasing Sn content correlates with higher fraction of divacancies (I1) and a decreased fraction of larger vacancy clusters, interpreted as Sn reducing vacancy clustering rather than driving Sn loss or precipitation under the reported conditions. |
| measurement_methods | Depth-profiled pulsed positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS/PAS), variable-energy Doppler broadening (S-parameter), X-ray diffraction (RSM, 2θ-ω), cross-sectional TEM, and references to prior structural/chemical studies (literature). |
| evidence_for_sn_vacancy_binding | Indirect experimental evidence in this paper: the fraction of large vacancy clusters (τ2 component) decreases as Sn content increases while the divacancy-related component (τ1 ≈ 335 ps) becomes dominant (I1 up to ~83%), suggesting Sn locally 'freezes' or stabilizes vacancies and limits their clustering. The paper also cites prior work (Refs. 37, 38) reporting an affinity of Sn to attract/trap vacancies from experiments and ab initio calculations (emission channeling and DFT), supporting Sn–vacancy interaction hypotheses. No direct measurement of Sn–V binding energy in this study. |
| sn_vacancy_binding_energy | None |
| vacancy_concentration_or_generation | No absolute vacancy concentrations reported. Relative PAS-derived metrics: average positron lifetime τ_AV = 380–395 ps near surface decreasing to ~350 ps near the Ge-VS; Ge reference bulk lifetime τ_b ≈ 224–228 ps. Decomposition: divacancy-related lifetime τ1 ≈ 335±2 ps (I1 increases from ~65% to ~83% with Sn content). Larger vacancy-cluster lifetime τ2 > 450 ps with low intensity I2 that decreases with Sn content. No numeric vacancies/cm^3 provided. |
| sn_diffusion_mechanism_claim | The paper does not directly measure Sn diffusion; it discusses literature and plausible mechanisms: Sn can trap vacancies (Sn–V complexes) and occupy bound-centered or vacancy-split configurations (literature cited), implying vacancy-mediated processes could be relevant for Sn mobility or stabilization. The authors mention high activation energies for divacancy migration (>1 eV, Ref. 35), arguing vacancy mobility (and therefore vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion) is limited under small growth-temperature changes in their experiments. |
| sn_diffusion_coefficients | None |
| activation_energies_diffusion_or_reaction | No activation energies measured for Sn diffusion/segregation in this work. The paper cites literature value/order: divacancy migration in Ge involves activation energies above 1 eV (Ref. 35). |
| models_or_simulations_used | No models/simulations performed in this paper. The authors cite prior DFT/ab initio studies (Refs. 38) and thermodynamic considerations from literature regarding Sn preference for substitutional sites and possibility to trap vacancies. |
| capping_effect_on_defects_or_diffusion | Not studied; samples were uncapped and no cap experiments were reported. Paper does not provide data on how capping would influence vacancy concentration or Sn loss during annealing. |
| comparative_results_capped_vs_uncapped | None reported. |
| temperature_thresholds_for_instability | No thresholds for Sn precipitation/segregation in the 400–700 °C range reported. The paper cites literature that Sn–divacancy complexes formed in irradiated Ge anneal out at 220 K (Ref. 39), i.e., a low-temperature anneal-out, but provides no high-temperature stability thresholds for substitutional Sn in epitaxial GeSn. |
| role_of_strain_and_relaxation | Authors note compressive in-plane strain < -0.3% across samples. They propose that the larger size of Sn relative to Ge makes Sn–vacancy pairing a plausible local stress-relief mechanism; this is invoked to explain reduced vacancy clustering as Sn increases. Dislocations near the GeSn–Ge interface are noted, but are argued not to significantly affect PAS signals under measurement conditions. |
| role_of_interfaces_and_surfaces | Depth-dependent PAS shows increased open-volume defects near the GeSn surface and a monotonic decrease toward the Ge-VS; the S-parameter increases up to ~310 nm mean depth and then decreases toward Si substrate values. The GeSn–Ge virtual substrate interface hosts dislocations, but the authors argue these do not dominate the observed PAS lifetimes. No observations of Sn pile-up at interfaces or cap/film reactions are reported. |
| counterevidence_or_alternative_explanations | The authors consider and discount a simple temperature-driven explanation for reduced vacancy cluster formation (i.e., lower growth temperature reducing mobility), arguing the 300–330 °C growth-temperature range is too narrow and that migration barriers are high (>1 eV). Thus they favor an Sn–vacancy attractive interaction explanation. They also note that monovacancies are not observed at room temperature (monovacancies pair to divacancies above ~200 K), consistent with PAS lifetimes recorded. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 (Fig.2: S-parameter vs positron energy; Fig.3: τ_AV vs depth and vs Sn content; Fig.4: lifetime decomposition for Ge-VS; Fig.5: lifetime/intensity decomposition for 13 at.% GeSn and composition dependence at 215 nm). |

paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f.displayLabel: Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation

s2Metadata.title: Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation
s2Metadata.abstract: $\text{SiGeSn}$ alloys are promising silicon-compatible semiconductors for monolithic infrared photonics. However, their metastable nature limits the thermal budgets available for post-growth device processing, and the mechanisms governing their thermal degradation remain unresolved. Here, we investigate the thermal stability of $\text{Si}_{0.08}\text{Ge}_{0.83}\text{Sn}_{0.04}$ alloys using in situ spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) during isothermal annealing at 550 {\deg}C. We show that adding an ultrathin oxide cap kinetically suppresses Sn exchange with the free surface while leaving bulk diffusion pathways largely unaffected. Uncapped films undergo phase separation after 50 min, accompanied by void formation, a 60% thickness reduction, and a 400 meV blueshift of the $E_{2}$ critical point (CP) transition, consistent with substitutional Sn depletion from the probed volume through surface segregation. In contrast, oxide-capped films exhibit a small compositional change (<1 at.% Sn) and optical shift (<20 meV) over the same period, with suppressed void formation, strain relaxation, and alloy decomposition. This surface-kinetic control additionally yields a 25-fold reduction in contact resistivity relative to annealed uncapped alloys. These results identify surface Sn transport as the dominant degradation pathway in SiGeSn and demonstrate that an ultrathin oxide cap extends the thermal stability of metastable group-IV alloys, providing a practical route toward their integration into advanced silicon photonic and electronic platforms.

paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1.displayLabel: Thermally activated diffusion and lattice relaxation in (Si)GeSn materials

s2Metadata.title: Thermally activated diffusion and lattice relaxation in (Si)GeSn materials
s2Metadata.abstract: Germanium-Tin (GeSn) alloys have emerged as a promising material for future optoelectronics, energy harvesting and nanoelectronics owing to their direct bandgap and compatibility with existing Si-based electronics. Yet, their metastability poses significant challenges calling for in-depth investigations of their thermal behavior. With this perspective, this work addresses the interdiffusion processes throughout thermal annealing of pseudomorphic GeSn binary and SiGeSn ternary alloys. In both systems, the initially pseudomorphic layers are relaxed upon annealing exclusively via thermally induced diffusional mass transfer of Sn. Systematic post-growth annealing experiments reveal enhanced Sn and Si diffusion regimes that manifest at temperatures below 600°C. The amplified low-temperature diffusion and the observation of only subtle differences between binary and ternary hint at the unique metastability of the Si-Ge-Sn material system as the most important driving force for phase separation.

paper-69932a46d534636de23ae1ff78e4eee472.displayLabel: The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers

s2Metadata.title: The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers
s2Metadata.abstract: We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. We investigated strained and partially relaxed epi-layers with Sn content in the 5 at. %-12 at. % range. In relaxed samples, we observe a further strain relaxation followed by a sudden Sn segregation, resulting in the separation of a β-Sn phase. In pseudomorphic samples, a slower segregation process progressively leads to the accumulation of Sn at the surface only. The different behaviors are explained by the role of dislocations in the Sn diffusion process. The positive impact of annealing on optical emission is also discussed.We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. We investigated strained and partially relaxed epi-layers with Sn content in the 5 at. %-12 at. % range. In relaxed samples, we observe a further strain relaxation followed by a sudden Sn segregation, resulting in the separation of a β-Sn phase. In pseudomorphic samples, a slower segregation process progressively leads to the accumulation of Sn at the surface only. The different behaviors are explained by the role of dislocations in the Sn diffusion process. The positive impact of annealing on optical emission is also discussed.

paper-050532416690efea233eb1e27bd9cd091d.displayLabel: Free-running Sn precipitates: an efficient phase separation mechanism for metastable Ge1−xSnx epilayers

s2Metadata.title: Free-running Sn precipitates: an efficient phase separation mechanism for metastable Ge1−xSnx epilayers
s2Metadata.abstract: The revival of interest in Ge1−xSnx alloys with x ≥ 10% is mainly owed to the recent demonstration of optical gain in this group-IV heterosystem. Yet, Ge and Sn are immiscible over about 98% of the composition range, which renders epilayers based on this material system inherently metastable. Here, we address the temperature stability of pseudomorphic Ge1−xSnx films grown by molecular beam epitaxy. Both the growth temperature dependence and the influence of post-growth annealing steps were investigated. In either case we observe that the decomposition of epilayers with Sn concentrations of around 10% sets in above ≈230 °C, the eutectic temperature of the Ge/Sn system. Time-resolved in-situ annealing experiments in a scanning electron microscope reveal the crucial role of liquid Sn precipitates in this phase separation process. Driven by a gradient of the chemical potential, the Sn droplets move on the surface along preferential crystallographic directions, thereby taking up Sn and Ge from the strained Ge1−xSnx layer. While Sn-uptake increases the volume of the melt, single-crystalline Ge becomes re-deposited by a liquid-phase epitaxial process at the trailing edge of the droplet. This process makes phase separation of metastable GeSn layers particularly efficient at rather low temperatures.

paper-35dd505a98166b99ccf5ae96a6952433f5.displayLabel: Structural changes in Ge1-xSnx and Si1-x-yGeySnx thin films on SOI substrates treated by pulse laser annealing

s2Metadata.title: Structural changes in Ge1-xSnx and Si1-x-yGeySnx thin films on SOI substrates treated by pulse laser annealing
s2Metadata.abstract: Ge1-xSnx and Si1-x-yGeySnx alloys are promising materials for future opto- and nanoelectronics applications. These alloys enable effective band-gap engineering, broad adjustability of their lattice parameter, exhibit much higher carrier mobility than pure Si, and are compatible with the CMOS technology. Unfortunately, the equilibrium solid solubility of Sn in Si1-xGex is less than 1% and the pseudomorphic growth of Si1-x-yGeySnx on Ge or Si can cause in-plane compressive strain in the grown layer, degrading the superior properties of these alloys. Therefore, post-growth strain engineering by ultrafast non-equilibrium thermal treatments like pulse laser annealing (PLA) is needed to improve the layer quality. In this article, Ge0.94Sn0.06 and Si0.14Ge0.8Sn0.06 thin films grown on silicon-on-insulator substrates by molecular beam epitaxy were post growth thermally treated by PLA. The material is analyzed before and after the thermal treatments by transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD), Rutherford backscattering spectrometry, secondary ion mass spectrometry, and Hall effect measurements. It is shown that after annealing, the material is single-crystalline with improved crystallinity than the as-grown layer. This is reflected in a significantly increased XRD reflection intensity, well-ordered atomic pillars, and increased active carrier concentrations up to 4x1019 cm-3.

paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae.displayLabel: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys

s2Metadata.title: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: GeSn alloys are among the most promising materials for the fabrication of high-efficiency silicon-based light sources. However, due to the tendency of Sn to segregate to the surface during growth, it is challenging to achieve a high Sn concentration while maintaining high-quality GeSn alloys. Both theoretical and experimental studies have confirmed that non-substitutional Sn defects (VSnV) are the primary driving factors in Sn surface segregation. However, there is a discrepancy between existing theoretical and experimental findings regarding the variation in VSnV concentration with total Sn concentration. To clarify this issue, we first prepared GeSn materials with varying Sn concentrations using molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and subjected them to annealing at different temperatures. Subsequently, we characterized the VSnV concentration and Sn surface segregation. The results indicate that a higher total Sn concentration and temperature lead to an increased VSnV concentration, and the proportion of VSnV relative to the total Sn concentration also increases, which is consistent with existing theoretical research. To explain these phenomena, we employed first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the effect of varying the total Sn concentration on the formation of substitutional Sn (Sns) and VSnV in GeSn alloys, while simultaneously studying the migration kinetics of Sn atoms. The results demonstrate that as the total Sn concentration increases, the formation of Sns becomes more difficult, while the formation of VSnV becomes easier, and Sn atoms exhibit enhanced migration tendencies. The analysis of binding energies and charge density distribution maps reveals that this is due to the weakening of Ge-Sn bond strength with increasing Sn concentration, whereas the binding strength of VSnV exhibits the opposite trend. These findings demonstrate excellent agreement with experimental observations. This study provides both theoretical and experimental references for GeSn material growth and VSnV defect control through a combined theoretical–experimental approach, offering significant guidance for enhancing device performance.

paper-d2af7876dbf4ce6fbc25ba658f331ccada.displayLabel: Source/Drain Materials for Ge nMOS Devices: Phosphorus Activation in Epitaxial Si, Ge, Ge1−x Sn x and Si y Ge1−x−y Sn x

s2Metadata.title: Source/Drain Materials for Ge nMOS Devices: Phosphorus Activation in Epitaxial Si, Ge, Ge1−x Sn x and Si y Ge1−x−y Sn x
s2Metadata.abstract: This paper benchmarks various epitaxial growth schemes based on n-type group-IV materials as viable source/drain candidates for Ge nMOS devices. Si:P grown at low temperature on Ge, gives an active carrier concentration as high as 3.5 x 1020 cm-3 and a contact resistivity down to 7.5 x10-9 Ω.cm2. However, Si:P growth is highly defective due to large lattice mismatch between Si and Ge. Within the material stacks assessed, one option for Ge nMOS source/drain stressors would be to stack Si:P, deposited at contact level, on top of a selectively grown n-SiyGe1-x-ySnx at source/drain level, in line with the concept of Si passivation of n-Ge surfaces to achieve low contact resistivities as reported in literature [K. Martens et al. Appl. Phys. Lett., 98, 013504 (2011)]. The saturation in active carrier concentration with increasing P (or As)-doping is the major bottleneck in achieving low contact resistivities for as-grown Ge or SiyGe1-x-ySnx. We focus on understanding various dopant deactivation mechanisms in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx alloys. First principles simulation results suggest that P deactivation in Ge and Ge1-xSnx can be explained both by P-clustering and donor-vacancy complexes. Positron annihilation spectroscopy analysis, suggests that dopant deactivation in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx is primarily due to the formation of Pn-V and SnmPn-V clusters.

content.text: A free surface lets Sn escape; oxide caps largely stop the escape; Ge caps stop surface escape but let Sn spread into nearby Ge.
**Supporting evidence:**

- At 550 °C isothermal anneal of Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04, uncapped sample shows ~50 min incubation then rapid collapse (t0 = 74.2 ± 0.5 min; collapse width 1.86 ± 0.15 min), large E2 blueshift (+423 meV), ~60% thickness loss, voids with oxygen, filamentary Sn-enriched paths, and formation of a Ge0.99Sn0.01 segregation layer; with a 3 nm SiO2 cap, compositional change <1 at.% Sn over 140 min, |ΔE2| < 20 meV, no voids, limited strain relaxation, and much lower contact resistivity degradation.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- Screening result: 5 nm Al2O3 also suppresses segregation after 550 °C / 30 min (ex situ SE), consistent with nm-scale oxide capping acting as a strong throttle of surface-mediated loss.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- In RP-CVD pseudomorphic diffusion experiments, uncapped samples show surface segregation above ~600 °C, whereas Ge/GeSn/Ge and Ge/SiGeSn/Ge sandwiches with thick in-situ Ge caps suppress surface segregation and instead exhibit Sn redistribution into cap/buffer (e.g., >2× reduction of Sn peak after 10 min @ 600 °C).  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- Thermal stability study of GeSn: relaxed (dislocated) layers show Sn-rich clusters at both free surface and GeSn/Ge interface (MD cores as sinks/fast paths), while pseudomorphic layers show Sn accumulation mainly at the surface; segregation occurs above a composition-dependent critical temperature T_C(x).  <paper entityId="paper-69932a46d534636de23ae1ff78e4eee47265ecd8" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="105474679" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Zaumseil et al., 2018</paper>

- Conceptual/literature discussion that capping or H-termination is expected to suppress surface segregation and delay precipitation/phase separation by removing the surface source/sink of Sn and reducing point-defect-assisted pathways (qualitative support for boundary-condition control).  <paper entityId="paper-050532416690efea233eb1e27bd9cd091db28159" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="25636372" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Groiss et al., 2017</paper>

- PLA studies in air show Sn out-diffusion to the surface and Sn-rich oxide formation at higher pulse energies, highlighting that surface oxidation can be an irreversible sink for Sn when present.  <paper entityId="paper-35dd505a98166b99ccf5ae96a6952433f53304e0" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="270440900" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Steuer et al., 2024</paper>
Nothing seems to change for a while, then Sn loss suddenly accelerates once a fast escape network effectively connects to the surface sink.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Uncapped SiGeSn at 550 °C shows ~50 min incubation then rapid collapse with a fitted logistic width of ~1.9 min; TEM/EDX show filamentary Sn-enriched paths and widespread voids containing oxygen in the degraded region, consistent with a sudden transition to an efficient short-circuit/sink-coupled transport mode.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- Relaxed/dislocated GeSn layers exhibit sudden segregation above a critical temperature T_C(x), with clustering at surfaces and interfaces around dislocation cores (fast paths/sinks), consistent with threshold-like onset behavior when channels become effective.  <paper entityId="paper-69932a46d534636de23ae1ff78e4eee47265ecd8" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="105474679" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Zaumseil et al., 2018</paper>

- In uncapped MBE GeSn at higher Sn, rapid surface segregation and substitutional Sn loss can appear already at 400–600 °C for 60 s anneals depending on composition, consistent with a threshold in the effective transport/instability pathway versus composition and temperature (although the detailed channel physics differs by microstructure).  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

- This connectivity interpretation is consistent with (but distinct from) the droplet-mediated rapid transformation observed above the eutectic in high-Sn MBE GeSn, where once a new fast transport state (liquid droplet) nucleates, transformation proceeds quickly after a short onset.  <paper entityId="paper-050532416690efea233eb1e27bd9cd091db28159" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="25636372" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Groiss et al., 2017</paper>

content.title: Cap-induced sink relocation and two-regime activation law

content.text: With a thick Ge cap, Sn doesn’t form surface piles; it spreads into the surrounding Ge, and the measured diffusion shows a high-T ‘normal’ regime and a low-T ‘enhanced’ regime.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Ge/GeSn/Ge and Ge/SiGeSn/Ge capped sandwiches suppress surface segregation and show two Arrhenius regimes for Sn: high-T EA = 3.10 ± 0.07 eV (Ge/GeSn/Ge) and 2.87 ± 0.03 eV (Ge/SiGeSn/Ge); low-T EA = 1.81 ± 0.09 eV (Ge/GeSn/Ge) and 1.13 ± 0.11 eV (Ge/SiGeSn/Ge).  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- In capped Ge0.94Sn0.06, the Sn peak concentration decreases by >2× after 10 min at 600 °C, indicating redistribution into adjacent Ge layers rather than surface pile-up.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- Uncapped counterparts show surface segregation above ~600 °C, demonstrating that the cap changes the boundary condition and thus where Sn accumulates (surface vs buried Ge sinks).  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_013" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- Oxide-capped SiGeSn at 550 °C maintains composition uniformity (<1 at.% Sn change) over 140 min and avoids voiding/segregation, showing that some caps can largely suppress not only surface pile-up but also catastrophic redistribution on these timescales.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_014" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- The diffusion study itself notes that the low-T enhanced regime cannot be explained by vacancy-mediated diffusion alone and invokes metastability/chemical potential gradients as major drivers (supports the ‘effective’ low-T EA interpretation).  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_015" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- H9: For Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 held at 550 °C, a continuous 3 nm SiO2 cap will suppress the near-surface substitutional Sn-loss signal relative to uncapped. The uncapped film will show a visible change after an incubation time on the order of tens of minutes (∼50 min scale), whereas the capped film will show no visible change (or a much longer incubation) over the same observation window.
- If dislocation density is increased (partially relaxed vs pseudomorphic) in uncapped films at fixed T (e.g., 550 °C), incubation time will decrease and near-surface Sn loss will accelerate; with a high-quality oxide cap, this dependence will be strongly reduced because the surface sink is throttled.
- Replacing 3 nm SiO2 with ~5 nm Al2O3 on the same SiGeSn stack will similarly suppress near-surface Sn-loss kinetics at 550 °C provided the layer is continuous and stable (consistent with the screening result).
- In Ge/GeSn/Ge sandwiches, changing the Ge cap thickness primarily changes the spatial redistribution/symmetry of the final Sn profile (sink capacity), not the existence of surface segregation; surface pile-up should remain suppressed as long as no free surface is exposed.

- A nominally continuous oxide cap with a controlled density of engineered pinholes will restore incubation-then-collapse kinetics; the incubation time will scale inversely with pinhole density and pinhole opening size (a percolation-to-sink problem).
- A cap stack that blocks Sn transport but allows efficient vacancy/interstitial exchange (e.g., via a defect-rich interlayer) could allow voiding/degradation without large net Sn loss, yielding a decoupled ‘voiding-without-Sn-depletion’ mode detectable by TEM/SE line broadening.
- Applying an oxygen-gettering interlayer below an oxide cap (e.g., ultrathin Si) could either stabilize further (suppress oxidation-assisted sink irreversibility) or destabilize (create interdiffusion-driven defect injection), producing a non-monotonic stability vs interlayer thickness.

- If a verified-continuous 3 nm oxide cap (no pinholes, no delamination) produces the same incubation time and collapse amplitude at 550 °C as an uncapped sample, then the boundary-condition/surface-sink premise is falsified for that system.
- If oxide-capped samples still develop the same Ge0.99Sn0.01 surface segregation layer and surface Sn clusters as uncapped samples without cap failure, then the proposed cap-throttled surface sink mechanism is wrong or incomplete.
- If a very-low-dislocation-density uncapped film still shows a short-incubation rapid collapse identical to a highly dislocated film, then channel connectivity via dislocations/short-circuits is not the controlling variable as proposed.

- DFT/NEB work in uncapped MBE GeSn reports very low derived activation energies (~0.83–0.93 eV) for vacancy-mediated Sn hops in VSnV-containing supercells, whereas SIMS-based interdiffusion in capped sandwiches yields much larger high-T activation energies (~2.9–3.1 eV). The present theory treats these as different ‘effective’ regimes/contexts (local hop vs macroscopic interdiffusion with vacancy formation contributions), but does not quantitatively reconcile them.  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_016" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.2">Zhou et al., 2025</paper> <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_017" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

paper-a43c2e298fb9654389ce73682a550fa534.displayLabel: Vacancy complexes in nonequilibrium germanium-tin semiconductors

s2Metadata.title: Vacancy complexes in nonequilibrium germanium-tin semiconductors
s2Metadata.abstract: Understanding the nature and behavior of vacancy-like defects in epitaxial GeSn metastable alloys is crucial to elucidate the structural and optoelectronic properties of these emerging semiconductors. The formation of vacancies and their complexes is expected to be promoted by the relatively low substrate temperature required for the epitaxial growth of GeSn layers with Sn contents significantly above the equilibrium solubility of 1 at.%. These defects can impact both the microstructure and charge carrier lifetime. Herein, to identify the vacancy-related complexes and probe their evolution as a function of Sn content, depth-profiled pulsed low-energy positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy and Doppler broadening spectroscopy were combined to investigate GeSn epitaxial layers with Sn content in the 6.5-13.0 at.% range. The samples were grown by chemical vapor deposition method at temperatures between 300 and 330 °C. Regardless of the Sn content, all GeSn samples showed the same depth-dependent increase in the positron annihilation line broadening parameters, which confirmed the presence of open volume defects. The measured average positron lifetimes were the highest (380-395 ps) in the region near the surface and monotonically decrease across the analyzed thickness, but remain above 350 ps. All GeSn layers exhibit lifetimes that are 85 to 110 ps higher than the Ge reference layers. Surprisingly, these lifetimes were found to decrease as Sn content increases in GeSn layers. These measurements indicate that divacancies are the dominant defect in the as-grown GeSn layers. However, their corresponding lifetime was found to be shorter than in epitaxial Ge thus suggesting that the presence of Sn may alter the structure of divacancies. Additionally, GeSn layers were found to also contain a small fraction of vacancy clusters, which become less important as Sn content increases.

content.title: VSnV favorability increases with total Sn concentration

content.text: More Sn in the alloy makes Sn–vacancy clustering easier and more likely.
**Supporting evidence:**

- DFT/PBE formation energies for VSnV become more negative as total Sn increases (Table 3): from −4.244 eV at 3.2% to −6.279 eV at 16.1% Sn; binding-energy trend in Fig.11 increases with Sn concentration; charge-density maps show increased electron density around VSnV with higher Sn.  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

- Experimentally (uncapped MBE GeSn), the inferred fraction of substitutional Sn converted to VSnV increases with anneal temperature and with higher initial Sn concentration, including complete loss of measurable substitutional Sn by 600 °C for the highest-Sn sample (8.6% Sn_s) after 60 s.  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

content.title: Vacancy-mediated Sn hop activation decreases with increasing Sn content (local mechanism)

content.text: Higher Sn content can make Sn-via-vacancy hops easier.
**Supporting evidence:**

- DFT/NEB: migration barrier decreases from 0.286 eV (Ge60Sn2-VSnV) to 0.179 eV (Ge55Sn7-VSnV); derived activation energies 0.927 eV to 0.832 eV for these models.  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.2">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

- O1: In Ge0.88Sn0.12, a substitutional Sn adjacent to a vacancy will be bound (positive binding) by at least 0–0.3 eV and plausibly >0.3 eV if VSnV-like stabilization dominates at this composition; the binding tendency should increase relative to lower Sn alloys.
- O2: In MD of Ge0.88Sn0.12 with vacancies at 500–700 K, observed Sn hops mediated by nearby vacancies will show an effective activation energy well below bulk Ge substitutional diffusion (2.9–3.3 eV), more consistent with the low-energy metastable/defect-assisted range (≈1.1–1.8 eV or below for local hops), depending on whether vacancy formation is implicit or fixed.
- Increasing total Sn content at fixed anneal temperature (e.g., 550–600 °C) will increase the fraction of Sn converted to non-substitutional Sn–vacancy clusters (VSnV-like) and will lower the temperature at which surface segregation features become visible in uncapped films.

- If vacancy concentrations are externally controlled (e.g., by pre-irradiation vs vacancy annihilation treatments), the same GeSn composition could switch between a ‘vacancy-sequestering’ regime (stable substitutional Sn) and a ‘vacancy-mobility’ regime (rapid Sn loss), producing hysteresis in stability vs pre-history.
- In ternary SiGeSn, repulsive Si–Sn interactions combined with Sn–vacancy clustering may create spatial anti-correlations that further lower effective barriers for Sn–vacancy complex migration compared with binary GeSn (beyond what is captured by effective Arrhenius fits).

- If direct binding-energy calculations at ~12% Sn show Sn–V is unbound (negative binding), the assumed thermodynamic tendency toward Sn–vacancy association at high Sn would be undermined.
- If varying total Sn at fixed microstructure and anneal temperature does not change the inferred non-substitutional defect fraction (contrary to the DFT+RTA trend), the proposed thermodynamic switch with x would be falsified.

- PAS/DFT on P-doped GeSn indicates Sn_n–V complexes are less favorable than P_n–V complexes, implying dopants can dominate vacancy trapping; the present theory does not explicitly incorporate dopant competition effects into stability predictions.  <paper entityId="paper-d2af7876dbf4ce6fbc25ba658f331ccada60eeb9" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="219060327" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Vohra et al., 2020</paper>

paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae.displayLabel: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys

s2Metadata.title: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: GeSn alloys are among the most promising materials for the fabrication of high-efficiency silicon-based light sources. However, due to the tendency of Sn to segregate to the surface during growth, it is challenging to achieve a high Sn concentration while maintaining high-quality GeSn alloys. Both theoretical and experimental studies have confirmed that non-substitutional Sn defects (VSnV) are the primary driving factors in Sn surface segregation. However, there is a discrepancy between existing theoretical and experimental findings regarding the variation in VSnV concentration with total Sn concentration. To clarify this issue, we first prepared GeSn materials with varying Sn concentrations using molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and subjected them to annealing at different temperatures. Subsequently, we characterized the VSnV concentration and Sn surface segregation. The results indicate that a higher total Sn concentration and temperature lead to an increased VSnV concentration, and the proportion of VSnV relative to the total Sn concentration also increases, which is consistent with existing theoretical research. To explain these phenomena, we employed first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the effect of varying the total Sn concentration on the formation of substitutional Sn (Sns) and VSnV in GeSn alloys, while simultaneously studying the migration kinetics of Sn atoms. The results demonstrate that as the total Sn concentration increases, the formation of Sns becomes more difficult, while the formation of VSnV becomes easier, and Sn atoms exhibit enhanced migration tendencies. The analysis of binding energies and charge density distribution maps reveals that this is due to the weakening of Ge-Sn bond strength with increasing Sn concentration, whereas the binding strength of VSnV exhibits the opposite trend. These findings demonstrate excellent agreement with experimental observations. This study provides both theoretical and experimental references for GeSn material growth and VSnV defect control through a combined theoretical–experimental approach, offering significant guidance for enhancing device performance.

paper-a43c2e298fb9654389ce73682a550fa534.displayLabel: Vacancy complexes in nonequilibrium germanium-tin semiconductors

s2Metadata.title: Vacancy complexes in nonequilibrium germanium-tin semiconductors
s2Metadata.abstract: Understanding the nature and behavior of vacancy-like defects in epitaxial GeSn metastable alloys is crucial to elucidate the structural and optoelectronic properties of these emerging semiconductors. The formation of vacancies and their complexes is expected to be promoted by the relatively low substrate temperature required for the epitaxial growth of GeSn layers with Sn contents significantly above the equilibrium solubility of 1 at.%. These defects can impact both the microstructure and charge carrier lifetime. Herein, to identify the vacancy-related complexes and probe their evolution as a function of Sn content, depth-profiled pulsed low-energy positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy and Doppler broadening spectroscopy were combined to investigate GeSn epitaxial layers with Sn content in the 6.5-13.0 at.% range. The samples were grown by chemical vapor deposition method at temperatures between 300 and 330 °C. Regardless of the Sn content, all GeSn samples showed the same depth-dependent increase in the positron annihilation line broadening parameters, which confirmed the presence of open volume defects. The measured average positron lifetimes were the highest (380-395 ps) in the region near the surface and monotonically decrease across the analyzed thickness, but remain above 350 ps. All GeSn layers exhibit lifetimes that are 85 to 110 ps higher than the Ge reference layers. Surprisingly, these lifetimes were found to decrease as Sn content increases in GeSn layers. These measurements indicate that divacancies are the dominant defect in the as-grown GeSn layers. However, their corresponding lifetime was found to be shorter than in epitaxial Ge thus suggesting that the presence of Sn may alter the structure of divacancies. Additionally, GeSn layers were found to also contain a small fraction of vacancy clusters, which become less important as Sn content increases.

paper-d2af7876dbf4ce6fbc25ba658f331ccada.displayLabel: Source/Drain Materials for Ge nMOS Devices: Phosphorus Activation in Epitaxial Si, Ge, Ge1−x Sn x and Si y Ge1−x−y Sn x

s2Metadata.title: Source/Drain Materials for Ge nMOS Devices: Phosphorus Activation in Epitaxial Si, Ge, Ge1−x Sn x and Si y Ge1−x−y Sn x
s2Metadata.abstract: This paper benchmarks various epitaxial growth schemes based on n-type group-IV materials as viable source/drain candidates for Ge nMOS devices. Si:P grown at low temperature on Ge, gives an active carrier concentration as high as 3.5 x 1020 cm-3 and a contact resistivity down to 7.5 x10-9 Ω.cm2. However, Si:P growth is highly defective due to large lattice mismatch between Si and Ge. Within the material stacks assessed, one option for Ge nMOS source/drain stressors would be to stack Si:P, deposited at contact level, on top of a selectively grown n-SiyGe1-x-ySnx at source/drain level, in line with the concept of Si passivation of n-Ge surfaces to achieve low contact resistivities as reported in literature [K. Martens et al. Appl. Phys. Lett., 98, 013504 (2011)]. The saturation in active carrier concentration with increasing P (or As)-doping is the major bottleneck in achieving low contact resistivities for as-grown Ge or SiyGe1-x-ySnx. We focus on understanding various dopant deactivation mechanisms in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx alloys. First principles simulation results suggest that P deactivation in Ge and Ge1-xSnx can be explained both by P-clustering and donor-vacancy complexes. Positron annihilation spectroscopy analysis, suggests that dopant deactivation in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx is primarily due to the formation of Pn-V and SnmPn-V clusters.

paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1.displayLabel: Thermally activated diffusion and lattice relaxation in (Si)GeSn materials

s2Metadata.title: Thermally activated diffusion and lattice relaxation in (Si)GeSn materials
s2Metadata.abstract: Germanium-Tin (GeSn) alloys have emerged as a promising material for future optoelectronics, energy harvesting and nanoelectronics owing to their direct bandgap and compatibility with existing Si-based electronics. Yet, their metastability poses significant challenges calling for in-depth investigations of their thermal behavior. With this perspective, this work addresses the interdiffusion processes throughout thermal annealing of pseudomorphic GeSn binary and SiGeSn ternary alloys. In both systems, the initially pseudomorphic layers are relaxed upon annealing exclusively via thermally induced diffusional mass transfer of Sn. Systematic post-growth annealing experiments reveal enhanced Sn and Si diffusion regimes that manifest at temperatures below 600°C. The amplified low-temperature diffusion and the observation of only subtle differences between binary and ternary hint at the unique metastability of the Si-Ge-Sn material system as the most important driving force for phase separation.

paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f.displayLabel: Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation

s2Metadata.title: Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation
s2Metadata.abstract: $\text{SiGeSn}$ alloys are promising silicon-compatible semiconductors for monolithic infrared photonics. However, their metastable nature limits the thermal budgets available for post-growth device processing, and the mechanisms governing their thermal degradation remain unresolved. Here, we investigate the thermal stability of $\text{Si}_{0.08}\text{Ge}_{0.83}\text{Sn}_{0.04}$ alloys using in situ spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) during isothermal annealing at 550 {\deg}C. We show that adding an ultrathin oxide cap kinetically suppresses Sn exchange with the free surface while leaving bulk diffusion pathways largely unaffected. Uncapped films undergo phase separation after 50 min, accompanied by void formation, a 60% thickness reduction, and a 400 meV blueshift of the $E_{2}$ critical point (CP) transition, consistent with substitutional Sn depletion from the probed volume through surface segregation. In contrast, oxide-capped films exhibit a small compositional change (<1 at.% Sn) and optical shift (<20 meV) over the same period, with suppressed void formation, strain relaxation, and alloy decomposition. This surface-kinetic control additionally yields a 25-fold reduction in contact resistivity relative to annealed uncapped alloys. These results identify surface Sn transport as the dominant degradation pathway in SiGeSn and demonstrate that an ultrathin oxide cap extends the thermal stability of metastable group-IV alloys, providing a practical route toward their integration into advanced silicon photonic and electronic platforms.

content.title: Sn concentration increases thermodynamic stability of VSnV-type complexes

content.text: With more Sn in the alloy, Sn–vacancy complexes are easier to form and more stable, so annealing converts more substitutional Sn into these defects.
**Supporting evidence:**

- DFT in GeSn reports VSnV formation energies becoming progressively more favorable with increasing Sn fraction (Table 3 trend from about −4.244 eV at ~3.2% to about −6.279 eV at ~16.1%) and shows increasing VSnV binding strength with Sn concentration (Fig.11 trend).  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

- NEB/DFT and accompanying discussion in the same study link increased Sn content to weaker Ge–Sn bonding and to increased tendency for non-substitutional Sn-vacancy clustering, consistent with a thermodynamic shift toward VSnV at higher Sn.  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

- Experiment (uncapped MBE GeSn) shows substitutional Sn retention decreases with increasing initial Sn and increasing anneal temperature (60 s RTA): the 8.6% sample loses measurable substitutional Sn already at 400 °C and is fully depleted by 600 °C, while 4.5% and 7.2% samples retain at 400 °C and partially retain at 600–800 °C. This is consistent with higher-x alloys being more susceptible to conversion away from substitutional Sn during anneal.  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

- PAS on CVD GeSn (6.5–13 at.% Sn) finds divacancies dominate and the intensity of larger vacancy clusters decreases as Sn increases, interpreted as Sn stabilizing vacancies in specific configurations and suppressing vacancy clustering—consistent with strong Sn–vacancy interactions affecting defect thermodynamics/assembly.  <paper entityId="paper-a43c2e298fb9654389ce73682a550fa5342d1603" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="128256592" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Assali et al., 2019</paper>

- PAS/CDOBS in GeSn:P detects Sn atoms adjacent to mono-vacancy-sized open volume in mixed Sn_pP_n–V complexes, demonstrating that Sn can occupy vacancy-neighbor environments in epitaxial GeSn.  <paper entityId="paper-d2af7876dbf4ce6fbc25ba658f331ccada60eeb9" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="219060327" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.1">Vohra et al., 2020</paper>

content.title: Vacancy-mediated Sn hop barrier decreases with local Sn content

content.text: In Sn-richer local environments, it takes less energy for Sn to hop with a vacancy, so diffusion speeds up.
**Supporting evidence:**

- DFT/NEB reports lower migration barriers for higher Sn content supercells: example barriers decrease from 0.286 eV (Ge60Sn2–VSnV) to 0.179 eV (Ge55Sn7–VSnV), with derived activation energies decreasing from 0.927 to 0.832 eV.  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.2">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

- The same MBE+DFT study reports that higher initial Sn content yields earlier and larger substitutional Sn loss and earlier surface segregation during 400–800 °C RTA (60 s), consistent with faster vacancy-mediated kinetics at higher Sn content.  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

- In coherent capped diffusion experiments, SiGeSn shows a lower low-T effective activation energy than GeSn (1.13 eV vs 1.81 eV), consistent with the broader idea that alloy chemistry/local environment can reduce effective barriers and enhance Sn mobility in metastable alloys.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

content.title: Two-branch Arrhenius behavior arises from a defect-population/complexation crossover

content.text: At high temperature diffusion looks like ordinary bulk diffusion, but at lower temperature the metastable alloy’s defect population and Sn–vacancy complex dynamics make diffusion appear much easier.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Capped sandwich diffusion experiments report two Arrhenius regimes: Ge/GeSn/Ge high-T EA = 3.10 ± 0.07 eV and low-T EA = 1.81 ± 0.09 eV; Ge/SiGeSn/Ge high-T EA = 2.87 ± 0.03 eV and low-T EA = 1.13 ± 0.11 eV.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- The diffusion study explicitly notes the low-T activation-energy reduction cannot be explained solely by strain-driven vacancy formation and emphasizes metastability/chemical-potential gradients as key drivers, consistent with an effective-EA crossover interpretation rather than a single-mechanism Arrhenius law.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- The oxide-capping stability study argues bulk substitutional diffusion is too slow at 550 °C to explain observed transport (estimated diffusion length ~0.3 nm over 50 min), implying that alternative fast paths and defect-controlled kinetics determine observed changes in uncapped samples—consistent with the general idea that measured kinetics can be controlled by defect populations and fast pathways rather than bulk hop barriers.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- O1 (Ge0.88Sn0.12, MACE-MP-0 static): a substitutional Sn adjacent to a vacancy is predicted to be bound (positive binding). Category-level expectation: 'bound by 0 to 0.3 eV' or 'bound by more than 0.3 eV' (leaning >0.3 eV given VSnV stabilization trends at higher Sn, but noting dopant-free context matters).
- O2 (Ge0.88Sn0.12 with vacancies, 500–700 K MD): effective activation energy for observed Sn hops is predicted to be well below bulk Ge substitutional diffusion (2.9–3.3 eV) and more consistent with a low-barrier regime (category: 'close to the low-temperature metastable-film value (1.1 to 1.8 eV)' rather than bulk-like).
- At fixed anneal temperature (e.g., 600 °C) and time (e.g., 60 s), raising initial Sn content from ~4–5% to ~8–9% in uncapped GeSn will increase substitutional Sn loss markedly and produce earlier surface segregation signatures (consistent with the reported 400–600 °C behavior).
- In coherent capped diffusion stacks, SiGeSn will continue to show a lower low-T effective activation energy than GeSn at similar Sn content, reflecting stronger low-T enhancement in the ternary (as already suggested by existing EA_low values).

- If the low-T regime is truly defect-population-controlled, then independently reducing vacancy availability (e.g., by growth at higher T to reduce vacancy supersaturation or by adding strong vacancy sinks) should selectively suppress the low-T enhanced diffusion branch while leaving the high-T branch relatively unchanged.
- At higher Sn contents (~12–16%), local Sn enrichment could create autocatalytic mobility: once small Sn-rich/vacancy-rich regions form, local barriers drop enough to accelerate further Sn rearrangement, potentially yielding sudden internal clustering even in capped stacks without a free surface sink.

- If MACE-MP-0 predicts the Sn–vacancy nearest-neighbor binding in Ge0.88Sn0.12 is unbound (negative binding), then the premise that Sn–V attraction/complexation controls low-T mobility becomes questionable (at least for that potential).
- If MD in Ge0.88Sn0.12 with vacancies yields Sn-hop activation energies close to bulk Ge (2.9–3.3 eV), then the proposed low-barrier complexation-controlled regime is not governing in the 500–700 K window.
- If strong low-T enhanced diffusion persists in samples where PAS (or other defect metrology) confirms very low vacancy-type defect density, then a non-vacancy mechanism must dominate the low-T branch.

- Oxide-capped SiGeSn at 550 °C shows near-complete suppression of near-surface substitutional Sn loss despite the theory focusing primarily on bulk Sn–V complexation; fully explaining the cap effect requires explicit surface-sink blocking and dislocation-pipe transport considerations (handled more directly by a separate surface-mediated degradation theory).  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

paper-69932a46d534636de23ae1ff78e4eee472.displayLabel: The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers

s2Metadata.title: The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers
s2Metadata.abstract: We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. We investigated strained and partially relaxed epi-layers with Sn content in the 5 at. %-12 at. % range. In relaxed samples, we observe a further strain relaxation followed by a sudden Sn segregation, resulting in the separation of a β-Sn phase. In pseudomorphic samples, a slower segregation process progressively leads to the accumulation of Sn at the surface only. The different behaviors are explained by the role of dislocations in the Sn diffusion process. The positive impact of annealing on optical emission is also discussed.We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. We investigated strained and partially relaxed epi-layers with Sn content in the 5 at. %-12 at. % range. In relaxed samples, we observe a further strain relaxation followed by a sudden Sn segregation, resulting in the separation of a β-Sn phase. In pseudomorphic samples, a slower segregation process progressively leads to the accumulation of Sn at the surface only. The different behaviors are explained by the role of dislocations in the Sn diffusion process. The positive impact of annealing on optical emission is also discussed.

paper-050532416690efea233eb1e27bd9cd091d.displayLabel: Free-running Sn precipitates: an efficient phase separation mechanism for metastable Ge1−xSnx epilayers

s2Metadata.title: Free-running Sn precipitates: an efficient phase separation mechanism for metastable Ge1−xSnx epilayers
s2Metadata.abstract: The revival of interest in Ge1−xSnx alloys with x ≥ 10% is mainly owed to the recent demonstration of optical gain in this group-IV heterosystem. Yet, Ge and Sn are immiscible over about 98% of the composition range, which renders epilayers based on this material system inherently metastable. Here, we address the temperature stability of pseudomorphic Ge1−xSnx films grown by molecular beam epitaxy. Both the growth temperature dependence and the influence of post-growth annealing steps were investigated. In either case we observe that the decomposition of epilayers with Sn concentrations of around 10% sets in above ≈230 °C, the eutectic temperature of the Ge/Sn system. Time-resolved in-situ annealing experiments in a scanning electron microscope reveal the crucial role of liquid Sn precipitates in this phase separation process. Driven by a gradient of the chemical potential, the Sn droplets move on the surface along preferential crystallographic directions, thereby taking up Sn and Ge from the strained Ge1−xSnx layer. While Sn-uptake increases the volume of the melt, single-crystalline Ge becomes re-deposited by a liquid-phase epitaxial process at the trailing edge of the droplet. This process makes phase separation of metastable GeSn layers particularly efficient at rather low temperatures.

content.title: Free surface acts as an absorbing sink that enables rapid Sn depletion via fast paths

content.text: If the surface is exposed, it can continually remove Sn, so Sn rushes there through fast paths and the film can suddenly degrade after some delay.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Uncapped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 at 550 °C shows ~50 min incubation then rapid collapse (midpoint ~74.2 min, collapse width ~1.86 min) in near-surface ellipsometry signal; post-mortem shows Sn depletion, voids with oxygen, filamentary Sn-enriched paths to surface, thickness loss, and formation of a Ge0.99Sn0.01 surface-segregation layer.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- The same study argues bulk substitutional diffusion is far too slow at 550 °C (estimated diffusion length ~0.3 nm in 50 min), implying fast pathways and surface-sink-driven kinetics dominate uncapped degradation.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- In pseudomorphic GeSn, uncapped samples show surface segregation above ~600 °C, whereas capped sandwiches suppress that surface accumulation, consistent with the free surface being the key sink in uncapped cases.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- In partially relaxed GeSn, Sn-rich clusters form at the surface and at interfaces correlated with dislocation networks; pseudomorphic films show surface accumulation only, supporting the idea that fast paths plus an available sink determine where Sn ends up.  <paper entityId="paper-69932a46d534636de23ae1ff78e4eee47265ecd8" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="105474679" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Zaumseil et al., 2018</paper>

content.title: Oxide caps kinetically block Sn escape and suppress Kirkendall voiding/runaway degradation

content.text: A thin oxide cap blocks Sn from reaching the surface and stops the voiding/rapid collapse that happens when Sn can escape.
**Supporting evidence:**

- 3 nm SiO2-capped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 shows <1 at.% Sn change over 140 min at 550 °C, |ΔE2| < 20 meV, no voids, preserved uniform Sn (EDX/APT), limited strain relaxation, and far lower contact resistivity than uncapped.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- Uncapped counterpart at 550 °C shows voids with oxygen, filamentary Sn-rich paths, Ge0.99Sn0.01 segregation layer, roughening, and severe thickness loss after the incubation/collapse event.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- Screening in the same work indicates 5 nm Al2O3 also suppresses segregation after 550 °C/30 min.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- Conceptual discussions elsewhere propose capping/H termination suppresses surface segregation and delays precipitation/phase separation, consistent with a surface-sink blocking mechanism.  <paper entityId="paper-050532416690efea233eb1e27bd9cd091db28159" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="25636372" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Groiss et al., 2017</paper>

- H9 prediction (Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 at 550 °C, uncapped vs 3 nm SiO2 cap, monitoring near-surface substitutional Sn loss): category = 'cap suppresses the change'; uncapped incubation time ≈ 50 minutes before the change becomes visible (order-of-magnitude tens of minutes, not seconds).
- Replacing SiO2 with Al2O3 of similar thickness (≈5 nm) will also suppress the near-surface change at 550 °C over at least ~30 min, consistent with screening evidence.
- For otherwise similar films, introducing a free surface (removing cap) will reintroduce incubation-and-collapse behavior, with earlier onset if dislocation density/fast-path density is higher.

- If an oxide cap is intentionally made leaky (patterned nanopores), degradation will initiate preferentially at those leakage sites and propagate laterally, allowing direct mapping of sink-gated kinetics to cap integrity.
- A cap that strongly getters vacancies (rather than only blocking Sn) could further stabilize the film even when some Sn transport through the cap is possible; distinguishing these would require independent vacancy metrology.

- If in-situ SE shows no difference between capped and uncapped at 550 °C (same incubation and collapse), then surface-sink gating is not the controlling factor and the dominant mechanism must be bulk or interface-limited.
- If capped samples still develop voids and rapid collapse without measurable Sn escape pathways, then voiding must be driven by another flux imbalance mechanism unrelated to Sn surface loss.

- In Ge/GeSn/Ge capped diffusion samples, the Ge cap suppresses surface segregation but still allows substantial Sn dilution into the cap/buffer (peak reduction >2× at 600 °C/10 min); the present theory explains this as sink redirection but does not quantify when redirection vs true retention should occur for different cap materials/thicknesses.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>
