paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f.displayLabel: Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation

s2Metadata.title: Enhanced thermal stability of SiGeSn by suppressing surface-mediated degradation
s2Metadata.abstract: $\text{SiGeSn}$ alloys are promising silicon-compatible semiconductors for monolithic infrared photonics. However, their metastable nature limits the thermal budgets available for post-growth device processing, and the mechanisms governing their thermal degradation remain unresolved. Here, we investigate the thermal stability of $\text{Si}_{0.08}\text{Ge}_{0.83}\text{Sn}_{0.04}$ alloys using in situ spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) during isothermal annealing at 550 {\deg}C. We show that adding an ultrathin oxide cap kinetically suppresses Sn exchange with the free surface while leaving bulk diffusion pathways largely unaffected. Uncapped films undergo phase separation after 50 min, accompanied by void formation, a 60% thickness reduction, and a 400 meV blueshift of the $E_{2}$ critical point (CP) transition, consistent with substitutional Sn depletion from the probed volume through surface segregation. In contrast, oxide-capped films exhibit a small compositional change (<1 at.% Sn) and optical shift (<20 meV) over the same period, with suppressed void formation, strain relaxation, and alloy decomposition. This surface-kinetic control additionally yields a 25-fold reduction in contact resistivity relative to annealed uncapped alloys. These results identify surface Sn transport as the dominant degradation pathway in SiGeSn and demonstrate that an ultrathin oxide cap extends the thermal stability of metastable group-IV alloys, providing a practical route toward their integration into advanced silicon photonic and electronic platforms.

paper-69932a46d534636de23ae1ff78e4eee472.displayLabel: The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers

s2Metadata.title: The thermal stability of epitaxial GeSn layers
s2Metadata.abstract: We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. We investigated strained and partially relaxed epi-layers with Sn content in the 5 at. %-12 at. % range. In relaxed samples, we observe a further strain relaxation followed by a sudden Sn segregation, resulting in the separation of a β-Sn phase. In pseudomorphic samples, a slower segregation process progressively leads to the accumulation of Sn at the surface only. The different behaviors are explained by the role of dislocations in the Sn diffusion process. The positive impact of annealing on optical emission is also discussed.We report on the direct observation of lattice relaxation and Sn segregation of GeSn/Ge/Si heterostructures under annealing. We investigated strained and partially relaxed epi-layers with Sn content in the 5 at. %-12 at. % range. In relaxed samples, we observe a further strain relaxation followed by a sudden Sn segregation, resulting in the separation of a β-Sn phase. In pseudomorphic samples, a slower segregation process progressively leads to the accumulation of Sn at the surface only. The different behaviors are explained by the role of dislocations in the Sn diffusion process. The positive impact of annealing on optical emission is also discussed.

paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1.displayLabel: Thermally activated diffusion and lattice relaxation in (Si)GeSn materials

s2Metadata.title: Thermally activated diffusion and lattice relaxation in (Si)GeSn materials
s2Metadata.abstract: Germanium-Tin (GeSn) alloys have emerged as a promising material for future optoelectronics, energy harvesting and nanoelectronics owing to their direct bandgap and compatibility with existing Si-based electronics. Yet, their metastability poses significant challenges calling for in-depth investigations of their thermal behavior. With this perspective, this work addresses the interdiffusion processes throughout thermal annealing of pseudomorphic GeSn binary and SiGeSn ternary alloys. In both systems, the initially pseudomorphic layers are relaxed upon annealing exclusively via thermally induced diffusional mass transfer of Sn. Systematic post-growth annealing experiments reveal enhanced Sn and Si diffusion regimes that manifest at temperatures below 600°C. The amplified low-temperature diffusion and the observation of only subtle differences between binary and ternary hint at the unique metastability of the Si-Ge-Sn material system as the most important driving force for phase separation.

paper-050532416690efea233eb1e27bd9cd091d.displayLabel: Free-running Sn precipitates: an efficient phase separation mechanism for metastable Ge1−xSnx epilayers

s2Metadata.title: Free-running Sn precipitates: an efficient phase separation mechanism for metastable Ge1−xSnx epilayers
s2Metadata.abstract: The revival of interest in Ge1−xSnx alloys with x ≥ 10% is mainly owed to the recent demonstration of optical gain in this group-IV heterosystem. Yet, Ge and Sn are immiscible over about 98% of the composition range, which renders epilayers based on this material system inherently metastable. Here, we address the temperature stability of pseudomorphic Ge1−xSnx films grown by molecular beam epitaxy. Both the growth temperature dependence and the influence of post-growth annealing steps were investigated. In either case we observe that the decomposition of epilayers with Sn concentrations of around 10% sets in above ≈230 °C, the eutectic temperature of the Ge/Sn system. Time-resolved in-situ annealing experiments in a scanning electron microscope reveal the crucial role of liquid Sn precipitates in this phase separation process. Driven by a gradient of the chemical potential, the Sn droplets move on the surface along preferential crystallographic directions, thereby taking up Sn and Ge from the strained Ge1−xSnx layer. While Sn-uptake increases the volume of the melt, single-crystalline Ge becomes re-deposited by a liquid-phase epitaxial process at the trailing edge of the droplet. This process makes phase separation of metastable GeSn layers particularly efficient at rather low temperatures.

paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae.displayLabel: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys

s2Metadata.title: Study on the Influence of Sn Concentration on Non-Substitutional Defect Concentration and Sn Surface Segregation in GeSn Alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: GeSn alloys are among the most promising materials for the fabrication of high-efficiency silicon-based light sources. However, due to the tendency of Sn to segregate to the surface during growth, it is challenging to achieve a high Sn concentration while maintaining high-quality GeSn alloys. Both theoretical and experimental studies have confirmed that non-substitutional Sn defects (VSnV) are the primary driving factors in Sn surface segregation. However, there is a discrepancy between existing theoretical and experimental findings regarding the variation in VSnV concentration with total Sn concentration. To clarify this issue, we first prepared GeSn materials with varying Sn concentrations using molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and subjected them to annealing at different temperatures. Subsequently, we characterized the VSnV concentration and Sn surface segregation. The results indicate that a higher total Sn concentration and temperature lead to an increased VSnV concentration, and the proportion of VSnV relative to the total Sn concentration also increases, which is consistent with existing theoretical research. To explain these phenomena, we employed first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the effect of varying the total Sn concentration on the formation of substitutional Sn (Sns) and VSnV in GeSn alloys, while simultaneously studying the migration kinetics of Sn atoms. The results demonstrate that as the total Sn concentration increases, the formation of Sns becomes more difficult, while the formation of VSnV becomes easier, and Sn atoms exhibit enhanced migration tendencies. The analysis of binding energies and charge density distribution maps reveals that this is due to the weakening of Ge-Sn bond strength with increasing Sn concentration, whereas the binding strength of VSnV exhibits the opposite trend. These findings demonstrate excellent agreement with experimental observations. This study provides both theoretical and experimental references for GeSn material growth and VSnV defect control through a combined theoretical–experimental approach, offering significant guidance for enhancing device performance.

content.title: Pipe-diffusion dominated Sn transport law (voiding/collapse mode)

content.text: When collapse behavior happens, Sn mainly travels along dislocations/fast paths rather than slowly through the perfect crystal lattice.
**Supporting evidence:**

- For uncapped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 at 550 °C, authors argue bulk substitutional diffusion cannot explain the kinetics, estimating a bulk diffusion length of only ~0.3 nm over the ~50 min incubation, while TEM shows filamentary Sn-enriched paths consistent with dislocation-mediated transport to the surface.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- Uncapped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 shows incubation (~50 min) then abrupt optical collapse; post-mortem TEM/EDX reveals filamentary Sn-enriched features and surface/near-surface segregation consistent with a connected fast-transport network feeding the surface sink.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- GeSn thermal stability study reports that partially relaxed (dislocated) GeSn exhibits much faster Sn transport/segregation and Sn-rich clustering at both surface and interface; pseudomorphic films (lacking dislocations) show surface-only accumulation and slower evolution, supporting a dislocation-enhanced transport picture.  <paper entityId="paper-69932a46d534636de23ae1ff78e4eee47265ecd8" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="105474679" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Zaumseil et al., 2018</paper>

- In uncapped pseudomorphic GeSn/SiGeSn diffusion work, surface segregation appears above ~600 °C, while capped sandwich structures suppress surface segregation and instead show smoother interdiffusion into Ge; this supports the idea that fast pathways plus a free-surface sink can dominate observed Sn redistribution when uncapped.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

content.title: Surface-sink–driven Kirkendall void nucleation and positive feedback

content.text: When the surface keeps removing Sn, vacancies pile up and form voids; voids then make Sn loss speed up suddenly.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Uncapped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 annealed 550 °C/140 min exhibits voids throughout upper region; voids contain oxygen by EDX, and authors interpret voiding as Kirkendall-type vacancy supersaturation caused by unbalanced outward Sn flux along fast paths to the surface.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- The same uncapped sample shows catastrophic thickness loss (~60%), strong ellipsometric E2 blueshift (+423 meV) and rapid collapse after incubation (t0≈74 min; incubation ~50 min; collapse width ~1.9 min), consistent with a nonlinear feedback process rather than steady Fickian diffusion.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- GeSn thermal stability study links enhanced Sn transport/segregation to extended defects (dislocations) and vacancy-mediated dynamics, consistent with a scenario where short-circuit transport can create strong fluxes that could generate vacancy imbalances.  <paper entityId="paper-69932a46d534636de23ae1ff78e4eee47265ecd8" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="105474679" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Zaumseil et al., 2018</paper>

content.title: Nm-scale oxide cap suppresses the sink/void feedback by blocking Sn egress

content.text: A thin, intact oxide cap removes the surface as a place for Sn to escape to, so the runaway voiding process never starts.
**Supporting evidence:**

- At 550 °C/140 min under N2 purge, uncapped Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 shows incubation (~50 min) then rapid collapse (t0≈74.2 min; width ~1.86 min), large E2 blueshift (~+423 meV), voids with oxygen, roughening, thickness loss, and formation of a Ge0.99Sn0.01 segregation layer; the 3 nm SiO2-capped sample shows <1 at.% Sn change over 140 min, |ΔE2|<20 meV, no voids, minimal relaxation and preserved uniformity.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- Screening in the same study indicates 5 nm Al2O3 also suppresses segregation after 550 °C/30 min, supporting the idea that an oxide barrier (not only SiO2 specifically) can block the relevant surface-mediated pathway.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- Conceptual discussions in GeSn droplet-mediated decomposition work suggest capping should suppress surface segregation and delay droplet/precipitate formation by reducing surface sink strength (though not experimentally tested there).  <paper entityId="paper-050532416690efea233eb1e27bd9cd091db28159" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="25636372" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Groiss et al., 2017</paper>

- Capped Ge/GeSn/Ge sandwich diffusion experiments suppress surface segregation and redirect Sn into adjacent Ge rather than allowing surface pile-up, consistent with the general principle that removing the free surface changes the dominant degradation pathway.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- For Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 annealed isothermally at 550 °C, a thin continuous oxide cap (e.g., 3 nm SiO2) will fall into the category 'cap suppresses the change' in in-situ SE, with the uncapped film showing a finite incubation time before the near-surface substitutional-Sn loss becomes visible (order: tens of minutes, comparable to ~50 min in the referenced 550 °C uncapped case).
- If the dislocation density (or connectivity of dislocations to the surface) is increased in otherwise similar uncapped films, the incubation time before collapse will decrease and the void density in post-anneal TEM will increase; capped films will show a much weaker dependence of kinetics on dislocation density (collapse suppressed).
- If an oxide cap is intentionally patterned with openings, degradation (Sn depletion, voiding) will initiate preferentially at openings and propagate laterally underneath as the local surface sink is reintroduced; capped regions away from openings remain comparatively stable.

- In an uncapped sample annealed under extremely low oxygen chemical potential (e.g., ultra-high purity inert gas with strong oxygen getter), collapse kinetics may slow substantially and voids may show reduced oxygen decoration; if collapse is still rapid, it would imply that oxidation is not required for sink strength (segregation alone suffices).
- Replacing oxide with a mechanically compressive but Sn-impermeable dielectric (e.g., thick SiNx) could either further suppress collapse (by sealing the surface) or accelerate it (if the stress generates cracks/defects that act as new fast paths). Outcome would strongly constrain whether mechanical integrity or chemical impermeability is the limiting factor.
- Electrostatic effects from high fixed-charge caps could modify vacancy charge states and thus vacancy mobility/aggregation; if true, identical impermeability caps with different charge states would yield measurably different incubation times, separating 'barrier' from 'defect-chemistry' contributions.

- If uncapped films that show SE collapse at 550 °C do not exhibit voids (confirmed by cross-sectional TEM across the affected region), then Kirkendall voiding is not necessary for collapse and the feedback-loop hypothesis is weakened.
- If capped films with verified continuous caps (no pinholes/cracks, verified by TEM/AFM and perhaps etch tests) still show the same incubation-then-collapse kinetics as uncapped, then suppression cannot be attributed to blocking the surface sink and the theory statements must be revised.
- If a verified dislocation-poor/pseudomorphic film (no connected dislocation network) nevertheless shows the same collapse kinetics and filamentary transport signatures, then pipe/short-circuit transport is not the dominant pathway in this regime.

- Droplet-mediated liquid-phase-epitaxy phase separation in high-Sn MBE Ge0.9Sn0.1 above the eutectic (~231 °C) proceeds by mobile liquid Sn droplets and is not explained by Kirkendall voiding feedback; it is a distinct degradation mode.  <paper entityId="paper-050532416690efea233eb1e27bd9cd091db28159" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="25636372" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Groiss et al., 2017</paper>

- Two-regime Arrhenius behavior (low-T enhanced diffusion with EA ~1.1–1.8 eV and high-T conventional with EA ~2.9–3.1 eV) in capped Ge/GeSn/Ge sandwich diffusion experiments reflects bulk/interdiffusion kinetics rather than collapse-mode voiding; this theory does not aim to explain those regimes quantitatively.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_013" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

paper-d2af7876dbf4ce6fbc25ba658f331ccada.displayLabel: Source/Drain Materials for Ge nMOS Devices: Phosphorus Activation in Epitaxial Si, Ge, Ge1−x Sn x and Si y Ge1−x−y Sn x

s2Metadata.title: Source/Drain Materials for Ge nMOS Devices: Phosphorus Activation in Epitaxial Si, Ge, Ge1−x Sn x and Si y Ge1−x−y Sn x
s2Metadata.abstract: This paper benchmarks various epitaxial growth schemes based on n-type group-IV materials as viable source/drain candidates for Ge nMOS devices. Si:P grown at low temperature on Ge, gives an active carrier concentration as high as 3.5 x 1020 cm-3 and a contact resistivity down to 7.5 x10-9 Ω.cm2. However, Si:P growth is highly defective due to large lattice mismatch between Si and Ge. Within the material stacks assessed, one option for Ge nMOS source/drain stressors would be to stack Si:P, deposited at contact level, on top of a selectively grown n-SiyGe1-x-ySnx at source/drain level, in line with the concept of Si passivation of n-Ge surfaces to achieve low contact resistivities as reported in literature [K. Martens et al. Appl. Phys. Lett., 98, 013504 (2011)]. The saturation in active carrier concentration with increasing P (or As)-doping is the major bottleneck in achieving low contact resistivities for as-grown Ge or SiyGe1-x-ySnx. We focus on understanding various dopant deactivation mechanisms in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx alloys. First principles simulation results suggest that P deactivation in Ge and Ge1-xSnx can be explained both by P-clustering and donor-vacancy complexes. Positron annihilation spectroscopy analysis, suggests that dopant deactivation in P-doped Ge and Ge1-xSnx is primarily due to the formation of Pn-V and SnmPn-V clusters.

Both the growth temperature dependence and the influence of post-growth annealing steps were investigated. In either case we observe that the decomposition of epilayers with Sn concentrations of around 10% sets in above ≈230 °C, the eutectic temperature of the Ge/Sn system. Time-resolved in-situ annealing experiments in a scanning electron microscope reveal the crucial role of liquid Sn precipitates in this phase separation process. Driven by a gradient of the chemical potential, the Sn droplets move on the surface along preferential crystallographic directions, thereby taking up Sn and Ge from the strained Ge1−xSnx layer. While Sn-uptake increases the volume of the melt, single-crystalline Ge becomes re-deposited by a liquid-phase epitaxial process at the trailing edge of the droplet. This process makes phase separation of metastable GeSn layers particularly efficient at rather low temperatures.

s2Metadata.title: Vacancy complexes in nonequilibrium germanium-tin semiconductors
s2Metadata.abstract: Understanding the nature and behavior of vacancy-like defects in epitaxial GeSn metastable alloys is crucial to elucidate the structural and optoelectronic properties of these emerging semiconductors. The formation of vacancies and their complexes is expected to be promoted by the relatively low substrate temperature required for the epitaxial growth of GeSn layers with Sn contents significantly above the equilibrium solubility of 1 at.%. These defects can impact both the microstructure and charge carrier lifetime. Herein, to identify the vacancy-related complexes and probe their evolution as a function of Sn content, depth-profiled pulsed low-energy positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy and Doppler broadening spectroscopy were combined to investigate GeSn epitaxial layers with Sn content in the 6.5-13.0 at.% range. The samples were grown by chemical vapor deposition method at temperatures between 300 and 330 °C. Regardless of the Sn content, all GeSn samples showed the same depth-dependent increase in the positron annihilation line broadening parameters, which confirmed the presence of open volume defects. The measured average positron lifetimes were the highest (380-395 ps) in the region near the surface and monotonically decrease across the analyzed thickness, but remain above 350 ps. All GeSn layers exhibit lifetimes that are 85 to 110 ps higher than the Ge reference layers. Surprisingly, these lifetimes were found to decrease as Sn content increases in GeSn layers. These measurements indicate that divacancies are the dominant defect in the as-grown GeSn layers. However, their corresponding lifetime was found to be shorter than in epitaxial Ge thus suggesting that the presence of Sn may alter the structure of divacancies. Additionally, GeSn layers were found to also contain a small fraction of vacancy clusters, which become less important as Sn content increases.

content.title: Vacancy capture hierarchy law (P dominates Sn in Ge/GeSn in studied regime)

content.text: With very high phosphorus doping, vacancies mostly bind to phosphorus; tin shows up mainly as an additional neighbor around those vacancy complexes rather than capturing vacancies first.
**Supporting evidence:**

- DFT formation enthalpy ranking: Pn–V complexes are most stable; mixed Sn–Pn–V intermediate; Sn-only vacancy complexes least favorable; authors conclude Sn does not efficiently trap vacancies compared to P and therefore does not improve P activation via vacancy trapping.  <paper entityId="paper-d2af7876dbf4ce6fbc25ba658f331ccada60eeb9" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="219060327" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Vohra et al., 2020</paper>

- PAS/coincedence Doppler shows mono-vacancy-sized open-volume defects decorated by multiple P atoms (2–4 depending on P level). In GeSn:P at highest P, PAS indicates at least one Sn atom near some vacancies (Sn_pP_n–V), consistent with Sn acting as a co-decorator around an already P-decorated vacancy complex rather than dominating vacancy capture.  <paper entityId="paper-d2af7876dbf4ce6fbc25ba658f331ccada60eeb9" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="219060327" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.1">Vohra et al., 2020</paper>

- PAS/DFT work notes inward Sn relaxation around vacancies (reducing open-volume and positron trapping), consistent with Sn being present around vacancies but not necessarily implying Sn is the dominant vacancy sink compared to Pn–V.  <paper entityId="paper-d2af7876dbf4ce6fbc25ba658f331ccada60eeb9" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="219060327" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Vohra et al., 2020</paper>

- Literature cited in the PAS/DFT work indicates undoped low-Sn GeSn (Sn ≤ ~6 at.%) can be stable up to 500 °C for up to 30 min (context that the relevant defect complexes persist without immediate macroscopic decomposition in this composition range).  <paper entityId="paper-d2af7876dbf4ce6fbc25ba658f331ccada60eeb9" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="219060327" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.2">Vohra et al., 2020</paper>

content.title: Dopant-controlled vacancy availability modulates vacancy-mediated Sn interdiffusion (under surface-sink-limited conditions)

content.text: If the main way tin moves is by exchanging with vacancies in the lattice, then adding a dopant that locks up vacancies should slow tin motion and help keep tin substitutional—provided the surface isn’t acting as an easy escape route.
**Supporting evidence:**

- This statement is logically inferred (abduction/deduction) from: (1) Pn–V complexes are thermodynamically preferred over Sn-only vacancy complexes in Ge/low-Sn GeSn (vacancy capture hierarchy), and (2) vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion requires accessible vacancies as mediators; therefore sequestering vacancies into dopant–V complexes reduces vacancy availability for Sn exchange hops and Sn–V complex formation.

- Vacancy-mediated Sn diffusion is identified as a relevant microscopic mechanism in GeSn stability literature; DFT/NEB in undoped GeSn shows low activation energies for vacancy-mediated Sn hops (~0.83–0.93 eV) and experimental RTA in undoped MBE GeSn shows substitutional Sn loss interpreted via formation of Sn–vacancy complexes (VSnV). These establish that vacancy-mediated routes can control Sn stability when not overridden by surface/pipe mechanisms, motivating why vacancy availability matters.  <paper entityId="paper-299b559155f3a1cf19af801e8a7eceb7ae7ee82e" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="278036911" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.2">Zhou et al., 2025</paper>

- Capped diffusion-sandwich experiments (Ge/GeSn/Ge; Ge/SiGeSn/Ge) demonstrate that removing the free-surface sink shifts behavior to bulk interdiffusion with measurable activation energies (two-regime behavior) rather than immediate surface segregation—consistent with a domain where bulk vacancy-mediated kinetics can matter and therefore where vacancy sequestration by dopants could modulate Sn mobility.  <paper entityId="paper-c5d7e9baabdb854a4a6de0f1ad8ccf2ab1f5bee7" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="207794174" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Driesch et al., 2019</paper>

- In a surface-sink-suppressed geometry (e.g., Ge/GeSn/Ge diffusion sandwich or an oxide-capped stack that blocks free-surface Sn escape), increasing P doping into the high-10^19 cm−3 regime will reduce the effective Sn interdiffusion rate at 500–650 °C relative to an undoped control with similar dislocation density, because vacancies are sequestered into Pn–V complexes.
- PAS/CDOBS vs P concentration in GeSn:P will show systematic increase in P decoration number (P2–V → P3–V/ P4–V) while the incremental Sn contribution around vacancies remains limited (mixed Sn_pP_n–V signal increases weakly or saturates), consistent with P-dominated vacancy trapping.
- If two films have similar Sn content and microstructure but one has much higher P, the higher-P film will show reduced signatures of Sn-only vacancy complexes (or reduced kinetic conversion to such complexes during mild anneals), with vacancies predominantly residing in Pn–V or mixed Sn–P–V states.

- Fermi-level engineering could change the vacancy charge-state distribution enough to alter the dopant–V vs Sn–V stability ordering; in some doping/strain conditions this could partially invert the hierarchy and enable electrically tunable Sn stability during annealing.
- In SiGeSn, the presence of Si may modify vacancy formation energies and dopant–vacancy binding enough that P trapping is less effective (or more effective) than in GeSn, leading to composition-dependent crossovers where dopant chemistry unexpectedly accelerates Sn loss (if it increases vacancy populations more than it traps them).
- Co-doping strategies (e.g., combining P with another species that preferentially binds vacancies or changes vacancy migration) might create a regime where vacancies are immobilized without generating compensating fast paths, enabling substantially higher thermal budgets for substitutional Sn retention.

- Prepare capped (surface-sink-limited) GeSn diffusion-sandwich samples with matched Sn content and dislocation density but different P levels; if heavily P-doped samples show equal or higher Sn interdiffusion rates than undoped samples across 500–650 °C, then vacancy sequestration by P is not limiting Sn mobility (or P increases vacancy supply/fast paths enough to dominate).
- Direct defect spectroscopy/DFT under relevant Fermi-level conditions: if Sn–V (or VSnV precursor) binding becomes stronger than Pn–V stability under the actual charge states in these films, contradicting the assumed hierarchy, the theory’s mechanism fails for that regime.
- If PAS after anneal shows a large increase of Sn-only vacancy complexes in heavily P-doped GeSn compared with undoped controls (at comparable vacancy supply), then P is not the dominant vacancy trap in the kinetic/thermodynamic regime relevant to annealing.

- Oxide capping (3 nm SiO2, 5 nm Al2O3) at 550 °C can suppress surface-mediated degradation/voiding and preserve substitutional Sn in SiGeSn for 140 min; this theory does not explain that effect because it concerns bulk vacancy-trap competition, not surface-sink blocking and pipe-diffusion shutoff.  <paper entityId="paper-a69e5fc44f308dc4e30100d14b6078f64f160354" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="292033613" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Attiaoui et al., 2026</paper>

- Droplet-mediated liquid transport above the Ge–Sn eutectic in high-Sn GeSn (e.g., Ge0.9Sn0.1) dominates decomposition and is not addressed by vacancy-trap competition.  <paper entityId="paper-050532416690efea233eb1e27bd9cd091db28159" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="25636372" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Groiss et al., 2017</paper>
